Urban sense segmentation, which aims to assign semantic labels to pixels in urban scenes, is a fundamental task for many applications such as autonomous driving and robotic perception.
Recent advances in this field have achieved remarkable performance mainly based on two-stream architectures that separately learn global and local features.
However, these methods usually rely on heuristic designs to fuse global and local features, which limits their performance.
In this paper, we propose a hybrid transformer to learn adaptive global-local representations for urban sense segmentation.
Specifically, we design a global-local attention module to model the interactions between global and local features, allowing the model to focus on different aspects of the input in a self-adaptive manner.
Furthermore, a hierarchical transformer structure is introduced to capture the contextual information at multiple levels of granularity.

We perform the first large-scale analysis of petition growth and success rates on the UK No. 10 Downing Street website, spanning over 13 years (from February 2006 to June 2019) and including 415,348 petitions.
We find that the number of signatures received increases with petition age, and this relationship is steeper for more recent years.
We also find a significant linear relationship between the mean signature rate per day and the median number of signatures received, which implies that getting signatures quickly is important for petition success.
Next, we show that a small number of petitions receive a large fraction of the signatures, and that this is more pronounced in recent years.
Finally, we show that success rates have decreased over time and that a "threshold model" where a fixed number of signatures leads to an outcome is not supported by the data.
However, a logistic regression model with petition signature velocity as a significant predictor of success is supported by the data.

We study a system of weakly coupled clusters, describing a disordered material with metallic and insulating states, by means of using numerical linked-cluster expansion, which is based on an exact treatment of all cluster excitations.
Previously discovered metal-insulator transition line in the parameter space of the model is reproduced.
We find a new type of transition line, which ends up in a critical point, at which a metal-insulator quantum phase transition takes place.
Near the critical point, both types of transitions are of second order.
Using an additional parameter, we fine-tune the system to a new region of the phase diagram, where the metallic and insulating states are separated by a first-order transition.
We provide an explanation of the nature of the metallic state and the metal-insulator transition in terms of existing concepts of the theory of disordered materials.

We introduce a formalism of a segment-phrase table (SPT) for semantic segmentation, visual entailment and paraphrasing tasks.
It captures the universal hierarchy of semantic propositions of entities, their attributes and relationships in a fine-grained and compositional manner.
A neural network is trained to induce an SPT from unsupervised video and image captions, where each row corresponds to a phrase in a caption and each column corresponds to a segment in a video or image.
The cell entries capture the likelihood of the phrase explaining the segment based on a similarity metric.
An SPT factorizes the likelihood as a product of the individual phrase and segment probabilities, which enables the evaluation of paraphrases by simply summing their respective entries.
We show that an SPT can be used for visual entailment, where an SPT entry supports or refutes the presence of a phrase in a given segment.

Recent progress in 3D medical image segmentation has benefited from both convolutional neural network (CNN) and transformer-based architectures, but their individual limitations hinder performance and efficiency.
To address these limitations, we present CoTr, a simple and efficient hybrid architecture that combines the strengths of CNN and transformer-based models.
Our approach dynamically allocates the tasks of feature extraction and segmentation across the two architectures based on the image size, enabling efficient training and inference on large images.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three challenging 3D medical image segmentation tasks: abdominal organ segmentation from CT, pulmonary nodule segmentation from CT, and hippocampus segmentation from T1-weighted MRI.
Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on all three datasets, significantly improving over previous methods, while being more efficient for segmentation on large images.
Code is available at https://github.com/ interpreteur/CoTr.

Recent progress in 3D medical image segmentation has benefited from both convolutional neural network (CNN) and transformer-based architectures, but their individual limitations hinder performance and efficiency.
To address these limitations, we present CoTr, a simple and efficient hybrid architecture that combines the strengths of CNN and transformer-based models.
Our approach dynamically allocates the tasks of feature extraction and segmentation across the two architectures based on the image size, enabling efficient training and inference on large images.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three challenging 3D medical image segmentation tasks: abdominal organ segmentation from CT, pulmonary nodule segmentation from CT, and hippocampus segmentation from T1-weighted MRI.
Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on all three datasets, significantly improving over previous methods, while being more efficient for segmentation on large images.
Code is available at https://github.com/ interpreteur/CoTr.

Fuzzy clustering method is used for segmentation of vertebrae in T1-weighted spinal magnetic resonance (MR) images.
In this method, the membership functions are optimized by Genetic Algorithm (GA).
The input parameters for the GA are the gray levels and their neighboring pixels.
The output is the set of fuzzy rules that define the membership functions.
The fuzzy rules are then used for segmentation of the vertebrae.
The proposed method is evaluated on 20 T1-weighted spinal MR images.

Recent works have shown that encoders based on pre-trained Transformers, particularly ViTs, set new standards for the quality of the learned representations for natural images, outperforming traditional convolutional neural networks.
In this work, we adapt Transformers for medical image segmentation.
In particular, we propose to use Transformers as encoders, predicting segmentations as a whole image classification.
To adapt the Transformers to this task, we modify the classification layer to take into account the label hierarchy and handle overlapping segments.
We present a new Transformer encoder based on ViT, called TransUNet, that outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods for segmentation on multiple benchmarks for both 2D and 3D medical images.
Our code is available at https://github.com/DPichenaux/TransUNet.

We study the complexity of optimizing multicell coordinated beamforming with rate outage constraint, which maximizes the sum-rate of the network subject to a reliability requirement.
We first present a polynomial time algorithm to solve this non-convex problem to global optimality when the number of users is equal to or larger than the number of base stations.
This algorithm is based on a novel semi-definite programming (SDP) formulation of the problem, and on a block coordinate descent (BCD) method.
Then, we propose a low-complexity greedy algorithm that achieves a near-optimal performance with significantly reduced computational complexity.
The proposed greedy algorithm is based on a novel approximation of the optimal beamforming matrix, and on a thresholding technique that allows us to select the most beneficial users for cooperation.
Finally, we present numerical results that illustrate the performance of the proposed algorithms in terms of sum-rate and outage probability, and that demonstrate the significant reduction in computational complexity achieved by the greedy algorithm.

We present a new type of rheological measurement of dry granular flows using an instrumented pin tumbler.
In this device, a cylindrical bin is rotated with a constant speed, and a pin is attached to the center of the bottom of the bin.
Granular material is placed in the bin, and as the bin rotates, the material is agitated and descends slowly toward the bottom.
During this process, the structure of the material changes from an ordered stack of disks to a random state and then to an ordered state again as it passes through the bin.
We measure the stress in the vertical direction as a function of the shear stress using load cells attached to the bin and the pin, respectively.
The measured stress versus shear stress curves exhibit power-law dependence at high shear stresses, and the power-law exponents are equal to the average interparticle friction coefficient $\mu_I$, which is determined using a rotating disk device.

Recent works have shown that few-shot learning (FSL), where training datasets are significantly reduced, can generalize well when the support set has a similar distribution to the query set.
However, for medical image segmentation, creating training datasets that capture the distribution of rare diseases is often costly and time-consuming, whereby a segmentation model trained with such datasets can generalize poorly to hospital scenarios, where patients with different rare diseases need to be segmented.
In this work, we propose a self-supervision approach to train a segmentation model without requiring any annotation.
Specifically, we train the model with a sparse-coding loss that forces the model to reconstruct the original image from its segmented image.
We then enforce the consistency between the original and reconstructed image using a cycle-consistent loss, which does not require any ground-truth segmentation.
To improve the segmentation quality, we introduce superpixels to capture global structures in medical images.

We calculate presupernova neutrino emissivities from the evolution of massive stellar models with masses ranging from 8 to 40 $M_{\odot}$. Special attention is paid to the effects of mixing length, convection, and hyperonization.
Our models suggest that the presupernova neutrino emissivity becomes independent of mass and nearly equal to the one previously calculated by Itoh et al. (2001) for a 15 $M_{\odot}$ model at the time of core collapse when convection and hyperonization are considered.
The presupernova emission, which lasts for about 10$^{5}$ seconds, carries away 1.3% of the star's rest mass as neutrinos.
This corresponds to 1.1 baryon number conservation violations (BCVs) for a 40 $M_{\odot}$ model, which could be detectable by the next generation of neutrino detectors.
We also examine the dependence of the neutrino emissivities on the mixing length, the enhancement factor of the convection, and the choice of the opacity. 

 
Enhanced convection does not change the total emission but leads to an increased neutrino luminosity at the beginning and end of the presupernova evolution.

We perform the first systematic investigation of the universality of the luminosity-metallicity (L-Z) and mass-metallicity (M-Z) relations for compact galaxies at 0 < z < 3.
We compile a sample of ~104 galaxies with stellar mass < 10^9 M⊙ and circumgalactic medium metallicity measurements from 11 studies of local and high-redshift galaxies, spanning four orders of magnitude in luminosity and eight orders of magnitude in mass.
In agreement with previous studies, we find that the L-Z relation for compact galaxies is not universal, but instead depends on luminosity, with the faintest galaxies exhibiting the highest metallicities.
However, we find that the M-Z relation is universal, independent of mass, and that this relation holds over an order of magnitude longer than previously reported, from the Milky Way to dwarf galaxies a factor of ~100 times less massive.
We show that this lack of evolution in the M-Z relation implies that the star-formation histories and chemical enrichment histories of these galaxies must be closely coupled over nearly all of their lifetimes.

We present a method for unsupervised learning of foreground object detection, based on clustering and density estimation.
It consists in the training of two components: a classifier that assigns to each pixel a label corresponding to the cluster to which the foreground object belongs, and a density estimator that models the background.
The labels are determined during training by a clustering procedure that identifies the regions of the image dominated by the foreground objects.
The resulting method is effective in detecting the foreground objects in a fully unsupervised manner.
We demonstrate the performance of the method on a synthetic dataset and on a difficult real-world dataset of people in crowded scenes.


Our method is related to the popular density-based clustering methods

Recent progress in convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture design has propelled the advancement of semantic segmentation, especially in the context of natural image datasets.
However, the assumption that the training data is abundantly labeled, which is often satisfied in natural image segmentation, does not hold for specialized domains such as food image segmentation, which demands much effort and expense to collect and label.
To overcome the lack of labeled training data, we can utilize the prior knowledge in the form of rules or culinary knowledge to learn a segmentation model.
In this work, we borrow ideas from the recent advancement in the field of salient object detection and propose a saliency-aware class-agnostic segmentation approach for food images.
Specifically, we first utilize a pre-trained CNN as a feature encoder to extract mid-level features and then build a segmentation model that is trained by explicitly incorporating the prior knowledge of food images, which is in the form of a global saliency map.
The global saliency map is learned in a class-agnostic manner, but is tailored to the food domain.

Recent advances in neuroimaging acquisition enabled large-scale recordings of neural activity in many regions across the entire human brain at increasing resolution.
While the field of connectomics aimed to map the intricate patterns of fiber connections across the entire brain, current state-of-the-art algorithms for reconstructing fiber tracts from diffusion MRI (dMRI) images are far from delivering feasible runtime performance for mapping ultra-large scale datasets, which typically consist of several thousands of images with each image requiring several minutes of computational processing.
In this paper, we present a deep learning based approach that aims to accelerate the reconstruction process of fiber connections across the human brain.
We exploit recent advances in image segmentation through structured loss functions that promote the reconstruction of anatomically meaningful segments while retaining the advantage of end-to-end differentiability.
We train our deep learning architecture on large-scale datasets of simulated as well as real dMRI images.
In contrast to related work, we provide a thorough evaluation of the algorithm's performance by comparing it to state-of-the-art methods on real datasets.

Recent developments in imaging medicine have led to a significant increase in the size of 3D medical images, posing a great challenge for efficient transmission, storage and segmentation in the clouds.
In this paper, we propose a machine vision guided 3D medical image compression approach to address this issue.
Our method leverages the power of deep learning to learn a compression model directly from the images, which is trained using a large number of images collected from clinical studies.
The compression model is designed to take into account the specific characteristics of medical images, such as their typically low entropy and the need for precise segmentation.
We evaluate our method on a large dataset of real clinical images and demonstrate that it achieves a significant reduction in the file size while maintaining high quality and enabling accurate segmentation in the clouds.
Our method can be seamlessly integrated into the existing workflow of medical imaging and has the potential to significantly reduce the storage and transmission costs of 3D medical images.

Deep learning is a promising method for tongue surface tracking from real-time ultrasound videos.
We present a simple yet effective method to train a deep neural network for tongue surface detection.
Unlike most previous methods that trace the contour of the tongue, our method detects the landmarks on the tongue surface.
It is more robust to the ambiguous contour around the tongue border in ultrasound videos, and it is more efficient in terms of computation and training data.
We evaluated our method on real-time ultrasound videos, and the experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.


Our tongue surface detection network is based on a modified version of the popular Faster R-CNN [1] with additional novel improvements.

Recent developments in neural network architecture have boosted the performance of image segmentation.
In this paper, we propose FusionNet, a deep fully residual convolutional neural network for image segmentation in connectomics.
FusionNet incorporates several techniques that have been shown to be effective in image segmentation, including an atrous convolutional layer, a residual block, and a dense connection pattern.
We evaluate FusionNet on the task of segmentation of neuronal structures in connectomic images, and show that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art models.
In particular, when applied to segmenting neurons in mouse cortical tissue, FusionNet achieves a precision of 94.3% and recall of 92.6% on cell bodies, and 85.5% precision and 88.4% recall on axon initial segments.
Code is available at https://github.com/andy-connectome/FusionNet.

Nature-inspired algorithms perform well in image segmentation, but the choice of a base algorithm has a significant impact on performance.
In this research, the application of four nature-inspired algorithms (particle swarm optimization, bacterial foraging optimization, cuckoo search, and firefly algorithm) for multi-threshold image segmentation is compared.
Metrics including computation time and segmentation quality are considered.
The results show that the firefly algorithm outperforms the others in both metrics.
Particle swarm optimization achieved the second best performance.
Cuckoo search and bacterial foraging optimization did not perform as well as the top two algorithms.

We give an introduction to stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs).
After recalling the definition and properties of classical Gaussian SPDEs, we discuss existence and uniqueness results for general nonlinear SPDEs in a Gaussian setting.
We then turn to a class of nonlinear SPDEs in the Gaussian setting which possess a unique solution and focus on the question of obtaining a probabilistic representation for the solution in terms of a stochastic flow of maps.
Here the underlying stochastic flow is solution to a stochastic differential equation with a countable number of Brownian drivers.
We present a general approach for obtaining such a representation under mild conditions on the coefficients of the SPDE. 


As a concrete example, we consider a class of nonlinear SPDEs that are associated to a stochastic flow of maps that is generated by a stochastic differential equation with a countable number of Brownian drivers.

Medical image segmentation is important in medicine yet suffers from human error introduced during manual labeling.
A significant challenge in training deep learning models for segmentation is the amount of ground truth (GT) required, which is time-consuming and expensive to generate.
As a result, there has been increasing interest in using synthetic data for training.
However, the quality of the GT in synthetic data is typically superior to that in real data, leading to the risk of overfitting.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to address both problems: the small amount of real GT and the error in the GT.
We first use a U-Net deep learning architecture to segment images and then use a multi-scale graph cuts algorithm to refine the segmentation results.

We present an efficient and accurate approach for colorectal tumor segmentation based on 3D U-Net.
Our method extends the 2D U-Net architecture to include 3D pooling and striding operations, enabling the network to effectively capture spatial dependencies and contextual information in volumetric data.
To enhance performance, we introduce a region-of-interest (RoI) pooling layer that allows the network to focus on the most relevant tumor regions.
Furthermore, we propose a 3D RoI-aware loss function that guides the network to learn more effectively from sparse ground truth labels.
Our method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on the benchmark CSI-MR colon tumor segmentation dataset, with a dice coefficient of 0.8218 and a sensitivity of 0.7383.
In terms of efficiency, our approach achieves a speed of ~40 ms per case on a standard GPU, making it suitable for real-time or batch processing of large datasets.

Recent advances in deep neural networks have achieved significant performance in biomedical image segmentation.
However, these models are data-hungry and require a large amount of labeled examples for training, which are difficult to obtain in the biomedical field due to the high cost of expert annotation.
In this paper, we propose a universal decoding method, called Cascade Decoder, for training data-efficient segmentation models that can be applied to any image domain with only a few annotated examples.
Cascade Decoder first utilizes a set of pre-trained decoders to extract features from the input image, and then learns a new decoder to refine the predictions based on the segmented images and their annotations.
By cascading the decoders in a coarse-to-fine fashion, our method can effectively leverage both the global and local information in the image to achieve segmentation.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three different image segmentation tasks: tumor cell segmentation from confocal images, neuron segmentation from electron microscopic images, and white matter fiber tract segmentation from T1-weighted MRI images, with only 10%, 4% and 0.5% of the images in the training set, respectively.

We present a graph-based framework for natural image segmentation based on affinity fusion.
Our approach leverages the multi-scale graph structure to capture the image context and fuse the multi-scale segmentation results.
By iteratively refining the graph representation and updating the segmentation, our algorithm effectively combines both global and local information for accurate segmentation.
We introduce a novel affinity learning scheme to adaptively estimate the affinity matrix, which measures the similarity between pixels.
The proposed method is fully automatic, parameter-free, and is able to handle any image size.
We evaluate our approach on the VOC 2012 segmentation benchmark and achieve competitive results compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

Line patterns are very common in images.
They appear, for example, in aerial and satellite images, temperature maps, brightness temperature maps, and many other types of images.
The problem of line pattern delineation, i.e., segmenting a line pattern into individual lines, is therefore of practical importance.
In this paper we propose a new approach to line pattern delineation based on the use of B-COSFIRE filters.
These filters have good frequency response characteristics and are straightforward to implement.
In addition, a new gradient-based line selector is proposed.

Multi-channel image segmentation is a classical problem in image processing, with many applications in areas such as medical imaging, remote sensing, and video processing.
In this paper, we propose a new approach to multi-channel image segmentation based on component trees.
Our method utilizes the derivative information of the image channels to build a hierarchy of segments, which can be recursively split into smaller segments.
The proposed method is simple to implement and efficient to compute, and it can handle images with different numbers of channels.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on a number of challenging segmentation problems, including a remotely sensed image dataset and a multi-channel medical imaging dataset.
Our results show that the proposed method can achieve accurate segmentation results and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods.

Two-dimensional (2D) materials offer a unique opportunity to combine different atoms in a single van der Waals heterostructure, with atomic precision, to create engineered meta-materials with unprecedented electrical, optical, and magnetic properties.
One of the current challenges is the lack of understanding of the fundamental dielectric properties of these meta-materials and how they originate from the properties of the constituting 2D materials.
Here, we present a first principles theory to calculate the dielectric function of a van der Waals heterostructure made up of two different 2D materials.
We show how the fundamental dielectric response is influenced by the properties of the individual layers, such as the atomic structure, the electronic states, and the optical transitions.
As an example, we calculate the dielectric functions of van der Waals heterostructures made up of h-BN and graphene, and we show that the fundamental dielectric response is influenced by both the intralayer and the interlayer physics, which include resonant states in both regions and a strong interlayer coupling.
The results agree well with recent measurements.

Semantic image segmentation, which aims to assign semantic labels to every pixel in an image, is a fundamental problem in computer vision.
Recent progresses in this field are mainly driven by deep learning models, especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
However, directly applying CNNs on the pixel level prediction is computationally expensive, and the network architecture is difficult to extend to segment complex scenes.
In this paper, we present a progressively diffused network (PDNet) for semantic image segmentation.
PDNet employs a regional feature aggregation scheme to hierarchically refine the segmentation results and effectively capture long-range dependencies in an image.
A diffused structure is introduced to model the spatial variations of the image, which enables the network to focus on difficult regions and avoid unnecessary computations on easy regions.

Medical image segmentation is a fundamental preliminary step for computed tomography (CT) images towards computerized tumor diagnosis and therapy planning.
Recently, deep learning based on fully convolutional networks (FCNs) has produced significant advancements in medical image segmentation.
However, directly applying FCNs to segment CT images is challenging due to the substantial variability of tumor appearance, the presence of similar structures, and the reduced amount of manually annotated training data.
In this paper, we propose a novel mixed-supervised dual-network (MSDN) for automatic CT image segmentation.
Given the scarce amount of manually annotated data, our MSDN further utilizes a large set of automatically segmented images, which is obtained by a fully supervised deep learning algorithm, as additional weakly labeled training data.
We employ a dual-network architecture, where the prior network is trained in a fully supervised manner, and the latter network is trained with both the fully supervised and weak supervision.

Recent advances in deep learning have achieved great performance in medical image segmentation.
However, deep learning methods usually ignore the observer variation, which may lead to inconsistent segmentation results among different observers.
In this paper, we present a new framework to achieve observer- variation aware medical image segmentation, which combines deep learning and surrogate-assisted genetic algorithms.
Given the segmented images from multiple observers, our framework learns a deep neural network in a data-driven manner to capture the common patterns for segmentation, while genetic algorithms are used to optimize the segmentation protocols to achieve better segmentation consistency across observers.
We apply our method to segment lumbar vertebrae in CT images.
Experimental results show the effectiveness of our method in improving the segmentation consistency.

We reexamine the recently proposed Atrous Convolution (AC) for semantic image segmentation.
Despite its popularity, we show that the performance of AC deteriorates as the average stride length in the encoder increases, which is crucial for preserving spatial information and resisting overfitting.
Through analysis and experiments, we find that this limitation arises from the sharing of the atrous rate among different convolutional layers, which restricts the adaptability of the atrous rate to feature hierarchies.
To address this problem, we propose a simple yet effective method called Adaptive Atrous Rate (AAR), which adaptively estimates the atrous rate for each layer.
AAR not only improves the segmentation performance but also significantly reduces the memory usage and accelerates the training process.
We implement the state-of-the-art segmentation models with AAR and demonstrate its advantage over the models with the original AC on multiple datasets, including Cityscapes and ACDC.

We study interference between two single photons and two-photon spontaneous superposition using a polarization-based quantum eraser setup.
The two-photon state is produced by an spontaneous parametric down-conversion photon pair source, and the photons are sent through a polarization beam splitter, with one arm containing a quantum eraser and the other a half-wave plate, which can be used to change the polarization of a photon.
The two photons are then measured using two polarization-sensitive detectors.
We find that when the half-wave plate is not set to a special angle, the two-photon coincidence rate shows an interference pattern, with maxima and minima corresponding to the two different polarization settings of the quantum eraser.
However, when the half-wave plate is set to a special angle, we observe that the two-photon coincidence rate is always at its maximum, independent of the polarization setting of the quantum eraser.
This demonstrates a breakdown of the spontaneous superposition of the two-photon state, and is explained by a simple classical model.

Patterns are ubiquitous in natural language texts, formal languages, and biological sequences.
Furthermore, patterns can often be embedded within one another forming hierarchical structures.
For example, in a natural language sentence, individual words can form phrases, and phrases can form clauses, etc.
Similarly, in genetic sequences, motifs (short patterns) can form larger structures such as genes, which in turn form chromosomes.
These hierarchical structures can be represented as nodes in a tree, where each node has potentially multiple parent nodes and multiple child nodes.
Such tree structures are referred to as tree patterns.

A long-running webcam installed in 2007 at Lake Mendota, Wisconsin, has provided an opportunity to develop a time series of lake ice coverage and thaw dates.
Comparing webcam images with those from crowd-sourced volunteers using the same web interface shows that citizen scientists can provide useful data, but with considerable variability.
Guidance for volunteers on how to interpret webcam images of lake ice leads to more accurate and precise measurements, but variability in measurements persists.
Crowd-sourced data, if applied to a large region with adequate volunteer training, could provide a valuable supplement to satellite data for monitoring lake ice cover.
However, automated analysis of webcam images, as developed here, provides the most accurate and precise data.
The webcam-based time series reveals a significant shift toward later ice coverage in fall and earlier ice-out dates in spring over the 13-year record.

We show that linear dispersive filtering near atomic resonance can lead to time-reversal of light.
In particular, near the 1183 nm resonance in Xenon, a 1 nm thin layer of the gas achieves almost perfect time-reversal of the transmitted light.
We find excellent agreement between numerical solutions of Maxwell's equations and experimental measurements.
Our results open new possibilities for time-reversal of light using readily available materials, with potential applications in optical imaging and communication. 


We further show that a thin layer of any linear material, regardless of its atomic or molecular composition, can be used to reverse the group velocity of light.
Finally, we discuss the limitations of our experimental approach, and outline future directions.

Recent progress in deep learning allows training models to learn image segmentation from labeled images, but training data with ground truth is often not available in practice.
Unsupervised learning offers a appealing alternative but learning meaningful representations of images without guidance remains challenging.
In this paper, we exploit differentiable kernel clustering as a building block for learning an effective image representation without any labels.
Our method clusters image patches in a way that captures local structures and, at the same time, is differentiable with respect to the inputs.
This property enables training by minimizing an appropriate energy function on a graph, which is defined by the image gradients.
We show that the resulting algorithm is capable of simultaneously clustering image patches and segmenting the image in a supervised manner, given only the image itself as input.

Abstract:

Deep learning (DL) has recently emerged as a powerful tool for machine health monitoring (MHM).
In this survey, we provide an overview of the current state of the art in DL for MHM, including key research challenges, opportunities, and limitations.
We begin by introducing the basic concepts of DL and MHM, and then review the different ways in which DL has been applied to MHM, including fault detection, diagnosis, and prognosis.
We then discuss the advantages and limitations of DL for MHM, and highlight key research challenges such as data acquisition, model selection, and deployment.
Finally, we provide a brief overview of the current state of the art in DL for MHM, and highlight potential research directions.
We hope that this survey will provide a comprehensive and informative overview of the current state of the art in DL for MHM, and inspire further research and development in this exciting field.

Arxiv abstract:

We present a novel semi-supervised learning framework for few-shot medical image segmentation, which we refer to as PoissonSeg.
In medical image analysis, acquiring manually annotated images for training can be expensive, and transferring pre-trained models to new sites and modalities is challenging.
To tackle these problems, we exploit a recently proposed poisson learning framework, which enables us to leverage abundant unlabeled data and prior knowledge, and develop a new framework that is suitable for few-shot learning.
In our method, we minimize a poisson loss that enforces the agreement between segmentations and the prior knowledge, and a segmentation difference loss that encourages the agreement between predictions and a few labeled images.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three different abdominal image segmentation benchmarks, and show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches for few-shot learning.

Articular cartilage plays an essential role in the functioning of joints, as it allows for smooth articulation and dissipation of loads.
However, it is highly susceptible to injury and degradation, particularly in the presence of repetitive loading.
In this research paper, a comprehensive finite element model is presented to investigate the effects of cyclic loading on articular cartilage lesion formation.
The model incorporates the material properties and morphology of articular cartilage, allowing for a realistic representation of the tissue's behavior.


The results of the simulation show that cyclic loading significantly contributes to the formation of articular cartilage lesions.
The model was able to capture the progression of damage in the cartilage tissue, highlighting the regions of highest stress and strain that were susceptible to injury.

Chilies are one of the most important cash crops in Mexico and it is the second most important vegetable after the tomato.
Time consuming and tedious manual inspection is currently done in agriculture to estimate the percentage of defects in the harvested produce.
Defect inspection is needed for proper grading and to determine if the produce meets the stringent quality requirements of the exporter.
This work focuses on defect segmentation of chili pepper X-ray images.
Successful segmentation was achieved using a texture based approach.
A Gabor filter is used as a texture descriptor.

Deepfake refers to the phenomenon of maliciously manipulating multimedia contents, especially image and video data, using artificial intelligence techniques to impersonate a person doing or saying something they never did or said.
Detecting deepfake contents is of paramount importance to uphold the integrity of media communication.
In this paper, we focus on detecting forged facial expressions in still images, which is a fundamental yet challenging task.
We propose a novel approach to detect forged facial expressions using a separable convolutional neural network (SCNN) and image segmentation.
Our approach first extracts a compact feature vector from the input image using a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN).
Then, we apply image segmentation to extract the regions of interest (ROIs) from the input image.

We present a fast constraint propagation algorithm for image segmentation based on label fusion of watershed segments.
The approach is motivated by the shape prior of watershed segments, which reflects the local connectivity of the image pixels.
The proposed algorithm efficiently computes a score for each pixel based on the constraints from the watershed segmentation and fuses the scores of neighboring segments to obtain the final segmentation.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach on a variety of images, and show that it produces a segmentation that is more accurate and coherent compared to existing algorithms.
The proposed algorithm is fast enough to be used in real-time applications.

Arxiv abstract:
Most existing single image haze removal algorithms rely on a sufficient density of haze-free/low-haze image pairs to learn the transmission map for restoration.
In this paper, we propose a fast single image haze removal algorithm that does not require any image pairs at all and is specifically designed to be fast in practice.
The algorithm optimizes the haze visibility measure directly in the wavelet domain, resulting in a fast implementation.
Furthermore, to overcome the drawback of the wavelet domain, i.e., non-differentiability, we propose a multilevel wavelet decomposition, where the optimization is performed at different levels of decomposition, yielding a successively differentiable algorithm.
In addition, to further accelerate the optimization process, we propose an auxiliary function method that converges faster than simply using the non-differentiable wavelet domain haze visibility measure as the objective function.
Our method is fast, with less than 0.1 seconds to remove haze on a single image, and can be readily used in any device, even on mobile devices.

Recent progress in the controlled generation of individual x-ray photons for imaging at a free-electron laser (XFEL) facility lays the foundation for a new regime of imaging – single-photon counting (SPC) imaging.
In SPC imaging, the detected intensity at each image pixel is determined by counting the number of detected photons arriving within a fixed-length shutter time.
In this paper, we investigate the benefits as well as the associated challenges of SPC imaging, as compared to conventional (i.e. integrating) imaging, in a variety of scientific applications.
To this end, we have developed a simulation framework, which models the entire photon generation, propagation, and detection process at an XFEL facility, and which is suitable for performing fully-sequential simulations, wherein each detected photon's arrival time and pixel position is determined stochastically.
In this paper we present the formalism and the numerical methods employed in this simulation framework.
We then explore, through a series of numerical simulations, the relative benefits of SPC imaging as compared to conventional imaging in the context of three scientific applications: (a) phase imaging to recover a weak object transmission function; (b) diffraction imaging to determine an object's lattice; (c) imaging through strongly scattering media.

Abdominal CT images provide fine-grained details of the liver anatomy, which is widely used for clinical diagnosis and intervention.
However, the complex anatomical structures in CT images make liver segmentation a challenging task, even for expert radiologists.
In this paper, we present an auto-context neural network together with a self-supervised contour attention module to address the segmentation challenge.
The auto-context module captures the global context by aggregating all positions and channels of the input features, while the self-supervised contour attention module is designed to capture the contour information of the objects, without any additional contour information in the training phase.
We evaluate our method on the 2018 ISBI Liver Segmentation Challenge.
Compared to the state-of-the-art methods, our approach produces segmentation results with better accuracy and spatial coherence, ultimately improving the F1-score from 87.1% to 89.4% on the challenge dataset.

Recent progress in deep learning has enabled the development of end-to-end trainable systems for self-driving.
However, training such systems is challenging due to the lack of large-scale, diverse, and realistic training data.
We introduce GeoSim, a video simulation system that generates geometrically-accurate, photorealistic training data for deep learning-based self-driving systems.
GeoSim is designed to address the limitations of current simulation systems, which often produce unrealistic and synthetic-looking images.
It uses a combination of geometric reasoning, physical simulation, and artistic rendering to generate realistic and diverse training data.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of GeoSim in generating realistic training data and show that it improves the performance of deep learning-based self-driving systems.

Semantic image segmentation, as a fundamental task in computer vision, aims at assigning semantic labels to each pixel in an image.
Recently, deep learning methods have shown promising results in this area.
However, most existing methods rely on greedy inference, which can result in suboptimal performance.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for semantic image segmentation based on Deep Gaussian CRFs (DGCRFs), which are a class of probabilistic models that leverage deep features learned by convolutional neural networks.
By formulating the segmentation problem as a probabilistic inference problem, our approach is able to produce more accurate and robust predictions.
We introduce a fast and exact inference algorithm that scales to realistic images.

Most existing works on clustering rely on distance functions to define a metric between data points, which assumes the data lies in a low-dimensional space and fails when the data lies on a manifold of higher dimension.
In this paper, we propose a new clustering framework that does not rely on distance functions and hence is capable of clustering points on a manifold of any dimension.
In particular, given a set of n points in d-dimensional space, our method first maps these n points to a kernel feature space, where kernel functions define a similarity metric between points.
Next, we propose a spectral clustering algorithm that clusters points based on the similarity metric in the feature space.
We show that the proposed method can be used to define a data-dependent metric between points, and hence can cluster points on a manifold of high dimension.
We present experimental results on synthetic and real-world data sets, and show that the proposed method gives better clustering accuracy compared with state-of-the-art clustering methods.

We introduce a new estimator for the intrinsic dimension of a finite collection of data points, induced by the Gaussian core model.
This model captures the local geometry around a data point through a truncated multivariate normal distribution.
The intrinsic dimension is the dimension of the smallest space in which the data can be embedded in such a way that each data point has a neighborhood that is an analog of the model.
We show that our estimator is consistently estimated, and suggest an iterative algorithm to compute it.
This algorithm is validated against synthetic data, and the model is applied to several real world data sets.
In particular, we show that on the "Ising" model, the intrinsic dimension grows as the dimension of the ambient space grows.

Abstract

We present a deep learning work flow for fast and robust segmentation of anatomical structures in CT images.
The network was trained on publicly available datasets with ground truth annotations for lung and spine.
Our network is based on a convolutional neural network architecture previously validated on the MIAS challenge.
We exploit existing clinically available delineations, which are used for treatment planning, for the initialization of the network.
The initializations are propagated through the network using a weighted vector flow scheme.

We present the results of deep X-ray observations of two cometary blue compact dwarf (BCD) galaxies, Mrk 59 and Mrk 71, aimed at studying the nature of the excess soft X-ray emission recently discovered in these objects.
The observations were performed with Chandra ACIS-S on 2005 November 22 (Mrk 59) and 2005 December 2 (Mrk 71) for a total exposure of ~70 ks and ~140 ks, respectively.
The X-ray images of both galaxies are well fitted by a model in which the emission is dominated by a point source, most likely the active nucleus, at the galaxy's center, and a diffuse, unresolved component.
The latter is spatially coincident with the optical emission and accounts for ~70% of the total X-ray flux in both galaxies.
The spectrum of this diffuse component is well fitted by an absorbed power law with a photon index of ~1 and a cutoff at ~1 keV.
The absorbed fluxes of the nuclei are ~2.5

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to revolutionise medical imaging, but also carries the risk of perpetuating and even increasing existing health inequalities.
An international collaboration of experts from diverse fields has come together to consider how to ensure that AI in medical imaging is developed and deployed to maximise the benefits and minimise the harms.
Following a two-stage online consultation, we used a modified Delphi method to achieve consensus on key issues, and we provide here a summary of our discussions and recommendations for future AI development and deployment.
Combining the principles of trustworthy AI with consideration of fairness and equity, we propose a framework to inform the development and deployment of AI in medical imaging.
To ensure the trustworthy and fair use of AI in medical imaging, developers, clinicians and researchers should consider the following: promoting health equality and equity; upholding data privacy and security; maintaining technical performance; supporting clinical performance and decision making; and being responsive to patients and the public.
In this report, we outline a consensus view on the key issues that need to be addressed, and make recommendations for the future development and deployment of AI in medical imaging.

Post-mortem identification is an important task of forensic science, and the iris is a biologically unique region for human identification.
However, the process of post-mortem iris image segmentation is extremely challenging due to the absence of ocular illumination and specularity.
In this paper, we propose a deep learning based approach for post-mortem iris image segmentation, which is lightweight and efficient.
Our approach is composed of a coarse segmentation network, which is a lightweight ResNet18 with an attention module, and a refined segmentation network, which is a U-Net with an attention module.
We train our networks using a hybrid loss function, which combines dice loss and mse loss.
Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on a public post-mortem iris image segmentation benchmark while being much faster than other approaches.

We present a comprehensive spectroscopic survey of stellar populations in the inner Galactic bulge, performed with the Fiber Multi-Object Spectrograph (FMOS) on the Subaru 8.2m telescope as a part of the Bulge Extinction Study (BES).
The sample includes 555 stars with extinction-corrected magnesium abundances [Mg/H] < -1.7, covering a magnitude range of 12 <
I < 17 mag.
This survey largely complements the previous works, especially the recent study by Saito et al., who targeted the redder bulge stars with [Mg/H] < -2.3.
Thanks to the large dataset, we can examine the stellar metallicity distribution in the inner bulge in detail, through construction of the MDF in several different ways.
An apparent bimodality is seen in the MDF, which reflects the well-known division of the Galactic bulge into a metal-rich component and a metal-poor component.

Recent experiments on magneto-dielectric particle chains have revealed intriguing phenomena, including the observation of single-mode propagation in certain frequency ranges and the existence of frequency bands with no propagating modes.
To explain these experimental observations, we have performed 3D full-wave simulations based on the transmission line model (TLM) and compared the results to those obtained from an effective continuum model.
By comparing the results for different geometries, we found good agreement between our simulations and the experimental observations.
The simulations show that the observed single-mode propagation is a result of the specific chain geometry and the choice of material properties.
In addition, we found that the absence of propagating modes in certain frequency bands is a result of the interaction between the magnetic and dielectric responses of the particles.
Our results suggest that the observation of single-mode propagation and the existence of frequency bands with no propagating modes can be explained by the specific chain geometry and the choice of material properties.

Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision, with a goal to assign semantic labels to every pixel in an input image.
Most existing works focus on designing complex models to learn direct mappings from images to segmentation labels, which limit their applicability in real-world applications due to the model's complexity and resource intensity.
In this work, we propose a novel approach to semantic segmentation that utilizes psychometric learning, a technique derived from perceptual psychology.
Our method leverages a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) and learns a hierarchical segmentation model using a psychometric learning framework.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, achieving competitive results compared to state-of-the-art methods while using a fraction of the model size and computational resources.
The proposed method is simple, efficient, and effective, making it suitable for real-world applications.

A deep learning based convolutional neural network (CNN) has been shown to achieve great performance for medical image segmentation.
However, it remains a challenge to train such networks with limited training data.
In this paper, we present a novel ensemble based deep CNN framework for semi-supervised medical image segmentation, which is trained on both labeled and unlabeled data.
Our framework utilizes an ensemble of CNNs to boost the segmentation performance.
We adopt a weighted majority voting scheme to combine the outputs from individual CNNs, where the weights are learned from the labeled data.
Furthermore, we introduce a novel data augmentation technique to generate more training samples from the unlabeled data.

Appearance contrast is a popular bottom-up cue used by visual attention models to simulate salient object segmentation, but it tends to produce fragmented saliency maps lacking global coherence, resulting in incorrect object identification.
In this paper, we propose PISA, a method that improves the coherence of appearance-based saliency maps by taking advantage of two types of complementary contrast information: pixel-level and edge-level.
PISA flexibly integrates different appearance contrast measures—such as intensity, color, and texture—with edge-preserving coherence modeling.
We introduce a pixel-level contrast aggregation module that computes saliency from pixel-level contrasts, and an edge-level contrast aggregation module that computes saliency from edge-level contrasts.
These two modules are subsequently combined to produce the final saliency map.
We demonstrate via extensive experiments on common benchmarks that PISA consistently improves performance of saliency detection over strong baselines in terms of both accuracy and coherence, without any parameter tuning.

We study a system of two-color fermions in a cold and magnetized state in the mean-field approximation.
By using the numerical linked-cluster expansion, we evaluate the thermodynamic potential for arbitrary values of the density and magnetization.
For large values of the magnetization, the system undergoes a transition from a normal fluid to a Bose-Einstein condensate.
On the other hand, for small values of the magnetization, the system stabilizes into a color superconducting state.
By comparing the free energies for the different phases, we determine the boundary of the coexistence region between the normal fluid and the superconducting phases, and between the normal fluid and the Bose-Einstein condensate.
We discuss the behavior of the order parameters and quasiparticle weights.

Model predictive control (MPC) is applied to a coupled tank liquid level system in this work.
In this system, the liquid levels in two tanks, which are connected by a pipe, are controlled.
The control objective is to transfer liquid from one tank to another while maintaining the liquid levels in both tanks at desired levels.
The model of the system is derived using a mass balance approach on the liquid levels in the tanks.
The controller is designed using a linear quadratic regulator (LQR) approach.
The controller is tested on a set of realistic scenarios, and the results are compared with those obtained using a PID controller.

We present a general, lightweight system for accurate 3D medical image segmentation.
Our system, called Network to Segment Them All (N2S2), is based on a single deep learning network that is capable of segmenting a wide variety of anatomical structures in 3D medical images.
The network is designed to be efficient, with a small number of parameters and a low computational cost, making it suitable for use on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones or tablets.


We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of 3D medical image datasets, including MRI, CT, and ultrasound images.
Our results show that N2S2 is able to achieve state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of anatomical structures, including the brain, lungs, liver, and heart.


We believe that N2S2 has the potential to revolutionize the field of medical image segmentation by providing a general and efficient solution that is capable of accurately segmenting a wide variety of anatomical structures in 3D medical images.

Recent progress in deep learning has enabled the development of powerful models for image semantic segmentation, i.e., assigning a label to each pixel in an image.
However, these models are trained on large datasets and require a significant amount of computational resources, making them difficult to deploy on resource-constrained devices.
In this paper, we propose a lightweight and efficient approach for image semantic segmentation based on personalized modeling.
Our approach is designed to reduce the computational cost and memory requirements of the model, while still achieving high accuracy.
We achieve this by combining a deep neural network with a set of personalized semantic prototypes, which are generated from a small number of labeled images.

Recent advances in MRI acquisition enable scanning of the entire heart at once, making it possible to reconstruct a volumetric model of patient-specific cardiac chambers.
This model can be used for help in surgical planning; however, it is challenging to manually segment the boundary of the cardiac chambers in the volume.
We present a method for automatic segmentation of the left ventricle (LV) and right ventricle (RV) in cardiac MRI volumes using a transformer-based model.
Our method reaches a F1 score of 0.91 on in-distribution testing data, and 0.80 on out-of-distribution data.
In addition, our model generalizes to segment the RV in datasets where the RV was not present in the training data.
We show that our model generalizes well to unseen datasets and out-of-distribution data in an open-world setting, despite only being trained on a fixed set of segments.

We present a new active contour model for image segmentation based on a generalized asymmetric dual-front approach.
In this model, the interface is described by two fronts, one for the exterior and one for the interior of the object, which move simultaneously toward each other or away from each other depending on the local gradient direction.
The front that is inside the evolving contour is always faster than the outside front.
This feature imposes a strong constraint on the contour evolution, resulting in a bias toward the formation of a global contour that is closed and does not leak out of the object boundary.
An important advantage of the proposed method is that it is very fast and easy to implement because it only involves a simple calculation of the gradient of the image and a marching process in the gradient direction.
Experimental results on several segmentation benchmarks show the efficiency of the proposed approach compared with state-of-the-art active contour models.

We present a systematic approach to scene understanding for autonomous manipulation, leveraging recent advances in deep learning.
In this work, we consider the task of picking objects from cluttered scenes, a key capability for autonomous robots.
We introduce a novel deep architecture, termed Object-Context Embedding (OCE), that fuses object detection and semantic scene understanding.
Our approach jointly reasons about the presence of objects, their contexts, and their interactions, enabling the robot to adapt its decisions to the scene at test-time.
We show that our approach outperform state-of-the-art on the task of picking objects from scenes, measured by success rate and pick success.
In particular, we achieve 79% pick success on the challenging Object Discovery and Learning (ODL) dataset, significantly improving upon the prior state of the art.

In this paper, we provide an overview of the most commonly used cardiac MR image segmentation techniques.
We discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each technique and provide examples of their applications in clinical and research settings.
We also discuss the future direction of cardiac MR image segmentation and potential applications in the clinic.
The goal of this paper is to provide a comprehensive understanding of the current state of the art in cardiac MR image segmentation and to highlight its potential for improving the diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular disease.
We conclude that manual segmentation techniques have the advantage of producing high-quality segmentations but are highly time-consuming and require expertise.
Automated techniques are a promising alternative with the advantage of being much faster and less expensive but suffer from the disadvantage of being less accurate.

We present a simple method to augment pretrained models with new anatomy and images, based on an in-depth analysis of the representations learned by the pretrained models.
Our method is motivated by the observation that while pretrained models are trained on a diverse set of images, they learn highly specific representations, making them ineffective when used out of distribution.
We find that this is because the representations learned are highly dependent on the presence of certain anatomy and that the absence of this anatomy often leads to the representations not being able to generalize well.
Our method addresses this limitation by learning a new representation that can exploit both the information in the pretrained model as well as the new anatomy and images.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on three different datasets: cardiac MRI, abdominal CT, and knee MRI.
For all three datasets, we show that our method improves performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods, while requiring less labeled data.

Recent progress in deep learning has boosted the development of medical image segmentation models.
However, most existing works focus on 2D images or 3D volumes without considering the inherent hierarchical structure of medical images.
In this paper, we present a Pyramid Medical Transformer (PMT) to effectively exploit the pyramid structure of medical images for segmentation.
Specifically, we design a Light-weight Attention Module (LAM) to capture the global and local information at different levels of the image pyramid.
Moreover, to effectively integrate multi-scale information, we propose a Scale-aware Attention (SA) module that can focus on different scales of features adaptively.
Furthermore, a Pyramid-aware Tokenization (PAT) strategy is proposed to selectively preserve the useful information from the low-level features for each token.

Head overcoat (HOC) thickness is an important diagnostic indicator for multiple sclerosis (MS), which can be automatically measured using magnetic resonance (MR) images.
However, existing methods usually require additional manual corrections or optimizations, which is inconvenient for clinical use.
In this paper, we propose a novel automatic HOC thickness measurement method based on deep learning.
Our method is based on a NASNet-Large-Decoder net pre-trained on a large dataset of abdominal MR images.
We fine-tune the pre-trained model on a small dataset of MS patients including T1-weighted (T1W), T2-weighted (T2W), and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images.
The proposed method was validated on MS patients and healthy controls, and compared with two commonly used methods: manual drawing of regions of interest (ROIs) and an automatic method based on random forests (RFs).

Abstract— We present a framework for training a deep neural network for automated weed detection in aerial imagery with context.
Our approach combines a convolutional neural network (CNN) for feature extraction with a support vector machine (SVM) for classification.
The CNN is trained on a dataset of aerial images containing a variety of weeds and background contexts.
The SVM is trained on the features extracted by the CNN from a separate dataset of images containing only weeds and background.
Our approach achieves a high accuracy rate of 92.7% for weed detection in aerial imagery.
Furthermore, our approach is able to detect weeds in imagery containing a variety of background contexts, such as fields, roads, and water bodies.

In this study, we investigate the effect of interface anisotropy on the precession of magnetization initiated by laser heating.
We find that a $\pi$ phase shift occurs in the precession of magnetization when the material is heated by a laser.
This phase shift is a result of the interface anisotropy and the resulting change in the magnetic easy axis.
We also find that the direction of the phase shift depends on the direction of the applied magnetic field, and that the phase shift can be controlled by the direction of the magnetic field.
These findings could be useful for controlling the magnetic properties of materials and devices.

We present a novel falling-ball algorithm for image segmentation based on the minimization of a cost function via a simulated annealing approach.
Our algorithm is inspired by the behavior of balls falling into a bowl of sand, where the sand is modeled as a smooth surface and the balls are initially placed on a grid overlaying the image.
By iteratively moving the balls downward, the grid cells corresponding to the boundaries between regions in the image are gradually revealed.
Our approach is able to handle a variety of segmentation scenarios and is particularly effective at segmenting images with complex and irregular boundaries.
We demonstrate the performance of our algorithm on a number of benchmark images and compare it to other state-of-the-art segmentation algorithms.
Our results show that our algorithm is able to produce high-quality segmentations that are comparable to or better than those produced by other algorithms, while being more efficient in terms of computation time.

An index is proposed to evaluate the validity of fuzzy-possibilistic C-means (FP-C) clustering.
The index is calculated based on a similarity measure between the true data and the data classified by FP-C clustering.
The proposed index gives a measure of the quality of clustering in terms of how well the clusters are defined by the data points they contain.
The index ranges from 0 to 1, with 1 indicating perfect clustering and 0 indicating no clustering.
The validity index is compared to the fuzzy validity index (FVI) and the possibilistic validity index (PVI) for FP-C clustering.
The results show that the proposed index is a good measure for evaluating the validity of FP-C clustering.

Abstract:
We introduce SemSegLoss, a Python package providing a collection of state-of-the-art loss functions for training semantic segmentation models.
It facilitates transfer learning and model evaluation by implementing popular loss functions associated with published semantic segmentation models.

Captions are a valuable source of information for semantic segmentation, despite most existing approaches treating them as auxiliary data or a weakly-supervised signal.
In this paper, we investigate methods for harvesting information from captions for semantic segmentation.
We propose a simple yet effective approach for utilizing captions in a weakly-supervised manner, by exploiting their temporal consistency and context information.
Our key insight is that the caption for a given frame is likely to contain information about the presence and location of objects in that frame.
We leverage this intuition to improve the performance of weakly-supervised semantic segmentation.
Our approach consists of two main components: (1) a spatial attention module that uses the caption to focus on the relevant regions of the image, and (2) a temporal attention module that uses the caption to determine the relevance of different frames in a video.

Copula correlation is a novel dependence measure for continuous variables that overcomes the limitations of traditional measures such as Pearson's correlation.
It provides a more accurate representation of the relationship between variables by measuring the equivalence of their cumulative distribution functions.
This new measure has applications in various fields, including finance, insurance, and statistics.
In this paper, we introduce copula correlation and demonstrate its advantages over existing dependence measures.
We also extend Pearson's correlation to a new measure called copula-based correlation, which incorporates the copula correlation concept.
This new measure is more flexible and can be applied to a wider range of variables than Pearson's correlation.

Most organisms use chemotaxis to detect and respond to chemical gradients, but collective decision-making processes that underpin swarm behaviour often appear to rely on other cues, such as mechanical signalling or social interactions.
Here we show that collectively migrating locusts respond to odour gradients under laboratory conditions that minimise mechanical and social cues.
We found that the chemotactic response of individuals was relatively poor, yet successful migration of the group relied on odour perception.
We show that the locusts' aggregation behaviour emerges from the noise in individual responses, which is regulated by a transient amplification of responses to odour, probably caused by positive feedback between odour and behavioural states.
Our results suggest that collective odour sensing can improve detection of odour gradients and provide the basis for reliable group navigation, despite individual responses being relatively poor.

In this paper, we present a parameter decoupling strategy for semi-supervised 3D left atrium segmentation.
Unlike most existing works that use a fully supervised approach, our method takes advantage of both supervised and unsupervised datasets for training.
We argue that the inconsistency between the two datasets is mainly rooted in the parameter settings (e.g., initial starting points, threshold values, and regularization weights) rather than the network architecture itself.
To tackle this issue, we propose a parameter decoupling strategy, in which we decouple the parameters into two parts: architecture parameters and appearance parameters.
We then fine-tune the network separately on both supervised and unsupervised datasets, with the architecture parameters kept fixed.
In this way, our method can effectively leverage the rich annotations from the supervised dataset and the abundant unlabeled samples from the unsupervised dataset, thereby achieving better performance in 3D left atrium segmentation.

A detailed and unified study of criteria for measures of quantum correlations is presented.
After briefly reviewing the fundamental limitations on measuring correlations, we analyze in detail several recently proposed criteria for measures of quantum correlations.
In contrast to previous studies, our analysis covers all major types of criteria, including those based on continuity, convexity, and contractivity conditions.
We show that most of the recently proposed criteria are inherently weaker than others and derive general necessary and sufficient conditions for these criteria in terms of simple mathematical operations.
We also present a new class of criteria that are applicable to any measure of quantum correlations and prove that they are all equivalent when the underlying measure is continuous, convex, and contractive.
Finally, we give a complete description of all possible criteria for measures of quantum correlations and illustrate our results through several examples.

Toward panoptic segmentation, which directly predicts instance-level segmentation masks and instance labels for each pixel, we find that existing methods suffer from two limitations: (1) Most existing methods rely on post-processing steps that are expensive in terms of computational cost, and (2) Existing panoptic segmentation benchmarks include only coarse pixel-level ground truth, which hampers the training of dense prediction models.
To address these issues, we present a simple but effective anchor-based approach for panoptic segmentation.
By adapting the mask-scoring module in the detection framework, our method achieves comparable performance to the state-of-the-art methods while being much faster.
In addition, to tackle the lack of dense ground truth, we present a new dataset, called , which has instance-level segmentation masks as ground truth.
The proposed method achieves top performance on the and benchmarks, while being more than 2x faster than the next best method.
Code is available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/panoptic-segmentation.

We show that QPL ensembles are as resilient as PLEs to attacks that have been previously considered for PLEs, such as the birthday attack and the subset attack, while requiring a smaller key space.
In addition, we show that QPL ensembles are useful for creating practical symmetric key generators, as they can be generated with a small number of bits and are highly resilient to attacks.
We present a way to generate QPL ensembles that is based on a new method for generating PLEs, which is more efficient than the previously known methods.

We present a novel class of algorithms for submodular optimization that is both simpler and more powerful than previous methods.
Our approach is based on reflecting the gradient of the objective function with respect to each decision variable.
This reflection has two benefits: it simplifies the optimization problem by transforming it into a convex problem, and it exploits the structure of the submodular function to obtain a better approximation guarantee.
Our reflection method can be easily incorporated into any first-order method, such as gradient descent or stochastic gradient descent.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a wide variety of submodular optimization problems, including submodular function optimization, matroid intersection, and minimax optimization.
We also show how to use our reflection method to solve the popular knapsack problem with fractional items, which has applications in numerous fields including robotics and finance.

A new approach to image segmentation based on the principal component analysis is presented.
This approach is applied to the segmentation of in vitro cell colonies in bright field images.
The individual cells are the basic elements for the segmentation, and therefore an appropriate estimation of cell regions is essential.
In order to achieve this goal, a new filtering technique that utilizes the spatial dependence of the pixel intensity in the image is proposed.
This technique, named as the self-guided filter, is used to preprocess the image, and the resulting image is then provided as the input to the proposed segmentation method.
In this method, the image is decomposed into its principal components, and the segmentation is performed on the dominant principal component, which carries most of the useful information for segmentation.

We present a long-term visual localization system that utilizes semantic segmentations of the training images to improve performance.
We pretrain a convolutional neural network (CNN) on the ImageNet dataset, and use the CNN to extract features from both the training and test images.
We then use a support vector machine (SVM) to classify the images into 1000 fine-grained object classes.
To segment the images, we propagate the activations of the last layer of the CNN through an iterative graph cuts algorithm.
To localize a query image, we first classify the query image using the SVM, then we segment the query image using the trained segmentations from the training images, and finally we localize the query image by matching the segmented query image with the segmented training images.
In addition, we implement several strategies to improve localization performance, including a prior based on the training images' geographic location information, and “in-session localization,” which utilizes object classes that are unique to the session to improve localization.

Medical image segmentation is prone to label corruption, which poses a severe impediment to clinical deployment.
In this paper, we tackle the challenge of label corruption by learning a cross-denoising network (CDN) with a denoising branch and a correcting branch, aiming to restore clean labels for corrupted ones.
Specifically, the denoising branch leverages the inherent smoothness of segmentations to remove noise, while the correcting branch focuses on the dissimilarity between the corrupted labels and their denoised versions to correct them.
To effectively train the correcting branch, we introduce a domain shift adaptation module to align the distributions of uncorrupted and corrupted data, enabling the network to learn from both sources of data without leaking the clean labels to the corrupted side.
We evaluate our method on three public medical image segmentation benchmarks with different degrees of label noise (20%, 40%, and 60%), and demonstrate its effectiveness against existing state-of-the-art methods.
Code is available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/CDN.

In this paper, we tackle the challenge of label corruption by learning a cross-denoising network (CDN) with a denoising branch and a correcting branch, aiming to restore clean labels for corrupted ones.
Specifically, the denoising branch leverages the inherent smoothness of segmentations to remove noise, while the correcting branch focuses on the dissimilarity between the corrupted labels and their denoised versions to correct them.
To effectively train the correcting branch, we introduce a domain shift adaptation module to align the distributions of uncorrupted and corrupted data, enabling the network to learn from both sources of data without leaking the clean labels to the corrupted side.
We evaluate our method on three public medical image segmentation benchmarks with different degrees of label noise (20%, 40%, and 60%), and demonstrate its effectiveness against existing state-of-the-art methods.
Code is available at https://github.com/VITA-Group/CDN.

cross-stain histopathology image segmentation based on a dual adaptive pyramid network (DAPNet).
The DAPNet is composed of two adaptive pyramid networks (APNs), each designed to segment a specific stain in the histopathology image.
The proposed method was tested on a dataset of 
histopathology images from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) project.
The experimental results show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and runtime.

Our method is inspired by the rate optimal convergence rate of the lasso estimator.
We derive the optimality in the sense that the expected number of false discoveries is minimized under a given power.
We show that the projection pursuit, which is the basis of our method, achieves the optimal rate.
We propose a multiple testing procedure that controls the false discovery rate (FDR) under the linear regression model with a potentially high-dimensional covariance matrix.
The proposed method is motivated by the projection pursuit, a convex optimization technique, to search for the important variables.
