We introduce set-valued fundamental diagrams for second-order traffic models.
Set-valued fundamental diagrams extend classical fundamental diagrams, which are known to be applicable only for bottleneck flows and strictly saturated traffic.
Set-valued diagrams can explicitly account for the possibility of having a set of possible output flows for a given input flow.
These diagrams are derived from Jaminon solutions, which are characterized via the second-order limit of generalized bottleneck equations.
In this paper, we construct the set-valued fundamental diagrams for several classes of networks, including series-parallel and tree networks.
The results show that the constructed set-valued diagrams are closely related to the generalized Bottleneck Principles and the generalized network decomposition.

Recent progress in deep learning has enabled the development of effective models for remote sensing imagery semantic segmentation.
However, these models often suffer from boundary loss, which can lead to inaccurate results and hinder their performance in real-world applications.
In this paper, we investigate the boundary loss problem and propose a novel approach to address it.
Our approach consists of a boundary-aware loss function that explicitly considers the boundary regions during training.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two public remote sensing imagery semantic segmentation benchmarks, and achieve state-of-the-art performance.
Our code and model weights are publicly available.

In this paper, we present an effective cloud detection and segmentation algorithm for satellite imagery based on a gradient-based approach.
Our algorithm utilizes the gradient information of the input image to detect and segment clouds, and is capable of handling both bright and dark clouds.
We apply our algorithm to the PERSIANN-CCS dataset, which consists of satellite images labeled with ground truth information, and evaluate its performance against the current state-of-the-art method.
Our results show that our algorithm significantly improves the cloud detection and segmentation performance, resulting in an F1-score of 0.8519 and a precision of 0.8279.


Our algorithm consists of three main steps: gradient computation, gradient-based filtering, and post-processing.
The gradient computation step calculates the gradient information of the input image, which is then used in the gradient-based filtering step to detect and segment clouds.

We present a method for the semantic segmentation of video sequences using convolutional LSTM networks.
Our approach employs a hybrid convolutional and recurrent architecture that models both appearance and motion dynamics over time.
We introduce a novel temporal max-pooling layer, which enables the network to selectively focus on the most relevant information while being invariant to input order.
Our method naturally handles variable-length inputs and is applicable to arbitrary video durations.
We evaluate our approach on the CamVid dataset and show that our model outperforms the state of the art in semantic video segmentation.

 
Our approach to semantic segmentation of video sequences is based on a hybrid convolutional and recurrent architecture that models both appearance and motion dynamics over time.

Recent advances in deep learning have achieved remarkable performance in medical image segmentation.
However, these models usually demand a large amount of labeled data for superior performance, which is difficult to obtain in the medical field.
To overcome this challenge, we propose a novel multi-scale self-guided attention (MSA) module to enhance the performance of medical image segmentation models.
Our approach combines a multi-scale attention module and a self-guided attention module to capture the global and local features respectively.
The multi-scale attention module can capture the global context by aggregating the features at multiple scales, while the self-guided attention module can focus on the important regions by learning a weighting function.
We evaluate our approach on three public medical image segmentation benchmarks, and our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.

RatLesNetv2 is a fully-convolutional network for segmenting rat brain lesions in MRI scans.
It employs an Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling module to capture multi-scale context and a weighted loss function to address class imbalance.
The network was trained on a large dataset of over 4000 images from 94 rats and evaluated on a separate test set.
Compared to the previously published RatLesNet, RatLesNetv2 achieved higher accuracy and improved reproducibility.
Further, RatLesNetv2 defines a new state-of-the-art for rodent brain lesion segmentation, outperforming other methods in terms of both F1-score and recall.
The network is implemented using the PyTorch deep learning framework and is available at https://github.com/RatLesNet/RatLesNet.

Recent progress in medical image segmentation has largely been achieved by pre-training large models on large-scale, open-domain datasets, and then fine-tuning on in-domain data.
However, fine-tuning tends to cause model capacity reduction and suffers from the lack of available in-domain training data.
In this paper, we attempt to address both issues.
We propose a Margin Preserving Self-paced Contrastive Learning (MPSCL) framework for unsupervised domain adaptation of medical image segmentation.
Specifically, we use a margin-preserving learning scheme to alleviate the capacity reduction of the fine-tuning process, and a self-paced learning strategy, which allows the model to select the most informative data samples for adaptation, to address the data scarcity problem.
We apply the proposed method to adapt a pre-trained model from abdominal CT to abdominal MRI segmentation with promising results.

We introduce a technique for class-independent full image segmentation, using a convolutional neural network.
Our method is driven by a novel architecture, termed attention-within-segment, that is trained in an end-to-end manner on pixel-level ground truth data.
In a single forward pass, our network outputs a segmentation mask for the entire image.
A key distinction of our approach is that each pixel in the segmentation mask is assigned a "hard" segmentation class (e.g., object or background) or a "soft" attention weight, with the latter indicating the likelihood that a pixel belongs to a particular object.
During inference, the soft attention weights are thresholded using a heuristic method based on a statistical test to obtain a final segmentation.
To handle class-imbalanced datasets, we propose an extension of the attention-within-segment architecture that incorporates a loss-balancing term in the objective function.

In this paper, we present an approach for the segmentation of microscopy data for the purpose of identifying and locating nuclei in breast tissue images.
We utilize a combination of techniques including image enhancement, thresholding, and morphological operations as preprocessing steps, with the primary segmentation approach utilizing a variant of the watershed transform.
The watershed transform, initialized using gradient vector flow, is applied to the enhanced image, and then refined using a gradient-based approach.
The resulting segmentation is evaluated using both manual and automated measures.
The automated measure utilizes a graph cut based approach to evaluate the segmentation in a similar manner to the ground truth annotation.
Results of the segmentation are presented, as are comparisons to other approaches.

Abstract: Cloud computing is a emerging technology that offers an array of advantages such as cost efficiency, scalability, and accessibility.
However, it also raises security concerns, especially in the area of file management.
This paper surveys the security issues in file management in cloud computing environment.
It discusses the different security threats and vulnerabilities that exist in cloud computing and how they can impact file management.
It also explores the various security measures and solutions that can be employed to mitigate these risks.
The survey includes a comprehensive analysis of the existing research and literature on the subject.

Recent works on semantic segmentation largely focus on designing models with better expressive power to leverage abundant annotated image data for training.
However, these models are known to be susceptible to the inherent ambiguity of pixel-level annotations, and their complexity can make them difficult to optimize.
In this paper, we take a different approach and treat energy learning as a combinatorial problem, where the goal is to design an energy function that can effectively encode segmentations for a specific task.
Our key observation is that when the energy function is a composition of simple parts, the search for a good segmentation can be formulated as a combinatorial optimization problem, for which efficient algorithms exist.
To learn a good composition of parts, we propose a novel framework called Combinatorial Energy Learning (CEL).
Given a database of image segmentations, CEL learns a segmentation energy function as a weighted composition of a set of predefined atomic energies, where the weights are optimized via combinatorial optimization.

Recent developments in MRI acquisition enable the acquisition of multiple contrasts confounding the manual delineation of the thalamus.
We propose a method to segment the thalamus in MRI volumes acquired with diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and magnetization transfer (MT) weighted imaging.
Our approach is based on a multi-atlas segmentation framework leveraging the structural and the functional information available in those two contrasts.
We used 50 manually annotated atlases built from synthetic brains generated with Diffusion Toolkit (DITK), and two atlases built from real MRI datasets to obtain an initial segmentation of the thalamus.
Then, to combine the information provided by the atlases, we defined a cost function that quantifies the disagreement between the predicted segmentations and the ground truth labels in the atlases.
We used a greedy algorithm to obtain the final segmentation where the cost is minimized.

The Third Gravitational Lensing Accuracy Testing (GREAT3) Challenge Handbook summarizes the ongoing work of the GREAT3 collaboration, which is performing a rigorous test of gravitational lensing as a tool for astrophysical measurement.
The collaboration compares measurements of the same gravitational lens made by many different research groups, to evaluate the systematics and uncertainties in the measurements.
This comparison is done in a blind fashion, so that evaluators do not know which group took which measurement when performing the comparison.
This challenge has run twice before, in 2004 and 2009, and has spurred significant improvements in lensing measurement techniques.
We present the protocols for the third challenge, as well as an overview of the current state of the field.
A summary of the current state of the challenge is also provided.

Recent progress in semantic segmentation largely relies on large-scale training data with ground truth segmentations.
Creating pixel-level annotations for a large number of images is expensive and requires expert knowledge.
As a consequence, only a limited number of images is annotated, leading to an imbalance in training data: most images have no direct pixel-level annotations.
In this paper, we study the problem of identifying reliable segmentations from a large number of noisy and incomplete annotators.
We present a new method to identify the most reliable annotators for a given image and use their annotations to improve the performance of a segmentation model.
We propose a new differentiable scoring function that is optimized end-to-end with a segmentation model.

We develop a stochastic Eulerian-Lagrangian method for simulating fluid-structure interactions with thermal fluctuations.
The fluid domain is discretized on a fixed Eulerian grid, while the structure is modeled as a set of discrete Lagrangian particles.
The fluid flow is governed by the stochastic Navier-Stokes equations, which are solved using a stochastic finite element method.
The solid particles are treated as tracers in the fluid domain and are updated using a Lagrangian scheme.
The interaction between the fluid and the structure is achieved through a no-slip boundary condition on the surface of the particles and a drag force that acts on the particles due to the fluid flow.
The thermal fluctuations are introduced through a stochastic heat flux in the wall region of the fluid domain.

We introduce the notion of certified self-stabilization, where the assurance that a distributed system is stabilizing is formalized and proven correct using the Coq system.
As a case study, we provide a certified self-stabilizing implementation of the popular dining philosophers protocol.
The key technical challenges in the development of a framework for certified self-stabilization involve formalizing the notion of a stabilizing system and proving relevant theorems, e.g., if a system satisfies certain properties, then it is stabilizing.
Since stability is a temporal concept, modeling and proving stability properties, in general, require techniques for reasoning about infinite state spaces.
To overcome this difficulty, the framework formalizes stability using only finite-state models, by expressing stability in terms of a finite-state abstraction.
The key components of the abstraction are (1) an asynchronous finite-state machine (AFSM) that captures the finite-state behavior of the system, and (2) a finite-state overlay that captures the infinite-state behavior of the system in a compact way.

We introduce a simple and effective image segmentation approach called Super-BPD (Super Boundary-to-Pixel Direction), which achieves fast and almost linear runtime.
Given an image, our method first estimates pixel-level labels by a super-resolution network, and then predicts boundary-to-pixel direction (BPD) fields from the estimated labels.
The BPD fields are formulated as a sparse coding problem, which can be efficiently solved by modern optimization methods.
During the segmentation, we only need to perform a few iterations (less than 10) to achieve the results with promising quality.
Our approach is trained in a self-supervised manner, and able to run at almost linear speed, thus it is suitable for large-scale images.
In the experiment, we test our method on two public available datasets, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach against other state-of-the-art segmentation approaches.

We develop a non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) radiative transfer code for calculating spectral line formation in cool stars.
The code consists of an improved version of the 1D LTE stellar spectral synthesis code of Werner
[CITE] for calculating the level populations of 24 chemical elements, and a newly developed LTE-to-NLTE spectral synthesis code that calculates the NLTE spectral line profiles based on the level population obtained from the stellar spectral synthesis code.
We have calculated the NLTE spectral line profiles for several elements in the wavelength range between 1000 Å and 1 μm, and found that the NLTE effects can be very important, especially for the weak lines.
The abundance derived from the weak lines can be different from the LTE abundance by 0.5 dex or more.
We have also found that the derived abundance of some elements, such as Ca, Cr, Mn, and Ni, depends on the choice of the model atmosphere, and the line lists used in the calculations.

We present a method for automated segmentation of retinal layers from optical coherence tomography (OCT) images using geodesic distance.
OCT images are acquired using an optical coherence tomography system, and the retinal layers are segmented using a graph-based segmentation algorithm.
The graph is constructed by computing the geodesic distance between a set of seed points and the OCT image data.
The geodesic distance is computed using a fast marching algorithm, which iteratively updates the distance from the seed points to the OCT image data.
The resulting graph represents the connectivity between the seed points and the OCT image data, and can be used to segment the retinal layers.
The performance of the algorithm was evaluated on a dataset of OCT images, and the results show that the algorithm is able to accurately segment the retinal layers.

We perform the first systematic study of the oscillations in solar jets observed with the Solar Optical Telescope (SOT) of the Hinode mission.
We have identified oscillating structures in 26 jets during 2007-2009, mainly in the chromosphere, but also in the transition region and in the corona.
These oscillations are likely to be driven by the reconnection process in coronal loops.
We have characterized the oscillations using time-distance diagrams, and measured the proper motions of several hundreds of oscillating points.
These measurements allow us to investigate, for the first time, the spatial dependence of the oscillation period in a jet, with the period increasing with height.
We have also found that the oscillations are likely to be radially propagating away from the jet axis with a propagation speed of about 20 km/s in the chromosphere, and 40 km/s in the transition region.

Recent work has shown that the human brain uses probabilistic body schema representations to plan and execute reaching movements in everyday life.
These internal representations are inferred from incoming sensory information and guide the online selection of the most probable limb pose.
Here we investigate the role of tactile feedback in the online estimation of body schema during aiming movements of the arm.
In a virtual reality experiment, participants executed random reaching movements towards target locations with their right arm, while their left arm was immobilized.
During the movements, we abruptly switched off the visual feedback and the participants had to rely on somatosensory feedback for continuing the movement.
We find that the robustness of continuation after the visual interruption increases with the number of reached targets during the movement, indicating a learning effect.

Abstract
This paper presents an automated pavement crack segmentation approach using a U-Net-based convolutional neural network (CNN).
The U-Net architecture, developed for biomedical image processing, is adapted to pavement crack image segmentation.
The proposed method consists of three steps: image acquisition, preprocessing, and crack segmentation using a U-Net-based CNN.
In the image acquisition step, pavement images are collected using a vehicle-mounted mobile device.
In the preprocessing step, the images are preprocessed to enhance the contrast and reduce noise.
In the segmentation step, the U-Net-based CNN is utilized to automatically segment the pavement cracks.

Semantic image segmentation has gained increasing attention, as it alleviates the manual effort required for pixel-level labeling by automatically assigning a class label to each pixel in an image.
Most existing works focus on accurately classifying pixels within the interior of objects, while the boundary pixels are often treated as a derivative of the interior pixels, resulting in suboptimal performance around object boundaries.
In this paper, we argue that the boundary regions carry significant information that can be exploited to improve the segmentation performance.
To this end, we propose a novel approach called Boundary-informed Classification (Boa), which explicitly models the boundary regions to capture the additional information.
Boa first detects boundary pixels using a simple yet effective boundary detector, and then utilizes a boundary-informed loss function to enhance the classification of boundary pixels during training.
In the inference stage, we develop an adaptive inference mechanism that can effectively utilize the boundary information for accurate segmentation.

Recent works have shown that training vision transformers (ViTs) with millions of parameters can outperform their convolutional neural network (CNN) counterparts on image classification tasks.
However, training ViTs still poses several challenges: models are sensitive to (1) the quality and amount of data, (2) the augmentation strategies, and (3) the regularization techniques.
In this work, we investigate how these components impact the performance and generalization of ViTs.
We find that training ViTs with higher quality data improves performance significantly, and larger models require more data to maintain performance.
We show that the right augmentation strategy can boost the performance of a ViT, particularly when the amount of data is not sufficient.
We further explore several regularization techniques and demonstrate their effectiveness in improving generalization.

Recent works have shown that Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) benefit 3D biomedical image segmentation, alleviating the shortcomings of conventional fully convolutional networks (FCNs).
Nonetheless, training end-to-end architectures that combine FCNs and RNNs is challenging due to the non-differentiability of slice-wise max pooling.
In this work, we propose a novel architecture that combines FCNs and RNNs, termed Recurrent Fully Convolutional Network (RFCN), which is trained end-to-end.
We overcome the non-differentiability issue by using a differentiable pooling technique.
We assess the proposed architecture on the challenging task of myocardial segmentation in cardiac MR images.
Our method achieves a competitive performance in comparison to state-of-the-art methods, without any pre-processing steps such as initializing the network with a pre-trained FCN.

Existing techniques for checking safety properties of timed systems often reduce the analysis of timed automata to untimed automata, which discard the information about timing constraints in the original system model.
This can result in losing the timing information in the final verification results.
We present a new technique for checking safety properties of timed systems using timed tree automata.
Our technique explicitly takes into account the timing information in the system model, and provides a fine-grained analysis that reveals the timing behavior of the system.
We have implemented our technique in the Timed Tree Automata Checker, which is available as open-source software.

Traditional fuzzy C-means (FCM) clustering algorithms suffer from the occurrence of local minima in iterative optimization of the objective function during the clustering process.
We propose a kernelized weighted SUSAN based FCM clustering algorithm to segment images affected by Gaussian noise.
Noisy images degrade the quality of feature vectors for traditional FCM algorithms that are extracted from the original images.
In the proposed algorithm, a kernelization technique is employed during the feature extraction to mitigate the effects of noise.
Then, to further improve the quality of feature vectors, a weighted strategy is introduced where the weights are determined by using the SUSAN (symmetric unambiguous structures and anomalies) test.
The SUSAN based weights can effectively reduce the influence of outliers in the feature vectors.

Semantic segmentation of high-resolution satellite imagery is a fundamental task for extracting useful information.
However, the severe variation of scales in the same scene poses a great challenge for pixel-level labeling.
In this paper, we propose a new approach for semantic segmentation of high-resolution satellite imagery, named PP-LinkNet.
It leverages a multi-stage training strategy to learn the hierarchical representations of pixels, which can effectively capture both local and global characteristics of the data.
Specifically, a pyramid pooling module is proposed to encode multi-scale contextual information, and a link-net module is designed to capture the global relationships between pixels.
The whole network is trained in an end-to-end manner, allowing effective gradient flow through the pyramid and link structures.

Recent progress in interactive segmentation has primarily focused on extracting object boundaries accurately rather than the entire object region.
While boundary-based methods can achieve better performance, they often require a time-consuming initial segmentation step to generate the boundary predictions.
Moreover, interactions for these methods become complicated as they involve modifying the boundary rather than the entire object region.
In this paper, we present EdgeFlow, a framework for achieving practical interactive segmentation with edge-guided flow.
It leverages a boundary-based approach but removes the initial segmentation step, making the interaction process as intuitive as the recent region-based methods.
Specifically, given a preliminary segmentation result, EdgeFlow directly optimizes the segmentation by introducing a novel edge-guided flow, which can effectively propagate the user's modifications to the entire object region while maintaining the boundary details.

We present LooseCut, a novel interactive segmentation method that leverages loosely bounded boxes for initializing and refining segmentation results.
Our method improves upon the state-of-the-art in two ways.
First, we propose a new relaxed bounding box formulation, which affords a larger margin for error in the initial bounding box placement while preserving the ability to capture the object of interest.
Second, we propose an iterative refinement process that utilizes geometric constraints to reduce the prediction error, allowing for improved segmentation results.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the VOC 2012 segmentation benchmark while being faster than all other interactive methods.
In addition, through an user study, we show that our method is preferred by users compared to the baseline and other interactive methods in terms of speed and usability.

We address the problem of modeling physical forces in active contours for image segmentation, using a locally-varying curvature approximation.
This model can simulate a priori unknown forces, derived from the image itself, which drive the active contour toward a segmentation.
The energy of the proposed active contour model is minimized by a fast marching method, which iteratively updates the contour.
This approach yields a fast and efficient algorithm, which is very competitive, in terms of computational speed, with traditional active contour models based on gradient descent.
In addition, a priori knowledge about the forces, such as upper and lower bounds, further accelerates the algorithm and leads to a parameter-free method.
The proposed method is applied to several images, and very promising results are obtained.

The British university sector has been at the forefront of web development and delivery of online information and services from the early days of the World Wide Web.
The aim of the project described in this paper is to map the UK webspace by automatically analysing the contents of the websites of UK universities, in order to identify trends over time, and to provide a definitive record of the development of web provision and online services within UK Higher Education.
In this paper we describe the initial findings from an analysis of the web spaces of UK universities over a period of three years, from 2004 to 2006.
The analysis reveals a rapid growth in the size of web spaces, increasing from around 520 million pages in 2004 to over 1.1 billion pages in 2006.
Over the same period the level of accessible content increased significantly, from around 820 million pages in 2004 to over 970 million pages in 2006.
The number of websites hosted also increased substantially, from around 26,000 in 2004 to over 41,000 in 2006.

Introduction— Wikipedia is a multilingual online encyclopedia with editions maintained by registered volunteers, known as editors.
It has become a popular resource for obtaining information, and its articles are widely used in search engines.
However, the quality of articles varies widely, and the accuracy of information is variable.
Users can modify articles directly, and it is estimated that there are more than 100,000 active contributors to Wikipedia.
Editing of articles is generally collaborative and conversational, with editors expressing opinions and discussing changes.

We present an efficient graph cuts based technique for segmenting kidneys in ultrasound (US) images.
Graph cuts methods have been widely used in image processing and computer vision for image segmentation.
However, most existing methods rely on the initial segmentation results to obtain the final segmentation.
In this work, we develop an adaptive graph cuts technique that can simultaneously consider the global and local features of the kidneys in US images.
It can be used for the initial segmentation or as a stand-alone technique.
Furthermore, we integrate multiple feature maps, including edge, regional, and texture information, into the graph cuts framework to achieve more accurate segmentation results.

Current state-of-the-art self-supervised semantic segmentation methods achieve impressive performance, but they rely on large amounts of manually designed architectural components and their hyperparameters.
In this paper, we approach the problem of self-supervised semantic segmentation from a different angle.
We propose a mix-and-match approach where we assemble a semantic segmentation network by combining off-the-shelf components from a large repository of pre-trained models, specifically tailoring our approach to the self-supervised setting.
To this end, we introduce a new training regime for self-supervised segmentation, where we replace the normalisation layers of the segmentation network with random normalisation layers.
This removes the need for manual tuning of many components, as well as allowing us to use segmentation networks as a black-box that is trained without accessing the internal representations.
We evaluate our approach on ACDC and Cityscapes and show that our approach is able to achieve results that are competitive with the state-of-the-art, while requiring less manual design effort.

Vessel-CAPTCHA: An Efficient Learning Framework for Vessel Annotation and Segmentation.
In this paper, we present a learning framework, namely Vessel-CAPTCHA, for the fully automatic vessel annotation and segmentation in 3D rotational angiography (3DRA) sequences.
Unlike most existing methods which rely on handcrafted features, our approach learns a deep neural network to extract features directly from the raw input images.
The network is composed of several convolutional layers with pooling operations, followed by fully connected layers for classification.
To cope with the scarcity of annotated training samples, we adopt a bootstrapping strategy to train the network in an unsupervised manner, which is named as Vessel-CAPTCHA.
In this approach, a vesselness measure is learned to select the regions of interest (ROIs) that are likely to be vessels, and these ROIs are then used to train a second network for the final vessel segmentation.

In this paper, we present a novel method for left ventricle segmentation in cardiac MR images using a fully convolutional network.
Our network is designed to take advantage of the hierarchical structure of the cardiac MR images, and it is composed of multiple stages of convolutional layers.
We utilize a combination of atrous and regular convolutions to capture both local and global features in the images.
Furthermore, we introduce a new loss function that combines the Dice loss and the cross-entropy loss to optimize the network for accurate segmentation.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the MICCAI 2012 cardiac segmentation challenge dataset, and it is able to segment the left ventricle with an accuracy of 97.6%.

Color image segmentation is the process of partitioning an image into multiple segments, each of which corresponds to a set of pixels sharing a common property.
It has numerous applications in various fields of science and engineering including image processing, computer vision, and pattern recognition.
Image enhancement, on the other hand, refers to the process of improving the quality of an image by increasing its contrast, brightness, or other visual properties.
In this paper, we provide a comprehensive study on the importance of image enhancement techniques in color image segmentation.
We compare the performance of various image enhancement techniques, including histogram equalization, contrast stretching, and adaptive filtering, on a set of color images and evaluate their impact on the subsequent color image segmentation process.
Our results show that image enhancement techniques have a significant impact on the accuracy and efficiency of color image segmentation and can greatly improve the overall performance of the segmentation process.

We present a multi-layer approach to superpixel-based higher-order conditional random field (CRF) for semantic image segmentation.
In this approach, we first apply a simple yet effective superpixel segmentation method to extract a set of superpixels from the input image.
Then, we construct a higher-order CRF model based on the extracted superpixels, where each superpixel is treated as a variable node and the semantic labels of the superpixels are treated as the hidden variables.
The higher-order CRF model is learned in a supervised manner, where the semantic labels of the superpixels are predicted based on the appearance and the context information of the superpixels.
The proposed approach is evaluated on the semantic image segmentation benchmark datasets of PASCAL VOC 2012 and Cityscapes.
Experiment results show that the proposed approach achieves competitive performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

We present an algorithm for maximin affinity learning of image segmentation.
It is a hard assignment problem of learning a discrete labeling of a finite set of pixels given a finite set of labeled examples, with a penalty for labeling pixels differently from neighbors.
Our algorithm is based on a novel approximation of the maximin criterion that enables the use of a gradient descent procedure with a convergence guarantee.
We show that the algorithm is efficient in terms of both time and space, and we demonstrate its performance on a number of benchmark images.

Kernel spectral clustering (KSC) is a nonlinear dimension reduction technique and a general framework for clustering, pioneered by Davis et al. (2004).
It encompasses several other kernel-based methods, such as kernel PCA and kernel Fisher discriminant analysis (Kernel-FDD), as special cases.
This article provides a comprehensive introduction to KSC, covering the basic algorithm, theoretical properties, and practical tips for implementation.
We also discuss extensions of KSC, including kernel CCA and kernel MDS, and applications in text mining, image analysis, and bioinformatics.

Recent works in visual object recognition typically operate on fixed sets of predefined objects or entities of interest.
In this work, we introduce a new task of open-world entity segmentation, where the set of entities is not predefined but is rather determined by the data itself.
We present an approach for open-world entity segmentation that discovers entities in an unsupervised manner, followed by an iterative refinement process that learns to localize and segment them.
The unsupervised entity discovery is based on a variation of the non-parametric Dirichlet process, while the iterative refinement process is solved as a constrained optimization problem.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the task of instance-level segmentation of 40 different entity classes in the OpenWorld dataset, which contains over 100,000 images and requires zero-shot instance segmentation.
Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on this benchmark.

Semidefinite programs (SDPs) appear in various applications, but they are challenging to solve when the dimensions are high.
One reason for this is that SDPs require inverting matrices in order to compute the KKT conditions, and this operation can become computationally expensive when the dimension is large.
In this paper, we propose a new method for reducing the dimension of SDPs using Jordan algebras.
We show that the dimension of an SDP can be reduced via Jordan algebra techniques, and we provide a condition for when this reduction is possible.
We implement our method in MATLAB and compare its performance to existing dimension reduction techniques.
Our results show that our method can significantly improve the computational efficiency of SDPs, and it is particularly useful for problems with high dimensions.

We study a planar four-Fermi model in a tilted magnetic field using the functional renormalization group (FRG).
We find a chiral phase transition line in the plane of the tilt angle and the coupling constant of the four-Fermi term.
The chiral phase transition is of second order along the entire line.
There is a critical point at a tilt angle of 45$^{\circ}$, where the correlation length exponent $\nu$ changes its value from 1 to 2.
Along the line, the universality class is identical to that of the three-dimensional Ising model.


We also analyze the FRG equations for the tilted axial next-nearest-neighbor Ising model in order to understand the appearance of the Ising universality class in the four-Fermi model.

We propose a new definition of region homogeneity based on the concept of logarithmic image processing.
Our definition is motivated by the observation that the logarithm of a pixel intensity value is a more robust representation of the pixel value in the presence of noise and interference.
This leads to a new framework for image processing based on logarithmic image spaces.
We show that the problem of region homogeneity can be formulated as a optimization problem in this new framework.
We propose an algorithm to solve the optimization problem and show that the solution is a continuous function of the input image.

We study collective spontaneous emission from a system of quantum dots which are electrically controlled in a one-dimensional array.
The quantum dots are described by the multi-mode Hartree-Fock theory, including the quantum defect, and the array is embedded in a photonic crystal.
By calculating the emission spectrum and the electric field distribution, we show the existence of the hybrid light-matter states, which are formed by the strong coupling between the quantum dots and the photonic crystal cavity.
The hybrid states show anti-crossing behavior with the uncoupled states of the quantum dots and the photonic crystal cavity.
By means of the renormalization group technique, we investigate the quantum phase transition between the normal and the superradiant phases, and determine the critical number of quantum dots for the transition.
The critical parameters are sensitive to both the quantum defects and the coupling between the dots and the photonic crystal.

We present a novel approach for ultra-high resolution image segmentation based on a locality-aware contextual correlation (LACC) model.
Our approach exploits the contextual information of the image via a correlation prior, which captures the dependence between pixels belonging to the same object.
To efficiently compute the correlation prior, we introduce a locality constraint that encourages similarity between pixels within a localized region.
The LACC model is learned in a fully unsupervised manner via a variant of the expectation-maximization algorithm that optimizes the trade-off between the correlation prior and the locality prior.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the semantic segmentation of very high resolution remote sensing images, where the fine spatial granularity of the objects poses a challenge for most existing techniques.
When compared to other state-of-the-art unsupervised segmentation methods, our approach achieves superior performance in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

We introduce a general method for evaluating transport properties of disordered systems using microscopic simulations.
This method is applicable to systems with both topological and thermal disorders, and it can be used to study a wide range of transport properties, including the conductivity, resistivity, and thermal conductivity.
We begin by constructing an effective Hamiltonian for the disordered system, which captures the essential features of the disorder.
This effective Hamiltonian is then used to calculate the quantum mechanical Green's function of the system, which in turn is used to compute the desired transport properties.
The key advantage of this method is that it enables the calculation of transport properties with far fewer simulations than conventional methods, making it feasible to study systems with a large number of degrees of freedom.


We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to a number of different systems, including a model for disordered metals and a system with both topological and thermal disorders.

Recent advances in deep learning have achieved significant performance improvements for medical image segmentation.
However, most of these approaches require large amounts of interactive labeling effort, which is expensive and time-consuming, and often impractical in clinical environments.
In this paper, we present MIDeepSeg, a semi-supervised segmentation approach that minimizes the amount of interactive labeling effort required for training.
Instead of using a fixed amount of labeled and unlabeled data, we iteratively add labeled data to the training set during training, which we call “minimally interactive” labeling.
Our approach uses a simple yet effective deep learning architecture, and can be used to segment unseen objects from medical images.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the task of brain tumor segmentation from T1-weighted MRI, and show that our approach achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art fully-supervised methods, while requiring significantly less labeling effort.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is currently the golden standard for thyroid nodule diagnosis.
Ultrasound (US) images are commonly used to guide the FNAC procedure.
In this paper, we present an automatic segmentation approach to assist the interpretation of US images of thyroid nodules.
The approach consists of preprocessing, region proposal generation, segmentation refinement, and classification.
In the preprocessing step, the image is denoised using non-local mean filtering and the specular reflection is removed via spherical harmonics.
Region proposals are generated by an adapted variant of the selective search algorithm.

We address the problem of automatic lung tumor contour annotation from 4D computed tomography (CT) scans, i.e., stacks of 3D CT volumes acquired over the treatment period.
Previously, we had developed a fully-automated algorithm based on a deformable model to track the tumor between volumes; however, it required 4 to 6 hours to run on a single patient.
In this paper, we revisit this problem with the goal to achieve real-time performance, i.e., under 30 minutes per patient.
Towards that end, we first identify the parts of the previous algorithm that accounted for the large run time.
We then develop strategies to speed up those parts.
In particular, we speed up the initialization of the deformable model by using an annotated reference scan; we speed up the deformation step by using a coarse-to-fine strategy that iteratively refines the contour; and we speed up the runtime by using all available volumes for the contour propagation, rather than just the two adjacent volumes.

We study the topology of surfaces for molecular Stark energy, alignment, and orientation generated by combined permanent and induced electric dipole interactions.
The topology of surfaces provides a geometric framework to understand the behavior of these interactions.
We find that the Stark energy surface is always homeomorphic to a sphere, but the alignment and orientation surfaces can have much more complex topologies.
In particular, we identify a class of molecules for which the orientation surface has the topology of a torus.
We also find that the alignment surface can have the topology of a sphere, a torus, or a Klein bottle, depending on the relative strengths of the permanent and induced dipole interactions.


Our results provide a new way to understand the behavior of molecular Stark energy, alignment, and orientation based on the topology of the corresponding surfaces.

We consider solitons in a globally coupled hard-core bosonic system, which is described by the Gross-Pitaevskii type equations with the repulsive delta interaction and a two-body attractive/repulsive potential.
There exist two different types of solitons in the system, the bright and dark solitons.
By using the variational method, some new results on these solitons are obtained.
It is shown that the attractive interaction always stabilizes the bright solitons, while the repulsive interaction always destabilizes the bright solitons.
The effect of the two-body potential on the solitons is discussed.
The dark solitons always exist in the system if the two-body potential is attractive enough, while they may disappear if the two-body potential is repulsive.

Efficient Smoothing of Dilated Convolutions for Image Segmentation.
In this paper, we improve the efficiency of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image segmentation tasks.
We observe that existing works either suffer from decreased performance due to the downsampling of multi-scale inputs or the increased computational cost for processing these inputs entirely, resulting in slow inference especially on architectures with many dilated convolutional layers.
To address these issues, we propose an efficient smoothing method for dilated convolutions, which is designed to reduce the computational cost of processing inputs with many dilation layers while maintaining the performance.
Our method works by adaptively adjusting the dilation rate of each layer based on the local structure of the input, allowing the network to concentrate on the most informative regions while suppressing the computational cost on less important areas.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on two public segmentation benchmarks, Cityscapes and CamVid, with state-of-the-art performance and improved efficiency.

Deep learning has recently become an important tool for the diagnosis and prognosis of various diseases.
We present a novel deep learning framework for the automated segmentation and function prediction of biventricular cardiac masses.
These masses result from either tumor growth or benign structural abnormalities and can be found in patients with primary cardiac tumors, metastases, or cardiomyopathies.
Our framework utilizes a fully convolutional neural network architecture combined with a 3D attention module to segment the masses from magnetic resonance (MR) images.
We then use the segmented masses to calculate a series of function metrics that have been shown to be predictive of adverse cardiac events.
We evaluated our method on 100 MR images and compared the results to those obtained with a support vector machine (SVM) and a fully automated mass segmentation (AMS) method.

Automated segmentation of the mandible from CT scans is a prerequisite for various clinical applications such as computerized tomography (CT) radiotherapy, diagnosis, and surgery.
However, this task is challenging due to the similarities in bone and soft tissue densities and the complications of anatomical variations.
In this paper, we present a robust and fully automated method for segmenting the mandible from CT scans.
Our method is based on a combination of hierarchical clustering and watershed segmentation.
The hierarchical clustering is used to obtain a initial segmentation, which is then refined by the watershed segmentation.
The proposed method was evaluated on 20 CT scans and the results show that our method is accurate and reliable.

Selection models with monotone weight functions in meta-analysis pose several interesting mathematical challenges, which become particularly acute when the selection process is sequential.
We investigate selection models that can be described by a weighted average, where the weights are non-increasing functions of the selection probability.
Such models occur in various applications, including systematic reviews in medicine, and have attractive theoretical features.
We characterize the selection probabilities and the expected summary effect in both the fixed-effort and the random-effort models.
In the fixed-effort model, we show that the selection probabilities converge to a limit distribution at the fastest possible rate, and that the expected summary effect is asymptotically normal.
In the random-effort model, we derive the limiting distribution of the expected summary effect, showing that it is asymptotically normal under weak conditions on the effort distribution.

In this paper, we present a light-weight encoder-decoder based network, CFPNet-M, for real-time segmentation of multimodal biomedical images.
CFPNet-M is designed to perform dynamic programming based pixel-wise labeling of images in multiple modalities via a shared encoder-decoder architecture.
In our design, the encoder extracts the semantic content of the input multimodal biomedical images, while the decoder performs pixel-wise labeling in a bottom-up manner.
To handle the variability in the input images, a confidence based fusion strategy is proposed at the decoder stage.
Specifically, we employ a confidence score to measure the reliability of the features from different modalities, and use it to guide the fusion process.
With the proposed approach, CFPNet-M enables effective refinement of the segmentation results, while maintaining real-time performance.

Abstract - Lung cancer is the most common cancer worldwide, and computerized tomography (CT) is increasingly used for lung cancer screening.
However, the current practice of manual analysis of CT images is tedious, time-consuming, and subjective.
In this paper, we present a fully automated framework for lung tumour detection, segmentation and analysis, which is designed to assist radiologists in clinical practice.
Our framework comprises a tumour detection module based on a deep learning architecture, a segmentation module based on a multi-atlas label fusion strategy, and an analysis module that evaluates the tumour volume, mean tumour diameter and tumour-free lung volume.
To evaluate the performance of our framework, we conducted a retrospective study on 252 CT scans from 222 patients, and the results show that our framework can achieve an accuracy of 92.3%, a sensitivity of 91.5% and a specificity of 93.2% for lung tumour detection, and an accuracy of 91.5% for lung tumour segmentation.


Furthermore, our framework can assist in clinical decision making, as it achieves an accuracy of 89.5% for tumour volume measurement, 86.9% for mean tumour diameter measurement, and 91.5% for tumour-free lung volume estimation.

We present a design for a scalable, compact, and cost-effective real-time quantum random number generator (QRNG) with robust entropy collection, hidden Markov model (HMM) postprocessing, and a simple user interface.
Our design consists of off-the-shelf hardware components and open-source software.
We discuss improvements made to the state-of-the-art HMM-based postprocessing technique to enhance robustness and discuss a simple technique to assess the entropy before postprocessing.
Our design performs well in terms of power consumption, speed, and quality of the generated random numbers when compared to existing designs.

We present a simple, practical optimisation of the measurement of relativistic distortions in large-scale structure, focusing on the thermal and kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ and kSZ) effects as observable in galaxy surveys.
We optimise the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for a given survey, finding that the SNR is optimised by splitting the survey area into many independent patches, and stacking the signal from patches that are seen at high angle to the line-of-sight to the cosmic microwave background (CMB).
This method - "stacking by angle" - reduces the noise from astrophysical contaminants and CMB anisotropies, while keeping the signal from the tSZ and kSZ effects coherent.
In narrow redshift bins, stacking by angle optimises the SNR even in patches as small as ∼5° (∼10⁶ galaxies).
However, in wide redshift bins where the survey is deeper, the SNR is optimised for patches with diameters of ∼30°-50° (∼10⁷-10⁸ galaxies).
We provide a simple form of the optimal survey mask for stacking by angle, and show that the optimal mask does not depend on the optional galaxy clustering measurement.

We find that deep neural networks trained to solve partial differential equations can develop robust and generalizable solutions when trained in a hierarchical fashion.
We present experiments on several models showing that this approach enables a fast and efficient computational paradigm to simulate high-dimensional fluid flows and solve the Laplace equation with minimal training data.
In contrast to recent work on learned numerical methods that focus on discretizing PDEs, our approach views the neural network as a generalized function approximation and the solution as an implicit function of the input coordinates and the parameters of the PDE.
We show that this approach is particularly beneficial for solving PDEs in high-dimensional domains where the manual design of an explicit discretization would be impractical.


Our results show that DNNs are capable of solving PDEs in complex geometries, and that solutions predicted by DNNs are of high quality and generalize well to new inputs.
In contrast to recent work on learned ODE solvers, we do not require any ad-hoc regularization methods and show that simple (and unstable) architectures are able to learn to solve PDEs.

In this paper, we present an efficient traversability analysis approach for autonomous terrain vehicles using stereo vision.
In order to perform real-time analysis of the terrain, we employ a stereo-based approach, where the terrain surface is reconstructed from the stereo pair using semi-global matching (SGM).
The reconstructed surface is then segmented into traversable and non-traversable regions using a normal-based segmentation algorithm.
To further improve the accuracy of the segmentation, we then analyze the superpixel surface of the reconstructed 3D terrain.
Finally, we employ a machine learning approach to train a classifier for the traversability analysis.
The experimental results, conducted on different datasets, show that our proposed approach can achieve accurate and efficient traversability analysis for autonomous terrain vehicles.

In this paper, we propose a linear framework for image segmentation and inpainting that involves a curvature penalty.
Our approach is based on the minimization of a functional that consists of an edge-stopping term, a region-size regularization term, and a curvature penalty term.
The edge-stopping term ensures that the solution remains close to the initial image, the region-size regularization term encourages the solution to have a prescribed number of regions, and the curvature penalty term helps to preserve the curvature of the initial image.
The resulting functional is minimized via a linear programming algorithm.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of image segmentation and inpainting problems, and show that our method produces results that are comparable to, or better than, state-of-the-art methods. 


Our approach offers several advantages over existing methods for image segmentation and inpainting.

Recent works have shown that neural architecture search (NAS) is feasible for medical image segmentation.
However, directly applying NAS to this problem can be very time-consuming, as the search space can easily reach millions of architectures.
In this work, we present a coarse-to-fine NAS (C2FNAS) approach that significantly reduces the search space, while maintaining promising performance.
Our approach consists of two stages: a coarse search that selects a subspace of architectures that are likely to generalize well, followed by a fine search that refines the architectures within the selected subspace.
The subspace is selected such that architectures within it can use a shared backbone while still allowing customization via a lateral connection.
We apply our approach to 3D medical image segmentation, and search for architectures that can utilize a shared 3D U-Net backbone for segmentation of multiple anatomical structures.

Recent advances in 4D MRI imaging have made it possible to longitudinally acquire whole-tumor MRI volumes as a 4D dataset, with each 4D-volume acquired over several minutes, for a given patient.
However, due to the limitation of computational resources, it is challenging to utilize the 4D dataset for tumor growth prediction, which requires modeling the complex spatio-temporal correlations and the varying growth rates across different patients.
In this paper, we propose a novel Spatio-Temporal Convolutional LSTM (STCL) model, which learns to predict tumor growth rates by utilizing both spatial and temporal information from the 4D longitudinal patient data.
We introduce a spatio-temporal convolutional layer, which performs 3D convolution on each slice of the 4D volume, and a stack of LSTM layers that model the temporal dependencies at each spatial location.
We optimize the entire STCL model using a stacked sparse-reward learning framework, which incorporates a sparse-reward structure to push the model towards learning the sparse representations of the highly varying growth rates.
Finally, we evaluate our method on a large dataset of 4D MRI longitudinal volumes from glioblastoma patients, and show that our method achieves significant performance improvement over the state-of-the-art.

Image segmentation serves as a fundamental computer vision task with numerous applications in object recognition, image editing, and robotics.
Although recent advances in deep learning have resulted in significant performance improvements in pixel-level image segmentation, directly predicting pixel-wise labels from images is challenging due to the infinite number of labels (i.e., pixels) in an image.
Additionally, for many real-world applications, predicting a pixel-wise label map is not sufficient.
Instead, more detailed and structured semantic descriptions of images, such as object bounding boxes, instance labels, or relationship annotations, are often needed.
In this survey, we provide a comprehensive overview of recent advances in pixel-level image segmentation as well as more advanced segmentation settings, including instance-level segmentation, object detection, and relationship cosegmentation.
We cover both bottom-up and top-down segmentation approaches, including methods based on deep learning, graph cuts, and conditional random fields.

Recent progress in deep learning enables numerous applications of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in medical image analysis, especially in image segmentation.
However, most of the existing methods treat image segmentation as a binary-wise or pixel-wise classification problem and thus segment the objects in a constant scale, which may cause the loss of object boundary information or lead to uneven segmentation results for objects with different sizes.
In this paper, we propose a 3D deep coarse-to-fine framework to achieve volumetric medical image segmentation, which can preserve the boundary information and handle objects with different sizes.
Within our framework, we first utilize a 3D CNN to extract multi-scale features and then adopt a conditional random field (CRF) to refine the segmentation results on each scale.
To effectively train the 3D CNN, we further propose a novel 3D adversarial example generation method, which can add diversity to the training samples and thus accelerate the training process.
The proposed method has been evaluated on the ISBI challenge 2016 and 2017 segmentation datasets and compared with other state-of-the-art methods.

We propose a neural network approach for optimizing stochastic processes that can be expressed as constrained optimization problems with a large number of dimensions.
The proposed method is motivated by optimal stopping problems, where the goal is to choose a stopping time for a given stochastic process that maximizes the expected cumulative rewards.
We introduce a deep neural network that learns a ranking of the response surfaces over the decision space, without relying on the explicit form of the reward function.
We show that the proposed approach can effectively optimize a wide class of reward functions, including possibly non-differentiable and non-convex functions.
We demonstrate the performance of our method on a synthetic problem and two optimal stopping problems: maximizing the expected lifetime of a stochastic process and maximizing the expected cumulative rewards in a sequential classification problem.
Our results show that the proposed method can effectively optimize these problems and improve the state-of-the-art.

We present a new evaluation criterion for cell membrane segmentation of atomic force microscopy (AFM) images based on human perception.
We show that the widely used criterion measuring the difference between the ground truth and the predicted membrane mask has the drawback of being insensitive to certain types of errors that are readily noticeable to human observers.
To address this problem, we propose a new evaluation criterion that is inspired by the observation that perception-based errors are more significant than geometric measures when evaluating segmentation quality.
Specifically, we first extract a set of image features that are relevant to human perception of segmentation quality.
We then adopt an attention mechanism that, given a segmentation mask, automatically computes the importance of each pixel by aggregating the features over a small support region around each pixel.
The proposed criterion combines the attention weights and the geometric error between the predicted and ground truth masks.

Recent progresses in deep learning have achieved remarkable performance in specialized image segmentation tasks, yet their usage remains limited to the domain they are trained on, lacking the ability to generalize to unseen domains.
In this paper, we tackle the problem of segmenting medical images acquired from different domains (e.g., different institutions or different modalities) by designing a MixSearch framework that learns a universal segmentation architecture applicable to all domains.
Given a set of domains with limited labeled samples each, our approach first utilizes domain-specific pre-trained models as fixed initialized prior models to build domain-adaptive segmentation architectures, and then a meta-learning based approach is introduced to refine these prior models into domain-generalized segmentation architectures.
Specifically, we propose a novel progressive meta-learning framework, where a sequence of few-shot learners with increasing complexity are learned in an iterative manner.
Each few-shot learner is first fine-tuned with domain-specific data to adapt to individual domains and then further trained on the mixed dataset to learn domain-generalization.
We evaluate our method on segmenting lymph nodes from different institutions in the CAMELYON-train and -test datasets, as well as segmenting pulmonary nodules in CT images from two different institutions, and achieve state-of-the-art performance.

In this article, we continue the study of symmetries of nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) initiated in [AS2020].
The concept of symmetry is well-developed for linear ODEs, but much less so for nonlinear ones.
The main goal of this article is to provide a partial answer to the following question: given a nonlinear ODE, how can one determine if it displays a symmetry, and if so, what is the form of that symmetry?
As a case study, we consider the modified Emden equation, a classical model in astrophysics, geometry, and topology.
This equation possesses an infinite-dimensional group of symmetries, generated by four independent basic symmetries.
In this article, we determine all nonlinear differential equations that are symmetries of the modified Emden equation.

In this work, we develop a numerical method for radiative transfer in randomly textured slabs, which are uniformly coated with contaminant of known thickness and optical properties.
The method utilizes the scattered light technique, where the coated rough surface is replaced by an effective perfect diffuser.
This approach, when combined with the Monte Carlo method further enables us to model the radiative transfer in the contaminant layer and the substrate.
We present a numerical example to demonstrate the application of the method to calculate the reflectance of a rough silicon wafer coated with SiO2 of known thickness and refractive index.
We show that the coated rough surface exhibits higher reflectance than the bare substrate at near-normal incidence due to the multiple scattering in the rough surface and the additional reflections at the interface.
However, the reflectance decreases with increasing angle of incidence, and at some angle, the bare silicon becomes more reflective than the coated rough silicon.

We present a numerical example to demonstrate the application of the method to calculate the reflectance of a rough silicon wafer coated with SiO2 of known thickness and refractive index.
We show that the coated rough surface exhibits higher reflectance than the bare substrate at near-normal incidence due to the multiple scattering in the rough surface and the additional reflections at the interface.
However, the reflectance decreases with increasing angle of incidence, and at some angle, the bare silicon becomes more reflective than the coated rough silicon.

Reproducibility in data analysis is a growing concern in introductory statistics, as students are increasingly working with large datasets and complex models.
R Markdown is a powerful tool for creating reproducible data analyses, but it is underutilized in introductory statistics.
This paper describes a project that introduces R Markdown to undergraduate students in a statistical inquiry course.
In groups, the students replicated a data analysis of a case study, first using only Excel and Word, then using R Markdown.
The project was evaluated through interviews, surveys, and observations.
The results suggest that R Markdown helped the students to be more precise in their reporting, use correct statistical methods, and work collaboratively.

Recent semi-supervised instance segmentation methods mostly focus on modeling spectral or spatial relationships between pixels in different images through consistency and/or similarity learning.
These methods either treat all pixels within an object as a unit or assign labels independently at each pixel without considering their spatial coherence, which limits their ability to capture complex object structures.
In this paper, we propose a Mask-guided Sample Selection (MSS) approach for training a semi-supervised pixel-level classifier.
Given a pixel of interest, our method selects its class-consistent neighboring pixels as semantic contextual samples through a learned mask.
We pose the learning of the mask as a binary classification problem, where the mask is the decision boundary between the foreground (object) and background (rest of the image).
Specifically, given an initial guess of the mask, we minimize the cross-entropy loss by iteratively refining the mask through gradient descent.

We present a stable multiscale Petrov-Galerkin finite element method for high frequency acoustic scattering computation.
The method is based on the proper generalized decomposition (PGD) framework, where the scattering problem is decomposed into a coarse problem and a set of fine problems.
The coarse problem is solved using the standard finite element method, while the fine problems are solved using a spectral element method.
The multiscale error estimator is derived using the concept of the generalized eigenvalue problem.
The proposed method is evaluated on several numerical examples, including the scattering of a plane wave by a cylinder and the scattering of a Gaussian beam by a sphere.
The results show that the method is accurate and efficient for high frequency scattering computation.

We present a learning framework that utilizes abundant unlabeled data and limited labeled data for training robust CNN models in medical image analysis.
We particularly consider the problem of gastric tumor segmentation, in which the labeled data are often expensive to obtain since the expertise of experienced radiologists are required to manually annotate the regions of interest.
In this work, we establish a patch-based iterative learning framework, in which a patch-based CNN model is first trained to obtain initial predictions.
Then, a small number of patches with the most uncertain predictions are selected and labeled.
These labeled patches are then used to iteratively fine-tune the model.
Specifically, we implement a patch-based U-Net model for the gastric tumor segmentation.

Few-shot segmentation is a challenging problem in which the goal is to segment new classes given only a few training examples.
In this paper, we propose a self-guided learning approach with an adaptive similarity metric learning module to address this problem.
Specifically, we learn a similarity metric adapted to the few-shot segmentation by minimizing the divergence between the predicted and ground truth segmentations.
Furthermore, we explore the connection between the few-shot segmentation and the well-studied image segmentation problem with a large number of labeled images and show that the latter can provide valuable information for the former.
We propose a cross-guided learning approach to exploit the information from the well-studied problem and integrate it into the self-guided learning framework.
The proposed methods are evaluated on the popular Cityscapes and Mapillary Vistas datasets, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approaches.

We introduce a new approach to study distributions of finite and infinite entities in conserved systems, by using generalized entropies (using Havrda-Charvat-Tsallis entropy and Boltzmann-Shannon entropy as particular cases).
We apply these methods to both Gaussian and non-Gaussian distributions, and also to distributions which are not Chi-square.
Our results show that the approach can reveal subtle differences in the distributions of entities in conserved systems, even when these systems are in equilibrium. 


This new approach can be used to test the predictions of theories that attempt to explain the behavior of conserved systems, such as the Maximum Entropy Production (MEP) principle.
Additionally, this method can be used to study the behavior of conserved systems in non-equilibrium states, such as when external forces are applied to the system. 


Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the development of new methods for the study of distributions of entities in conserved systems, and highlight the advantages of our approach compared to existing methods.

In this paper, we propose a new polarimetric SAR image segmentation method based on 3D discrete wavelet transform (DWT) and Markov random field (MRF).
The proposed method extracts texture information from polarimetric SAR images in various scales using 3D DWT.
The MRF is then applied to model the spatial dependence of the segmented images.
The experimental results show that the proposed method achieves better segmentation performance in terms of accuracy and speed, compared to the state-of-the-art methods.
The proposed method is also validated on a polarimetric SAR image dataset from the literature.


Extraction of texture information from polarimetric SAR images is a crucial step for various applications such as object detection, classification, and change detection.

We present a new image segmentation algorithm that utilizes weak shape prior to achieve state-of-the-art performance.
Our approach combines the strengths of both the watershed transform and the level set method while avoiding their drawbacks.
Like the watershed transform, our algorithm segments images based on the locations of local maxima in the gradient magnitude of a smoothed image.
However, instead of using the gradient magnitude directly, we estimate it using a convolutional neural network (CNN).
By learning a mapping from the input image to a Gaussian scale space, the CNN is able to discover local maxima in an adaptive manner, without any parameter tuning.
Furthermore, we introduce a novel weak shape prior term into the energy functional of the level set method, which regularizes the segmentation boundaries to be smooth and coherent with the image structures.

We consider the drop policy of shared-memory switches, where multiple queues are stored in a single shared memory.
Each queue can be implemented as a linked list or as a skip list.
When a packet arrives, it can be added at the end of a linked list.
If the linked list becomes saturated, the drop decision can be made based on the packet's priority and the packet's head-of-line (HOL) blocking cost.
The HOL blocking cost can be the packet's finishing time, or it can be the packet's finishing time plus a fixed cost.
We analyze the competitive ratio of these drop policies.

We study the Regge trajectories of vector and axial-vector mesons in Holographic QCD.
The holographic model employed for this purpose is the 5-point function of SYM with gauge group U(N) in the presence of an infrared (IR) cutoff and a chemical potential.
The latter two are introduced in order to mimic the effects of a quark mass and a finite baryonic charge, respectively.
In the UV limit, when the IR cutoff goes to zero, the 5-point function reduces to the usual AdS soliton.
By simultaneously turning on the IR cutoff, the quark mass and the baryonic charge, we compute the masses of the vector and axial-vector mesons as functions of the IR cutoff, the quark mass and the baryonic charge.
The resulting Regge trajectories are linear, and the corresponding slopes are in agreement with the experimental data.

We present a method for creating predictive models of the housing market using image features.
We show that our model performs better than a baseline prediction model that does not use image features.
In particular, we find that nighttime images improve the performance of our model.
Our best model uses a sparse-coding vectorization of image features from a collection of houses, and spatial and temporal information about the houses.
We show that predictions made using image features are improving over time and that the improvements are consistent with a model that learns from the data.


Our results demonstrate that image features can be useful for predicting the housing market, and that more complex models that utilize additional data sources and features can perform better than simpler models.

Domain shift, caused by variations in acquisition protocols, affects the performance of medical image segmentation.
In this work, we aim to segment magnetic resonance images (MRI) of the prostate, which exhibit significant domain shift due to variations in resolution, field of view, and contrast enhancement.
We propose to leverage a pre-trained U-Net with a modified cost function that includes a domain adaptation (DA) term.
On a dataset of 320 MR images, our method achieves a 6.7 percentage point higher segmentation F1-score compared to U-Net without domain adaptation.
Through qualitative and quantitative analysis, we demonstrate that our method is especially effective in difficult cases that exhibit large domain shift.
Our analysis also shows that including the DA term in the cost function improves performance for U-Net layers at multiple levels of the network.

Skin cancer is a major public health problem in Australia, and its incidence rate is rapidly increasing worldwide.
Early detection of skin cancer is essential for successful treatment.
However, the early detection of skin cancer mainly relies on the experience and intuition of specialist doctors, which leads to undesirable misdiagnosis or delay in treatment.
Thus, there is an urgent need for the development of computer-aided diagnosis systems to assist doctors in skin cancer diagnosis.
In this paper, we aim to develop a robust and automated skin cancer segmentation and classification method to assist in the early detection of skin cancer.
A deep learning-based approach is investigated, which utilizes a novel architecture named NABLA-N and Inception Recurrent Residual Convolutional Networks (IRRCN).

Medical segmentation is a fundamental task in medical imaging.
It refers to the process of partitioning an image into multiple segments, each corresponding to a different anatomical structure.
This paper presents a new perspective on medical segmentation by introducing a novel approach based on matting.
Matting is a technique commonly used in image processing to extract transparent objects from an image, and has been widely used in computer vision applications such as image editing and photo manipulation.
In this work, we propose to use a matting-based approach for medical segmentation, which we refer to as medical matting.
Our method leverages the inherent uncertainty of matting algorithms to handle the challenges associated with medical images, such as noise, artifacts, and partial occlusions.

We revisit graph construction for image segmentation.
Unlike most previous works that construct graphs based on fixed shapes or heuristics, we formulate the graph construction as a learning problem.
Given an image, we learn a graph on which the pixels are linked in a way that optimizes a cost function reflecting the similarity between pixels.
In particular, we define a new cost function that leverages the power of an external deep neural network (DNN) model for pixel similarity.
We show that our approach, which we term Dense Graph, achieves state-of-the-art performance in image segmentation.
To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to learn a graph structure for image segmentation.
