With the advent of anesthesia, surgery has become painless.
However, the underlying brain mechanisms supporting consciousness, which are perturbed by anesthesia, remain unclear.
Here, we aim to elucidate the spatiotemporal dynamics of brain networks supporting consciousness during the onset of anesthesia-induced loss of consciousness.
We applied a data-driven, hierarchical clustering approach to functional magnetic resonance imaging data obtained from healthy human volunteers, at the onset of unconsciousness induced by the intravenous administration of propofol.
We found that, as consciousness was lost, activity in the brain shifted from being organized by the known default mode and dorsal attention networks, to being organized by a novel unconscious network comprised of thalamus, brainstem, and dorsal cortex.
Furthermore, we found that the structure of brain networks at the onset of unconsciousness was related to the electroencephalographic latency of the participants, indicative of a relationship between the structure of brain networks and the neurophysiological measures of consciousness.

Abstract
Traditional image segmentation methods produce binary images, which
may not reflect the fuzzy regions in the original image.

Fuzzy segmentation methods can produce more accurate
segmentation results, but are often computationally expensive
and difficult to use.
In this paper, we present a new method
for fuzzy image segmentation that is both efficient and easy
to use.
Our method is based on a self-configuring fuzzy
segmentation algorithm that can evolve to produce a good
segmentation of the image.
The efficiency of the algorithm
comes from the fact that it only produces the necessary number
of segments, rather than segmenting the entire image.
The
ease of use of our method comes from the fact that it is a
fully automatic algorithm that does not require any user
interaction.

We introduce a new benchmark for weakly supervised medical image segmentation, which we call Segmentation of Synonyms (Segsyn).
Given a list of synonyms representing the labels for a given image, the goal is to produce a segmentation mask where each label is assigned to the regions containing the structure it denotes.
We show that while state-of-the-art medical image segmentation methods perform poorly on this benchmark, models pre-trained for natural image segmentation perform remarkably well.
We conduct an extensive study to identify and analyze the reasons behind these performance differences.
Finally, we propose a simple method to improve the performance of medical image segmentation models on Segsyn without access to any labeled medical data.
Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/BBillot/SegSyn.

Recent works in visual semantic segmentation have shown that the use of semantic segmentation as a teacher model helps virtual pilots learn to control in the real world.
In this paper, we argue that the use of virtual pilots i) limits the scalability of data collection, ii) limits the types of environments in which data can be collected, and iii) the policy learned with this approach is sub-optimal.
In contrast, we propose a framework where the teacher is trained directly in the real world.
Our framework performs convolutional neural network filtering of raw camera images and uses the output to train a policy in the real world.
We show that our method is able to learn a more robust policy end-to-end with only raw camera data and rudimentary sensing for state estimation.
We show that our method generalizes to unseen environments, and compare against state-of-the-art virtual-to-real methods on the semantic segmentation front.

A high-resolution, time-to-digital-converter-based (TDC-based) data acquisition board has been designed and built for the NA62 experiment at CERN.
It is equipped with three TDCs able to measure with picosecond resolution the arrival time of signals coming from the experimental apparatus.
The TDCs have been produced adopting a dedicated ASIC, featuring a 6 b resolution and a dead time of 3.3 ns.
The board is capable of acquiring eight analog signals with 12-bit resolution, digitizing them with a sampling frequency of either 40 or 80 MHz.
The board transmits the data through the PCI express bus to a commercial processor card where the data are stored and processed.
A software framework, based on the Linux OS and on the EPICS distributed control system, has been developed to control and read out the data from the TDC-based board.

Recent results on supervised learning with large datasets require an infeasible amount of human-labeled data.
To alleviate the labeling bottleneck, we propose DatasetGAN, a novel framework that leverages generative adversarial networks (GANs) to create labeled data efficiently.
It automatically identifies the underlying data distribution of the unlabeled data and synthesizes labeled data based on it, thereby converting unlabeled data into labeled data.
Compared to the conventional data co-training approach that uses GANs, DatasetGAN directly generates labeled data instead of unlabeled data, which is more efficient in terms of the data utilization.
We demonstrate the efficacy of DatasetGAN on four real-world datasets, in which it achieves up to 90% reduction in the labeled data requirement while maintaining the same accuracy.

In this paper, we present an effective 3D medical image segmentation method using elastic boundary projection.
Given a label image as input, our method estimates the gray level of the foreground object and then automatically detects the object boundary to separate it from the background.
Unlike the conventional techniques relying on accurate initialization, our method is capable of segmenting the object even when the initialization is far from the object boundary.
In particular, we estimate the gray level of the object using a robust weighted least square fitting between the observed image and the model image, where the weights are determined by the intensity similarity between the neighboring pixels.
Furthermore, the boundary of the object is detected by projecting the estimated gray level image onto the model boundary.
The proposed method has been evaluated on a number of 3D medical images obtained from real patients and it shows very promising results.

Recent progress in 2D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has led to state-of-the-art performance in many fields, including medical image segmentation.
However, directly applying 2D CNNs to 3D medical images is not efficient, as it requires voxel-wise predictions and extensive full-image connectivity, resulting in a large number of parameters and slow training.
In this paper, we explore the use of 2D CNNs with a spatio-temporal convolutional layer for efficient 3D medical image segmentation.
Our approach effectively reduces the number of parameters and improves training speed compared to fully 3D-convolutional networks.
We introduce a new architecture called the Thinned 3D Network (T3D), which comprises a 2D CNN with a spatio-temporal convolutional layer.
The T3D architecture significantly reduces the number of parameters and improves training speed compared to a fully 3D-convolutional network.

We present a simple yet effective method for semantic segmentation based on supervised learning of convolutional networks.
We train our networks using only image-level labels, which can be obtained easily through image annotation tools.
To deal with the lack of pixel-level labels, we introduce a novel supervision signal, called scribble-supervision, which uses image-level labels and human-provided scribbles on specific pixels as weakly-supervised information.
Our method performs favorably against the state-of-the-art in semantic segmentation, while requiring less labeled data and human effort.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the MIT-CBCL, PASCAL VOC 2012, and NYUDv2 datasets.
Code is available at https://github.com/bcj1012/ScribbleSup.

We introduce a new image segmentation framework called PointRend, which models image segmentation as a rendering problem, where the goal is to assign appropriate colors to the pixels of an input image based on the image's structure and existing object boundaries.
PointRend extends an existing approach called Semantic Softpooling, which uses a deep neural network to produce a soft segmentation label image that emphasizes regions with object boundaries.
These regions are then refined using a novel post-processing procedure involving a rendering step that assigns colors to pixels based on their proximity to object boundaries.
We show that the rendering step can be optimized end-to-end using a gradient descent algorithm that minimizes rendering energy.
This optimization procedure produces a segmentation that improves upon the input to the network and approaches the performance of a fully supervised energy-based method without requiring any ground truth segmentations at training time.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, obtaining state-of-the-art results.

Recent progress in clinical imaging, such as whole slide imaging and whole-body imaging, has resulted in a sharp increase in the size of pathological images, leading to large computational costs in training deep learning models.
To address this issue, we propose UCTransNet, a new model for clinical image segmentation that adopts the recently popular Transformer mechanism to enable effective skip connections.
Specifically, we decouple the channels in the skip connections from the spatial dimensions and then employ the attention mechanism to selectively aggregate the information.
This channel-wise transformer not only significantly reduces the computational cost but also helps the model to focus on important information, leading to improved performance.
We perform comprehensive experiments on four public whole slide image datasets, including two datasets with whole-slide images larger than 100 megapixels.
The results show that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance in all datasets with a significant reduction in computational requirements during training.

We consider the local quantum uncertainty (LQU) in two-qubit arbitrary pure states under the assumption of separability.
The LQU is shown to be extensively affected by the presence of the global phase factor associated with the two-qubit state.
For a given state, it is shown that the local quantum uncertainty is minimized when the global phase factor is equal to one.
We derive a simple explicit expression for the LQU of two-qubit states in terms of their entropy and a measure of non-separability.
Interestingly, this result generalizes to higher dimensions without any modification.
The case study of a two-qubit system helps reveal the underlying properties of LQU in high-dimensional systems.

Arrival time prediction of vehicles in traffic is an active research area, and several approaches have been suggested in the literature.
In this paper, we focus on the prediction of stop times of vehicles in traffic, which is a major component of the total travel time.
We suggest a novel hybrid method that integrates deep neural networks (DNNs) and random forests (RFs) to predict stop times.
DNNs can capture complex spatial-temporal relationships, but they are computationally expensive, whereas RFs are efficient, but they cannot capture complex relationships.
Our method first uses DNNs to extract spatial-temporal features from the traffic data, and then uses RFs to make predictions based on these features.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through extensive experiments on a real-world traffic dataset.

Recent works in dense image prediction typically exploit architectural arrangements at multiple scales to leverage multi-scale information and achieve better performance.
In this work, we perform an in-depth study and discover that the efficiency of multi-scale architectures varies significantly with different dense prediction tasks.
In particular, efficient architectures for natural image super-resolution (NI_SR) are not necessarily efficient for other tasks, and vice versa.
This inspires us to search for efficient multi-scale architectures for different dense prediction tasks.
We discover a few effective strategies for each specific task, including global information modulation, feature fusion, and spatial transformer networks.
Furthermore, we find that efficient architectures for dense prediction are typically composed of a small number of repeated modules with specific structures, which is different from the architectures designed for image classification.

We present a novel boundary-aware geometric encoding (BAGE) for efficient and effective semantic segmentation of point clouds.
BAGE utilizes a boundary-aware interpolation strategy to encode geometric information of point clouds into a continuous and dense feature space, where semantic segmentation can be performed.
Specifically, we design a boundary-aware weight function to emphasize the boundary points and grant more reliable predictions on object boundaries.
Furthermore, we propose a distance-weighted voting mechanism to refine the segmentation results and highlight the regions with complex shapes.
To evaluate the performance of BAGE, we conduct extensive experiments on the Semantic3D and S3DIS datasets, and the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in comparison to the state-of-the-art methods.
Our source code is available at https://github.com/AI4SEG/BAGE.

Abstract: With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, it has become possible to use big data and machine learning to identify and map vulnerable populations.
This paper explores the use of AI to map vulnerable populations in Chicago, Illinois.
We use a combination of demographic data, social vulnerability data, and AI to create a map of vulnerable populations in the city.
The map is then used to identify areas of the city that are most vulnerable to environmental and social stressors.
Our results show that the most vulnerable areas of the city are those with a high concentration of low-income and minority residents.
These areas are also the most susceptible to environmental and social stressors, such as air pollution and crime.

As distributed systems continue to grow in size and scale, ensuring consistency and correctness becomes increasingly challenging.
We present a new concurrency control protocol that provides consistency while allowing for high concurrency and low latency in distributed systems.
Our protocol is based on a new atomic commitment mechanism that is designed to work well with slow and unreliable networks.
We have implemented our protocol in a distributed database system and show that it can achieve high concurrency and low latency compared to traditional techniques.


In today's world, where distributed systems have become ubiquitous, it is more important than ever to ensure consistency and correctness.
Traditional concurrency control protocols, such as two-phase commit, are designed to provide consistency but can be limited in their ability to handle large-scale and high-latency distributed systems.

An Enhancement Neighborhood connected Segmentation (ENCS) is proposed for segmenting nuclei images.
It combines the advantages of existing algorithms such as Nuclear Density Based (NDB) technique, watershed transform and shortest path finding algorithms.
The proposed method consists of three steps.
Firstly, a thresholding technique based on Otsu's method is applied to the original image for obtaining an initial segmentation.
Secondly, the watershed transform is used to obtain the final segmentation.
Thirdly, the shortest path finding algorithm is applied on the watershed segmented image to obtain the final segmentation where the cells are connected according to their neighborhood.

We propose a deep neural network (DNN) for 3D surface segmentation based on contour tree hierarchy (CTH).
CTH is a data structure for 3D point cloud that encapsulates the hierarchical structure of contours, which can be used for efficient surface segmentation.
Our DNN takes a point cloud and outputs a segmentation of the surface, where each point is assigned a label indicating the surface region it belongs to.
The network is trained on a large dataset of synthetic point clouds with ground truth segmentation, and we evaluate the performance on a separate dataset of real-world point clouds with ground truth segmentation.
Our results show that the DNN can accurately segment the surface of various 3D objects, and the performance is significantly better than existing methods based on traditional machine learning and contour analysis.


Our method offers several advantages over existing approaches to 3D surface segmentation.

Biofilm is a causative factor for many oral diseases, and monitoring biofilm formation is crucial in understanding the disease progression.
The objective of this study was to develop a statistical modeling algorithm based on computer-aided tomography (CT) images for the quantification of dental biofilm.
Methods: In this cross-sectional study, we identified four regions of interest (ROIs) in each tooth of a subject and measured the mean Hounsfield unit (HU) values for each ROI.
The subject was then divided into four groups based on the presence of restorations.
A generalized linear model (GLM) was fitted between the HU values and the thickness of the biofilm.
The model was validated using an independent dataset.

We study the impact of sparsity in the dictionary on the sample complexity of online learning with kernels.
We consider the setting in which a fixed, known dictionary is used to encode the features, and the goal is to adapt an online classifier to a streaming dataset by selecting a small subset of dictionary elements.
This setting is motivated by applications such as recommender systems, where a sparse dictionary of user-item interactions is learned offline and used for online prediction.
We show that if the dictionary is sufficiently sparse, then an online classifier can achieve the same accuracy as its batch counterpart, while using only a fraction of the dictionary elements.
We also develop a practical algorithm that performs online selection of dictionary elements, and demonstrate its performance on a real-world dataset.
In particular, in experiments on a publicly available dataset from a real-world recommender system, we find that a sparse dictionary learned with the popular algorithm K-means++ provides substantial improvements over a dense dictionary in online prediction, while using only a fraction of the dictionary elements.

Let ${\mathcal}{A}$ be an arbitrary family of sets.
Sunflower-free sets are closely related to the notorious vector covering problem: Given a set $S$ of vectors, find the smallest subset of vectors that covers S.
This problem is known to be NP-hard, and it is believed that it is unlikely to have a polynomial-time solution.
In this paper, we present an upper bound on the size of a smallest sunflower-free set in terms of the size of the universe and the size of the ground set.
This bound shows that the size of a smallest sunflower-free set is essentially the same as the size of a smallest vector cover.
We also present a nearly matching lower bound.

Skin lesion segmentation is an important yet challenging task in medical image analysis.
We present an approach to handle inter-annotator agreement (IAA) for automated skin lesion segmentation.
Our approach is based on a fully-automated system that segments skin lesions in clinical images.
We use a deep learning architecture, called U-Net, to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the task.
To handle IAA, we propose to use a ensemble of segmentation models trained on different subsets of the available training data.
The proposed approach is evaluated on a large dataset of clinical images and compared to a single model trained on the full dataset.

We report on the timing jitter correction for a Ti:sapphire laser system operating at a 1 kHz repetition rate in the linear polarization regime.
The original timing jitter of the laser system is measured to be ≈ 190 fs rms using a home-built scanning Fourier transform spectrometer.
After the jitter correction, the rms timing jitter is significantly reduced to ≈ 18 fs, corresponding to ≈ 9° of stabilization of the polarization rotator.
This level of timing accuracy allows the simultaneous use of pump-probe experiments at different delay positions without the need for mechanical delay line adjustment.
Moreover, the femtosecond resolution allows the study of ultrafast phenomena such as carrier-envelope phase stabilization and four-wave mixing in nonlinear crystals.
The Ti:sapphire laser system is currently used as a pump laser for the Soft X-ray Laser (SXL) at the Free-Electron Laser (FEL) FACETS at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory.

Abstract: We present a fully-convolutional neural network (FCNN) architecture for joint segmentation of medical images: ACNN.
Architectures are described for the two major medical image types: scalar images (e.g., MRI) and vectorized images (e.g., CT).
For scalar images, an adaptive pooling module enables the network to handle images of different resolutions, while a multichannel input enables effective utilization of multi-contrast MRI scans.
For vectorized images, a hybrid FCNN architecture is proposed to handle both axial and coronal slices.
We evaluate ACNN on four public medical image segmentation benchmarks, ISBI 2011 Liver Tumor Segmentation, ISBI 2013 Pancreas Segmentation, MIAS 2016 Liver and Lung Segmentation, and 2018 Cardiac Tissue Segmentation, and achieve top performance on all datasets, significantly improving over the state-of-the-art.
In particular, on the MIAS 2016 Liver and Lung Segmentation dataset, our method achieves a high segmentation F1-score of 92.43%, significantly outperforming the next best method by 5.7%.

We show that a simple assumption on the quantum effective action, namely that it is bounded below, is a strong indication for the avoidance of singularities in Quantum Einstein Gravity.
This is in sharp contrast to classical general relativity, where non-trivial bounds on the effective action are not known to exist.
We discuss under which assumptions on the UV-completion of quantum gravity one may prove the avoidance of singularities and provide an example where the assumption of a lower bound on the effective action is not satisfied.
We also give a heuristic argument, based on the existence of a UV-completion containing only marginal operators, for the avoidance of singularities in Quantum Einstein Gravity.

 
classically, general relativity does not impose any restrictions on the existence of singularities nor on the behavior of the effective action.
Different scenarios for resolving the big bang singularity have been proposed within general relativity, but none of them can be considered satisfactory so far.

We present a novel framework for automatic prostate segmentation in ultrasound (US) images.
Our method is based on fine-grained recurrent neural networks (RNNs), which are designed to capture the complex anatomical structures and patterns in US images.
The proposed method consists of two main components: a coarse segmentation network and a fine-grained segmentation network.
The coarse segmentation network is based on a conventional RNN, while the fine-grained segmentation network is based on a long-short term memory (LSTM) RNN.
We evaluate our method on a large dataset of US images and compare it to other state-of-the-art methods.
Our results show that our method achieves competitive performance and is able to handle large variations in the appearance and shape of the prostate.

An original technique named tunable coupled-mode dispersion compensation is proposed and demonstrated in this work.
Unlike the conventional dispersion compensation techniques, this new method can intrinsically and simultaneously compensate the material and waveguide dispersion, which arises from the intrinsic nature of the proposed dispersion compensator.
The device is composed of a pair of essentially linear waveguides that are coupled by an adjustable air-gap.
By adjusting the air-gap, the coupled-mode dispersion of the proposed device can be tuned in a wide range.
The device is designed by using a dispersion-relation approach, and the basic operating principle is verified by employing a finite-difference time-domain simulation.
Furthermore, the proposed device is applied to on-chip resonant four-wave mixing, and an ultra-flat dispersion profile is obtained over a wide band.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach towards clustering based image segmentation.
Our approach is based on a new clustering algorithm that we call the Generalized Median Clustering (GMC).
The GMC is a variation of the K-Means clustering algorithm.
It is designed to work well with high-dimensional data such as images.
We evaluate the performance of our approach using a variety of images.

Recent progress in semantic segmentation largely relies on large-scale labeled datasets, which are usually expensive to collect and annotate.
As a result, most prior works focus on datasets where the objects of interest are represented in a fixed set of classes, limiting their applicability to unseen classes.
Furthermore, the choice of training and testing datasets often leads to biased and mismatched distributions between the source and target domains, adversely impacting the performance of segmentation models.
To address these issues, we propose a source-relaxed domain adaptation approach for image segmentation, which relaxes the requirement of having corresponding object classes between the source and target domains.
Our key insight is that, even in the absence of shared classes, it is still possible to exploit label correlations across different classes for domain adaptation.
Specifically, we leverage the label relationships (e.g., mutual exclusivity and inclusion relationships) among objects of different classes to align distributions between the source and target domains, leading to better generalization performance on unseen classes.

Recent progress in medical image segmentation has largely been driven by supervised learning, but the availability of labeled images remains a bottleneck.
In this work, we tackle the semi-supervised segmentation problem where only a sparse set of training images is labeled.
Our approach leverages unlabeled images to augment the training set and improve performance.
We propose a self-ensembling contrastive learning framework that maximizes the agreement between segmentations of the same patient while minimizing the disagreement between segmentations of different patients.
To effectively capture the underlying structure and achieve per-pixel segmentation, we aggregate predictions from multiple self-ensembled models.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three public abdominal CT datasets and achieve state-of-the-art performance.

We present a novel method to approximate the spatial probability of inclusion for a set of points inside partial contours.
It is well known that the inclusion probabilities inside full contours can be accurately computed using the Fourier Mellin transform (FMT), but this approach fails when the contour is partial.
In this paper we propose to extend the use of the FMT to partial contours by computing the inclusion probabilities in the Fourier domain across the contour, and then extending the resulting function throughout the entire image domain.
This is achieved by fitting a suitable function in the Fourier domain that satisfies the constraints of the problem across the contour and then extrapolating it in the spatial domain.
The proposed method is evaluated on two different datasets, and compared against state-of-the-art methods using four different evaluation metrics.
The experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.

We present algorithms for scheduling moldable tasks on homogeneous multiprocessors.
In many practical cases, the tasks arriving at a scheduler can be modified to increase their feasibility for the available resources.
We refer to such tasks as moldable.
We first present a polynomial-time algorithm that computes an online optimal schedule for moldable tasks under sum-completion-time (SCH) scheduling, which minimizes the makespan.
This algorithm is based on an optimal offline-algorithm that computes a schedule in which tasks are released at their release times.
We then consider the more practical scenario where the arrival times of tasks are given and the tasks may be modified only within a given preprocessing time.

We study the following basic question in geometric network design: in a given network topology how to distribute a given amount of traffic over routes such that the total length (or cost) of the routes is minimized?
We allow the topology to vary in order to find the best routes for the given amount of traffic.
This problem is known as the shortest path problem with given traffic, or in the literature as the traffic assignment problem.
We study this problem from a stochastic perspective.
We allow the network topology to be random, and we assume that the traffic per edge follows some known probability distribution.
The goal is then to find the optimal routes, i.e., the routes with minimum total length, on the average, or with some high probability.

We consider the problem of learning conditional random fields (CRFs) via the Bethe approximation.
Previous work has shown that the Bethe free energy has a simple expression in terms of marginals of the CRF, and that these marginals can be efficiently computed via the forward-backward algorithm.
However, computing the free energy still requires performing summations over the entire CRF, which can be computationally expensive.
In this paper, we propose an alternative expression for the Bethe free energy based on the concept of message passing, and show that it can be efficiently computed via the map decoding algorithm.
Our approach is based on the observation that the Bethe free energy can be viewed as the difference between the marginal likelihoods of two CRFs, one in which all variables are conditioned on, and one in which a subset of variables is conditioned on.
We show that the map decoding algorithm can be used to efficiently compute these marginal likelihoods, and that the difference between them corresponds to the Bethe free energy.

Abstract: We consider the setting of subspace learning where the data matrix has a sparse latent rank-one structure in an unknown subspace, which is contaminated by a small fraction of outliers and noise.
This setting is motivated by applications such as text classification, where instances are often sparse in feature space and prone to labeling errors.
In such situations, we show that spectral regulars for subspace learning, such as the nuclear norm heuristic (NNH) and its variants, are locally robust in the presence of outliers.
Specifically, we establish that when the data matrix has a sparse latent rank-one matrix in an unknown subspace, with outliers and noise lying in a union of subspaces, the NNH is robustly convex, i.e., its local optimizer is asymptotically rank-one, as the number of outliers and noise goes to zero.
We further show that our result can be attained by a simple reweighting scheme, where the data matrix is reweighted by the square root of its nuclear norm, and present an algorithm to approximate the reweighted matrix.

Recent results on semantic segmentation largely benefited from the use of large datasets and powerful models, such as Encoder-Decoder based models like U-Net or more recent object detection architecture adaptations.
However, acquiring a large amount of labeled data is expensive and time-consuming, especially when only a small amount of initial training data is available.
In this context, active learning appears to be a promising solution.
Nevertheless, most of the state-of-the-art active learning methods for semantic segmentation are based on point-based approaches, which require a dense annotation for each pixel, and often rely on heuristics that may not perform well in many cases.
In this paper, we present MetaBox+, a new region-based active learning approach for semantic segmentation.
MetaBox+ leverages an innovative priority map that is built from both a global and local perspective, and a novel sampling strategy that aims to minimize the risk of missing hard positive and negative examples.

Recent progress in sensor technology has enabled the collection of subdecimeter aerial images, with centimeters-level precision in pixel-level localization of trees.
However, the precise segmentation of trees in such images remains a challenge.
We present TreeSegNet, a deep learning based approach that is trained end-to-end to segment trees in subdecimeter aerial images.
TreeSegNet adapts Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to align with the tree structures by a tree-structure-aware loss function.
Furthermore, it incorporates geometry information in the learning process to improve performance.
We evaluate TreeSegNet on a large dataset of subdecimeter aerial images collected over several sites in the northeastern US.

We present a new numerical method for solving the spherical harmonics moment equations of radiative transfer in the Earth's atmosphere.
The new method, called StaRMAP (STAGgered Radiative Moments APproach), is a second-order accurate approximation of the exact radiative transfer equation.
It is based on a staggered grid arrangement of the spherical harmonics moments, which allows for an efficient and accurate solution of the radiative transfer equation.
We describe the basic idea of StaRMAP and present a set of test problems to evaluate the accuracy and performance of the new method.

Semantic image segmentation of urban street scenes is a fundamental step towards intelligent transportation systems.
In this paper, we present a real-time high-performance method for semantic image segmentation of urban street scenes.
Our method is based on a deep learning architecture called Convolutional Neural Network (CNN).
We use a pre-trained CNN model trained on the ImageNet dataset to extract features from the input images.
We then fine-tune the CNN model on a new dataset specifically designed for semantic image segmentation of urban street scenes.
Our method achieves accurate segmentation results and runs in real-time, making it suitable for applications such as autonomous driving and traffic monitoring.

Interactive image segmentation differs from automatic segmentation in that it allows the user to impose his or her prior knowledge on the segmentation process.
In many real-world applications, the user has specific prior knowledge about the regions of interest in the image and can provide initial segmentations.
Once an initial segmentation is provided, an interactive segmentation algorithm propagates this prior information in order to produce a final segmentation.
The success of the interactive segmentation algorithm depends on the accuracy of the initial segmentation and the robustness of the propagation process.
In this paper, we propose a new interactive image segmentation algorithm that combines advantages of gradient-based and texture-based approaches to segmentation.
In particular, we propagate user markings based on image gradients when the image regions have distinct gradients, and based on image texture when gradients are absent.

We present stellar population models based on APOGEE data for the innermost regions of 17 nearby S0 galaxies, aiming to quantify the impact of various environmental factors on the evolution of their central stars.
Combining the data with literature multiband photometry, we derive the stellar ages and abundances in the galaxies' bulges and inner disks.
We find that the central regions of S0 galaxies are generally dominated by old ( ≳ 10 Gyr) stars, albeit with significant internal variations, and that these galaxies typically lack young (≲ 1 Gyr) stars.
Comparing the stellar populations in the inner disks of S0s with those in the outer disks of spiral galaxies, we find that the onset of star formation in the outer disks typically occurs at a younger age and higher gas surface density.
This suggests that environmental factors play a crucial role in shutting down star formation in S0s, perhaps by accelerating the expulsion of gas from their inner regions.


Our results imply that the cessation of star formation in S0s occurs at an earlier time and higher gas surface density than predicted by simple cosmological simulations.

Comparing the stellar populations in the inner disks of S0s with those in the outer disks of spiral galaxies, we find that the onset of star formation in the outer disks typically occurs at a younger age and higher gas surface density.
This suggests that environmental factors play a crucial role in shutting down star formation in S0s, perhaps by accelerating the expulsion of gas from their inner regions.

The learning of image dehazing models is important for segmentation tasks.
A new method for learning dehazing models is proposed based on the observation that the haze-free image can be generated by two different processes: restoration and separation.
The proposed method learns a dehazing model by minimizing the difference between the predicted haze-free image and the ground truth image, where the ground truth image is obtained by combining the restoration and separation processes.
The proposed method has been tested on the haze-free image dataset of 100 images and the results show that the method can learn a dehazing model that can improve the performance of segmentation tasks.

We present a customizable architecture search method for semantic segmentation.
Unlike existing works which adopt an architecture search strategy specific to the design space, our approach allows the user to customize the search process with different strategies, including evolutionary algorithms (EAs) and reinforcement learning (RL).
To achieve this, we first formulate the architecture search as a meta learning problem, such that different search strategies can be used to optimize the same objective.
We then develop a meta trainer that learns a good policy network from a user specified search strategy in a few iterations.
With the policy network, the search strategy is then fine-tuned within a few more iterations to find the optimal architecture.
We show that our approach allows the user to not only customize the search process, but also achieve better performance compared to the state of the art methods on the Cityscapes dataset with MobileNetV2 as the backbone.

We report on spin-dependent transport through a silicon double quantum dot defined by epitaxial SiGe/Si heterostructures.
A clear signature of Pauli spin blockade is observed in a low-temperature magnetotransport measurement.
The spin blockade is attributed to the spin-dependent tunnel coupling between the quantum dots and the leads.
By tuning the gate voltages, the tunnel coupling can be controlled, which leads to tunable spin blockade.
The low-temperature behavior of the spin blockade is consistent with a model taking into account the spin-dependent tunnel coupling and the hyperfine interaction.
The results demonstrate the feasibility of using silicon quantum dots to manipulate the spin degree of freedom of electrons, showing promise for spin-based quantum technologies.

We consider the problem of detecting anomalies in a sequence of independent observations, where the anomalies are rare events and the observations are drawn from a known family of distributions.
We propose a sequential testing procedure that performs optimally in the limit as the sample size goes to infinity, with the cost metric being the total false alarm rate over the sample interval.
Our approach is motivated by the observation that the false alarm rate of any sequential testing procedure is proportional to the likelihood of the observations under the null hypothesis, and we seek to minimize this quantity by optimizing the test procedure over all possible sequences of observations.
We show that the optimal test procedure has a simple form, and we provide a closed-form expression for the optimal false alarm rate.
We also show that our approach is asymptotically optimal in the sense that the total false alarm rate of our procedure converges to zero as the sample size goes to infinity, and we provide a bound on the convergence rate.
Finally, we demonstrate the performance of our procedure on a simulated data set and compare it to existing sequential testing procedures.

We consider the problem of making a minimum number of moves to transform a given initial configuration of objects into a target configuration, where each move may involve flipping an edge between two objects (e.g., swapping the two objects).
This may model, for example, inserting a barrier between two objects in a network, or moving them closer together.
We seek a solution that minimizes an energy function that generalizes the submodular pairwise energies, and is defined using a symmetric and monotone set function that is not necessarily submodular.
This energy may model, for example, the total length of the edges involved in the moves.


We first present a polynomial-time algorithm that outputs an optimal solution when the energy function is submodular.
This algorithm extends a recent algorithm of Feige, Krause, Naor, and Ron for the special case in which the energy function is the sum of edge weights.

Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a sequentially compact space.
We study products $\mathbb{K}^{X}$, where $X$ is any set, with respect to the topology of pointwise convergence.
We show that if $X$ is at most countable, then $\mathbb{K}^{X}$ is compactly generated.
However, in general, $\mathbb{K}^{X}$ is not compactly generated.
On the other hand, we show that if $\mathbb{K}$ is a compactly generated compact space, then $\mathbb{K}^{X}$ is compactly generated for all sets $X$. 

We also consider the compactness with respect to a set of filters.
Let $\mathcal{F}$ be a family of filters in a Boolean algebra $\mathbb{B}$. We say that a subset $\mathbb{A}$ of $\mathbb{B}$ is $\mathcal{F}$-compact if for every filter $\mathcal{G}$ in $\mathbb{B}$ that contains $\mathbb{A}$, there exists $F \in \mathcal{F}$ such that $\mathcal{G} \supseteq F$.

Brain tumor segmentation is a fundamental step in clinical MRI analysis, and an accurate and automatic segmentation method is demanded.
In this paper, we propose a deep learning model integrating fully convolutional neural networks (FCNNs) and conditional random fields (CRFs) for brain tumor segmentation.
Our model is based on the U-Net architecture, which is a FCNN that uses skip connections to capture multi-scale contextual information.
We modify the U-Net architecture to incorporate CRFs, which model the spatial dependencies between pixels and provide global constraints on the segmentation.
The proposed model is trained on a large dataset of MRI scans and evaluated on the BraTS 2018 validation dataset, which contains a wide variety of tumor types and clinical modalities.
Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the BraTS 2018 validation dataset, with an F1-score of 0.9143 and an area under the ROC curve (AUC-ROC) of 0.9149.

We present hydrogen index (HI) measurements for a sample of blue compact dwarf (BCD) galaxies observed with the Green Bank Telescope (GBT).
These galaxies are among the most metal-deficient systems known and span a wide range in metallicity (-5.3 <
[Fe/H] < -1.7).
The BCDs, on average, follow the well-known correlation between HI content and metallicity observed in larger galaxies, despite their low masses and modified star formation histories.
This result demonstrates that the HI content-metallicity relationship is a fundamental one for galaxies independently of their mass and star formation history.
We also find that the scatter around the HI content-metallicity relationship is much larger among BCDs than in larger galaxies, increasing from 0.19 dex in galaxies >10^10^M_☉ to 0.3 dex in BCDs.

Recent results on salient object detection take a top-down approach, in which the model first detects the foreground and then refines it to obtain the final salient regions.
Most existing works focus on designing effective refinement modules to improve the quality of the predicted saliency maps.
In this work, we argue that a key problem of current top-down methods is the quality of the initial foreground map, which is usually obtained by thresholding or clamping the output of an encoder.
To address this problem, we propose a classifier-guided approach that refines the initial foreground map with a classifier.
Specifically, we train a support vector machine (SVM) classifier with image-level labels to predict whether a pixel is in the foreground or not.
Since the classifier is trained with image-level labels, it is able to exploit global information and capture the underlying object-like structures.

Deep learning has recently achieved great performance in image segmentation, but the mechanisms that lead to these results are not well understood.
In this paper, we investigate the utilization of a deep structured prediction model for fine image segmentation that inherently promotes complex relationships between labeled pixels.
We introduce a novel architecture that combines ideas from set propagation - allowing the model to reason about relationships between pixels - with an attention mechanism over object instances.
We show that our model discovers an interpretable hierarchy of object instances and pixel relationships, while achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes segmentation benchmark.
In a thorough empirical analysis, we uncover that (1) set relationships derived by the model correspond to meaningful object structures, (2) these relationships are crucial for segmentation performance, and (3) our model's attention over object instances is able to learn contextual object interactions.
Finally, we present an analysis of what limits the performance of our model on the Cityscapes dataset and discuss potential ways to overcome these limitations.

Recent progress in deep learning has led to significant advances in medical image segmentation.
However, fully automated segmentation algorithms still face challenges in dealing with anatomical variation, lesion appearance, and similar tissue structures.
While manual segmentation by domain experts is accurate and robust, it can be tedious, time-consuming, and suffers from intra- and inter-user variability.
There has been a growing interest in interactive segmentation techniques that seek to combine the strengths of both fully automated and manual segmentation methods.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach for interactive medical image segmentation that combines point-based interaction and sequential patch learning.
Our method enables the user to quickly highlight points on the image to define an initial segmentation boundary.

Quantum cryptography, in its original form of quantum key distribution (QKD), can provide two remote parties with a common secret key known only to them.
This key is then used as a one-time pad for encrypting messages.
QKD is information-theoretically secure against any attack, including those with quantum computers.
Unfortunately, it requires the establishment of a quantum channel between the two parties, which is not under active development for long-distance communication.
It has therefore been generally assumed that quantum cryptography is useful only for short-distance applications.
In this survey, we show that this assumption is incorrect.

Efficient piecewise training of deep structured models for semantic segmentation

Semantic segmentation is the task of assigning semantic labels to each pixel in an input image.
While deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable performance in this task, training such models is still a computationally expensive task, especially for large datasets and models.
In this paper, we present a method for training deep structured models for semantic segmentation that is more efficient than existing methods.
Our method is based on the idea of training the model in a piecewise fashion, where the model is trained on a subset of the data and then the trained model is used to predict the labels for the remaining data.
This allows us to train the model on a much smaller subset of the data, which reduces the computational cost of training.
Our experiments show that our method is able to achieve comparable performance to existing methods while reducing the computational cost of training by up to 50%.

Automated iris recognition has been successfully used in many applications, but it typically relies on live iris images taken under controlled conditions.
Post-mortem iris images, taken after death, present additional challenges that require new techniques for segmentation and recognition.
In this paper, we propose a data-driven approach for the segmentation of post-mortem iris images.
Our approach is based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) that has been trained on a large dataset of post-mortem iris images.
The CNN learns to predict pixel-level segmentation labels for each input image, resulting in a binary mask that highlights the iris region.
We evaluate our approach on a new publicly available dataset of post-mortem iris images and show that it achieves a high degree of accuracy compared to the state-of-the-art.

Recent advances in semantic segmentation of medical images have relied on large datasets collected from different domains, i.e., different hospitals or institutions.
However, directly applying models trained on one domain to another domain may result in poor performance due to the domain shift.
In this work, we aim to learn a domain adaptation model to improve the performance of semantic segmentation on target domains while preserving privacy of both the source and target domains.
We propose a two-stage adaptation method: (1) a global adaptation stage that learns a shared feature representation across all domains via a non-private dataset, and (2) a private adaptation stage that fine-tunes the shared feature representation with a domain-specific dataset without revealing the domain-specific data.
We implement the private adaptation stage using differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD), which adds noise to the gradients of the learning objective with respect to the model parameters.
The noise magnitude is carefully chosen to strike a balance between utility and privacy.

Arterial spin labeling (ASL) allows for non-invasive estimation of arterial blood flow without the need for contrast agents.
However, at lower arterial input pressures, the flow in the arteries is characterized by a transition from steady flow to unsteady flow, which manifests as a decorrelation of the ASL signal in space and/or time.
In this work, we derive a new generalized model for the flow-independent ASL signal, which we show captures the decorrelation due to unsteady flow.
The proposed model can be fit to ASL data in a least-squares sense, resulting in a spatial map of the effective input arterial blood flow, which we term the arterial input function (AIF).
We show via simulation that the AIF is capable of recovering the ground truth input flow in the presence of both spatially-varying and time-varying decorrelation.
We further validate our method on both simulated and in vivo ASL data.

A hybrid approach based segmentation technique in MRI images of brain tumor is proposed in this paper.
The proposed method shows that the combination of an anatomical and a probabilistic approach can produce accurate and reliable segmentations of brain tumor MRI images.
In our method, the MRI image is first preprocessed then, it is segmented by using the Anatomical network and finally, the probabilistic approach is used to obtain the final segmentation.
The proposed method is evaluated using MRI images of brain tumors and the results are compared with manual segmentation done by the experts.
The performance of the proposed method is evaluated in terms of the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC), sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy.
The proposed method achieves an average DSC of 0.91, sensitivity of 0.92, specificity of 0.87 and accuracy of 0.91.

Recent progresses in deep learning greatly advanced the performance of single-modal segmentation.
However, existing methods usually assume paired annotations, which are difficult to obtain, especially for medical images.
In this paper, we attempt to learn a universal multi-modal segmentation network with unpaired annotations via knowledge distillation.
Given a pair of domains A and B, we train a teacher network with ground truth annotations of domain A, and a student network with unpaired annotations of domain B.
We further introduce a domain classifier as the teacher to classify the domain of the input image.
The student network focuses on segmenting the object with the similar structure as the teacher network.

The student network focuses on segmenting the object with the similar structure as the teacher network.

Recent progress in semantic segmentation is primarily driven by two types of contextual information: image-level and semantic-level.
However, existing methods usually integrate the two types of contextual information separately on either feature level or decision level.
In this paper, we argue that the complementary information between image-level and semantic-level contexts could be further exploited by jointly integrating them into a unified framework.
Specifically, we develop a novel Integration of Semantic-level and Image-level Networks (ISNet), which integrates image-level and semantic-level contexts in a symmetric and cooperative way for semantic segmentation.
It not only effectively combines the advantages of both contexts but also provides an explicit integration mechanism to balance their contributions.
The proposed ISNet is simple to implement and can be conveniently embedded into any existing segmentation frameworks.

Recent progress in image co-segmentation has primarily focused on developing effective models for pairwise similarity learning.
However, most existing works assume that the similarity between image regions is independent of the image's context, which is not necessarily true in real applications.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to image co-segmentation via deep metric learning, which takes into account the contextual information of images.
Specifically, we propose to use a convolutional neural network (CNN) to learn a context-dependent distance metric between image regions.
The proposed metric takes pairs of regions and their corresponding images as input and learns to measure the similarity between the regions while considering the contextual information of the images.
To optimize the proposed metric, we develop a new co-segmentation loss function that encourages consistent and coherent segmentations across images.

We present a new model reduction technique for efficient simulation of flow in heterogeneous porous media, which accounts for both the nonlinearity of the flow and the heterogeneity of the medium.
Our method combines a global nonlinear model reduction technique, which captures the overall behavior of the flow, with a local model reduction technique, which captures the fine-scale behavior of the flow in each individual cell of the porous medium.
The global model reduction is based on a nonlinear singular value decomposition (SVD) of the flow equation, which identifies the most important modes of the flow and allows for the reduction of the flow problem to a small number of dimensions.
The local model reduction is based on a cell-specific approximation of the flow equation, which captures the fine-scale behavior of the flow in each individual cell of the porous medium.
The cell-specific approximation is constructed using a local nonlinear SVD of the flow equation, which identifies the most important modes of the flow within each cell.
The global-local model reduction technique is demonstrated on a variety of example flows in heterogeneous porous media, and it is shown to provide significant improvements in computational efficiency compared to conventional full-scale simulations, while maintaining accurate predictions of the flow behavior.

We present results from a direct numerical simulation of a turbulent channel flow at a Reynolds number $Re_\tau=5200$, based on the friction velocity and the channel half-height.
The DNS was performed in a domain with a span close to the ceiling and the floor and a periodic domain in the streamwise direction with no-slip boundary conditions.
The Prandtl number was set to $P_r=5$ and the simulations were carried out with a parallelized code based on the finite-volume method on a cubic grid with $512 \times 128 \times 64$ points, which resolves the channel half-height.
The velocity field was interpolated onto a finer grid with $1024 \times 256 \times 128$ points for the statistical analysis.
The production of turbulence kinetic energy and its dissipation were measured in the wall region and used to characterize the turbulence anisotropy and the formation of the buffer layer.
The friction factor and the Nusselt number were computed over a range of grid resolutions and compared to available empirical correlations.

We present a simple but effective approach to salient object detection, which is built upon a discriminative regional feature integration framework.
Unlike most existing works that treat saliency detection as a bottom-up process and accumulate evidence from low-level to high-level features, our approach works in a top-down manner, where the goal is to directly predict the final saliency map from the input image with the global context information carefully preserved.
In particular, we first generate a series of initial saliency maps at multiple abstraction levels by feature encoding modules.
Then, we introduce a regional feature integration module to selectively integrate the regional features across these abstraction levels in a top-down manner.
The regional features are aggregated such that the most discriminative ones are given higher weights, and that the global context information can be effectively preserved and propagated through the integration process.
In this way, our approach can effectively concentrate on the most salient objects and avoid the excessive response to non-salient regions.

Semantic image segmentation has achieved remarkable performance on various benchmarks,
driven by deep learning with ever-growing model complexity.
However,
training these complex models is computationally expensive, and they
tend to overfit the specific training datasets, thereby hindering their
performance on new datasets or in realistic applications.
In this
paper, we investigate methods to reduce model complexity, both
during training and inference, while maintaining high segmentation
quality.
We introduce a context module that captures high-order
context with a small number of parameters, and show that it
improves performance over representative baselines.
We then
capitalize on the guidance property of the context module to
develop an adaptive inference strategy that selectively applies
filtering to improve accuracy with minimal computational overhead.

Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes
dataset with a model that is an order of magnitude smaller
than the current leaders.

Semantic image segmentation has achieved remarkable performance on various benchmarks,
driven by deep learning with ever-growing model complexity.
However,
training these complex models is computationally expensive, and they
tend to overfit the specific training datasets, thereby hindering their
performance on new datasets or in realistic applications.

paper, we investigate methods to reduce model complexity, both
during training and inference, while maintaining high segmentation
quality.

context with a small number of parameters, and show that it
improves performance over representative baselines.
We then
capitalize on the guidance property of the context module to
develop an adaptive inference strategy that selectively applies
filtering to improve accuracy with minimal computational overhead.

We present a simple and efficient foreground clustering approach for joint segmentation and localization of objects in videos and images.
Our method leverages the prior knowledge of object geometry and motion to achieve robust and accurate results.
Given a set of initial segmentations, our approach iteratively refines the segmentations and localization by clustering the foreground regions in a joint spatial-temporal space.
We introduce a novel distance measure that considers both the spatial and temporal coherence of the pixels.
This allows us to efficiently handle objects that exhibit complex shapes, appearances, and motions.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of challenging video and image sequences, and show that our method compares favorably to the state-of-the-art in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

We propose a new algorithmic framework for exact and approximate testing of functional inequalities, motivated by several concrete applications that we have in mind in the theory of special functions, in particular the gamma and beta functions.
Instead of simulating the integral/derivative evaluation nodes of the discretized inequality, as it is usually done, we propose to simulate the nodes of the difference between the left-hand side and the right-hand side of the inequality.
This new approach allows one to test several functional inequalities for systems of several functions at once, with a computational cost that is linear (instead of quadratic) with the number of functions in the system.
We present implementations of our method in Matlab and C, that we make publicly available.
We also propose a variant of our method that allows one to test, on a grid of points, several functional inequalities against systems of tests that involve only a small number of functions in the system.
This is useful when one has a specific set of functions that are expected to satisfy a given functional inequality, and wants to test this inequality against a large number of tests using only evaluations of the given set of functions.

Driver distraction is a major contributor to traffic accidents.
In this paper, we present a non-intrusive approach for detecting driver distraction in a vehicle.
Our approach is based on image segmentation using the histogram of depth.
We use a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract the depth map from a single monocular image.
The depth map is then histogrammed to obtain a histogram of depth.
We propose a new segmentation method called thresholding on histogram of depth (THD) for partitioning the histogram into two regions corresponding to the foreground and the background.

Color image segmentation has always been an active research topic due to its wide applications in image processing area.
In this paper, we present a color image segmentation method based on seeded region growing and merging technique.
Specifically, we propose to use square elemental regions as the basic unit to extract the region information.
In the proposed method, the color image first undergoes the Gaussian smoothing operation, and the smoothing result is followed by the binary thresholding process to produce the initial segmentation.
Then, the seeded region growing and merging technique is applied to the binary image sequentially to produce the final segmentation result.
In the proposed method, the region growing process is performed within each square elemental region, and the region merging process is performed among the adjacent square elemental regions.

We present a novel framework for learning to segment neurons in 3D electron microscopy images.
Our approach is based on a metric graph learned by a convolutional neural network (CNN) from synthetic training images.
During training, the CNN is taught to generate simulated images from a metric graph, which encapsulates the spatial relationships between neurons.
Given a new image, our method estimates a metric graph that captures the local geometric structure of neuron branches.
This graph is then searched to find the optimal segmentation.
We show that the proposed approach is effective in segmenting neurons, even in challenging cases where other state-of-the-art methods fail.

Towards semantic video segmentation, the state-of-the-art primarily relies on dense optical flow for effective motion compensation.
However, computing optical flow is memory-intensive and computationally costly, especially for video frames of high resolution.
In this paper, we tackle the challenge of developing an effective and efficient framework for semantic video segmentation, which can readily take advantage of compressed-domain motion knowledge without requiring optical flow.
To this end, we propose TapLab, a semantic video segmentation framework that taps into compressed-domain motion knowledge by extensively exploiting motion compensation mechanisms available in modern video coding standards (e.g., MPEG).
Specifically, we reformulate the traditional semantic video segmentation pipeline by integrating compressed-domain motion compensation at each step, ranging from feature extraction to spatial propagation and temporal aggregation.
Furthermore, we introduce a novel sparse-grid optical flow field, which is efficiently computed from the compressed video stream and aids in refining the motion compensation.

We present a semi-supervised learning method for the segmentation of eye images.
We utilize a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, referred to as the Augmented CNN (ACNN), which leverages the power of supervised learning and the robustness of unsupervised learning.
Our approach is based on the assumption that eye images can be represented in a low-dimensional feature space where data points of the same class are closer to each other than data points of different classes.
The ACNN utilizes a low-dimensional embedding function to map input eye images into a low-dimensional feature space, where a linear classifier is then applied for segmentation.
To train our embedding function, we utilize a small set of labeled eye images and a large set of unlabeled eye images.
Our experimental results show that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ISBI eye segmentation benchmark.

Our approach is based on the assumption that eye images can be represented in a low-dimensional feature space where data points of the same class are closer to each other than data points of different classes.
The ACNN utilizes a low-dimensional embedding function to map input eye images into a low-dimensional feature space, where a linear classifier is then applied for segmentation.
To train our embedding function, we utilize a small set of labeled eye images and a large set of unlabeled eye images.
Our experimental results show
that the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ISBI eye segmentation benchmark.

Recent works have shown that training deep neural networks (DNNs) for image segmentation from scratch can be very time-consuming due to the large amount of labels required for supervised learning.
In this paper, we show that pre-trained models, especially those trained on large-scale datasets like ImageNet, can be used as strong initializations for training deep segmentation models.
We propose a simple yet effective approach to fine-tuning pre-trained models for image segmentation.
Our method first applies an initial segmentation model to segment the images into super-pixels.
Then, a pre-trained model is fine-tuned using the segmented images.
Experiments on two public segmentation benchmarks, PASCAL VOC 2012 and Cityscapes, show that our approach can significantly speed up the training process while maintaining high quality segmentation results.

We review the progress in computing weak decays using the method of regions, both at next-to-leading order (NLO) and at next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO).
After recalling the formalism of the method of regions, we present some selected results, mostly for decays of τ leptons and B mesons.
We also discuss on-going improvements to the methods and highlight a few outstanding challenges.

We present an object detection method that can be used for an efficient cluster initialization.
Our method is based on deep learning and unsupervised learning.
We use a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from the input images.
The extracted features are then processed by a region proposal network (RPN) to generate object proposals.
Finally, a support vector machine (SVM) is used to classify the proposals into different categories.
We evaluate our method on the VOC 2007 dataset.

Fast neutron detectors are essential for the characterization of nuclear data and have significant applications in nuclear security.
In this work, we present a new approach to fast neutron tracking that utilizes an array of plastic scintillator detectors, each equipped with a single-photon avalanche diode readout.
This approach offers distinct advantages in terms of cost, scalability, and portability.
We present detailed characterization measurements of the plastic scintillator and diode, which demonstrate that they perform similarly to their liquid organic and photomultiplier tube counterparts, as well as a methodology for embedding the detectors in various materials.
Using measurements obtained with embedded detectors, we present a reconstruction algorithm that utilizes a list-mode based approach to identify and track neutron trajectories in three dimensions.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using a series of tests with sources of various strengths and demonstrate its use in a large-scale experiment.

Deep learning methods have achieved tremendous success in image segmentation in recent years.
However, directly applying deep learning models on resource-constrained devices, such as smartphones, is impractical, due to their huge model size and high computational complexity.
In this paper, we aim to explore an efficient yet effective image segmentation method for screen content, which is composed of texts, graphics, and images.
It is highly challenging since the variety of screen contents makes it difficult to design hand-crafted features and the small dataset size makes it unsuitable for deep learning methods.
We propose a screen content image segmentation method based on least absolute deviation (LAD) fitting.
It is efficient because it only uses 1-D kernels and a small number of parameters.

We present an approach for dense 3D visual mapping of indoor scenes.
We aim at building a compact 3D model of the environment that replaces the original photometric and geometric texture with a simplified yet semantically coherent one.
In this way, our model is able to capture the intrinsic organization and structure of the scene, producing a coherent and recognizable 3D map.
To achieve this, we start by learning an overcomplete dictionary of atoms via sparse coding, i.e., finding the best low-dimensional representation of the training data.
Atoms are synthesized by combining a set of pre-defined 3D geometric primitives that are learned from the dataset.
In order to enforce semantic coherence, we then optimize the dictionary atoms to conform to the scene structure, leveraging on a dense 3D reconstruction of the environment.

Graphene, a single layer of graphite, has attracted extensive interest due to its unique properties.
Although graphene is known to be thermally and chemically stable, it can be oxidized to graphite by a laser irradiation in oxygen atmosphere.
In this study, we present a systematic in-situ Raman study of laser-induced graphene oxidation.
Unlike the previously reported random graphene oxidation, we find that a continuous graphene oxide layer is formed due to oxygen diffusion through the graphene membrane when the sample is oxidized at a sufficiently high temperature.
The graphene oxide layer is composed of a few graphene oxide sheets stacked together.
We discuss the formation of a continuous graphene oxide layer on the basis of our experimental results and previous studies.

Although graphene is known to be thermally and chemically stable, it can be oxidized to graphite by a laser irradiation in oxygen atmosphere.
In this study, we present a systematic in-situ Raman study of laser-induced graphene oxidation.
Unlike the previously reported random graphene oxidation, we find that a continuous graphene oxide layer is formed due to oxygen diffusion through the graphene membrane when the sample is oxidized at a sufficiently high temperature.
The graphene oxide layer is composed of a few graphene oxide sheets stacked together.

Graph entropies: recent progress in estimating graph entropies from data and applications in image processing is surveyed.
Graph entropy is a measure of randomness in graph structures.
Various entropy estimates are reviewed, including the spectral entropy, the distance-based entropy (also known as cut-entropy), and the recently developed interference-based entropy.
Applications of graph entropies in image processing, such as image segmentation and edge-preserving image filtering, are discussed.
In particular, a new edge-preserving smoothing filter based on the estimated cut-entropy is presented.
The new filter is shown to be effective in reducing the noise in the image while preserving the edges.

Recent advances in deep learning have achieved significant performance improvements in medical image segmentation.
However, training these models usually requires large amounts of manually annotated medical images, which are difficult to obtain.
In this paper, we present an approach for interactive medical image segmentation using deep learning with image-specific fine-tuning.
We start by training a deep learning model on a large dataset of synthetic images to obtain a good initial estimate of the segmentation.
We then fine-tune the model using a small number of manually annotated medical images specific to the patient and clinical site.
The fine-tuning process is performed using a small number of interactions with the user, who provides feedback on the initial estimate.

We present a novel architecture for cell image segmentation called Feedback U-net (F-U-net).
F-U-net combines the strengths of the U-net and CycleGAN architectures to create a robust and accurate cell image segmentation model.
The U-net architecture allows for the use of an encoder-decoder structure with skip connections, which helps to improve the model's performance by providing high-level features to the decoder network.
The CycleGAN architecture enables the model to learn a mapping between the source and target domains, which is useful for segmenting cells in images from different modalities or with different characteristics.
We evaluate F-U-net on two cell image segmentation datasets, and results show that it significantly improves over the U-net architecture in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

Recent progress in image segmentation, especially for nuclei images, has
been driven by large-scale annotated datasets.
However, manual
annotation is costly, and the resulting datasets are subject to
annotation errors and bias.
We present a data augmentation
approach to address these issues: given a nuclei image and its
ground truth segmentation, our algorithm generates new nuclei images
with the same segmentation.
Our method is based on a
generative neural network that learns to convert label maps to
images.
Because our network is trained to preserve the segmentation
rather than the appearance of individual nuclei, it can also
correct segmentation errors in the input image, and it is
capable of generating images with nuclei of different sizes and
shapes.
We show that our method, when used for data augmentation
during training, improves the performance of a U-Net
segmentation model for in vitro and in vivo nuclei images,
leading to significant improvements in segmentation accuracy
and speed.

Recent progress in image synthesis through the use of GANs provides a new opportunity for image understanding.
In particular, we show that the image representation learned by GANs can be used to produce state-of-the-art performance on semantic image segmentation, a task that is fundamental to many applications in computer vision.
We achieve this by proposing a new framework that leverages the rich structural information encoded in the generative models of GANs.
Our approach, which we term "Segmentation in Style", combines an adversarial reconstruction loss with a discriminator that performs segmentation.
This framework is applicable to any GAN architecture and we demonstrate its effectiveness on top of StyleGAN2 and CLIP, a recently proposed GAN-based image representation.
Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the ACDC and Cityscapes segmentation benchmarks without requiring any labeled data for training, but rather only a few images for initialization.

We present a method for real-time prediction of segmentation quality while the network is training.
Given a set of training images, we train a student-teacher network with an auxiliary segmentation branch whose sole purpose is to predict segmentation quality.
Since the teacher network is defined in terms of the student network, the two networks can be trained jointly in an end-to-end fashion.
During training, the predicted quality metric provides reinforcement signal to guide the training process of the student network and it could be used to protect the regions of interest.
In the test phase, the segmentation quality predictor can be used for active learning and selective sampling.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes dataset.

Recent works on portrait segmentation usually emphasize the accuracy of the segmentation results, while ignoring the boundary sensitivity of the predicted masks.
In this paper, we present a boundary-sensitive network (BSNet) for portrait segmentation, which effectively improves the boundary accuracy of the predicted masks.
Specifically, we propose to use a boundary-sensitive loss (BSLoss) to optimize the network.
In addition, we introduce a boundary-sensitive module (BSM) into the network architecture, which is designed to refine the boundaries of the predicted masks.
By combining the BSLoss and the BSM, our BSNet can produce much more accurate boundaries without sacrificing the overall segmentation performance.
In the experimental part, we conduct comprehensive experiments on the publicly available Portrait Segmentation Benchmark.
