The paper presents a computer vision pipeline for the automated determination of cardiac structure and function and the detection of disease by two-dimensional echocardiography.
The pipeline consists of three main components: image preprocessing, feature extraction, and machine learning.
The image preprocessing component includes methods for image enhancement, segmentation, and registration.
The feature extraction component extracts relevant features from the preprocessed images, including shape, texture, and motion features.
The machine learning component uses a deep learning model to classify the extracted features and determine the presence of disease.
The pipeline was evaluated on a large dataset of echocardiography images and achieved high accuracy and specificity in the detection of cardiac disease.

Abstract:
Noisy annotations in medical imaging, particularly in computed tomography (CT) imaging, can lead to inaccurate analysis and diagnosis.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to clearing noisy annotations in CT imaging using a combination of algorithmic and crowdsourcing techniques.
First, we use a deep learning-based approach to identify and remove noisy annotations from the CT images.
This is followed by a crowdsourcing step, where a large number of users are asked to review the remaining annotations and provide feedback on their quality.
The feedback is then used to further refine the annotation clearance process.
The proposed approach is evaluated on a large dataset of CT images and the results show that it significantly improves the quality of the annotations, leading to more accurate analysis and diagnosis.

Below is an abstract for the academic paper titled, "A dynamic graph-cuts method with integrated multiple feature maps for segmenting kidneys in ultrasound images:

Recent progress in ultrasound (US) image segmentation has achieved remarkable performance in various applications.
However, most existing methods are dedicated to specific organs and lack the generalization ability to other organs or pathologies.
In this paper, we propose a dynamic graph-cuts method with integrated multiple feature maps for segmenting kidneys in US images.
Our method incorporates multi-scale convolutional neural network (CNN) feature maps and anatomical knowledge into the graph-cuts framework.
The multi-scale CNN feature maps capture the global and local structures of the US images, while the anatomical knowledge improves the accuracy of the segmentation by enforcing the consistency of the predicted contours with the expected kidney shapes.
We evaluate our method on a public US image dataset and compare it with state-of-the-art segmentation methods.

An important problem in computer vision is saliency detection, i.e., predicting which pixels in an input image are most salient, or foreground, and which are least salient, or background.
We approach this problem in a top-down manner, first detecting objects of interest in the image, and then computing saliency within each object region.
Our approach is motivated by the observation that objects in images often carry important saliency information and are of primary interest in many applications.
We allow the set of objects of interest to be specified by the user, and we perform saliency detection within each object region using a classifier-guided approach.
Our method first uses a deep neural network to classify the objects in the image.
We then use the object class predictions to guide our saliency detection process within each object region.

Automated quality control (AQC) methods are crucial for effective and efficient image analysis in large-scale imaging studies.
In this paper, we present a comprehensive AQC framework for cardiac magnetic resonance (MR) imaging data in the UK Biobank imaging study.
Our AQC approach focuses on four key aspects: (1) image properties, including size, orientation, and slice location; (2) cardiac structure analysis, including heart rate and left ventricle segmentation; (3) quality of MR images, including image contrast and artifacts; and (4) comparison of manual and automated segmentation results.
We provide a detailed evaluation of our AQC framework using a large subset of the UK Biobank cardiac MR imaging study data (N=318).
Our results show that our AQC approach can effectively identify potential issues in the data and improve the consistency and quality of the image segmentation results.
We believe that our AQC framework will be useful for large-scale imaging studies and can potentially enhance the reproducibility and reliability of image-based research.

Abstract:
Traditional image segmentation approaches tend to perform poorly on food images, as they generally lack the ability to adapt to the variability and complexity of food objects.
In this paper, we present a saliency-aware approach for segmenting class-agnostic food images.
Our approach leverages the recently proposed Deep Graphical Feature Learning (DGFL) framework to extract robust and generalizable features from food images.
We then use a fully connected conditional random field (CRF) to refine the segmentation results and improve the accuracy.
Furthermore, we propose a saliency-aware module that highlights the regions of interest in the image and guides the segmentation process.
Our approach is evaluated on the publicly available Food-101 and Breakfast-102 datasets, and the results show that our approach significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art.

LeViT-UNet: Make Faster Encoders with Transformer for Medical Image Segmentation

Abstract:

We present a simple yet effective encoder augmentation for semantic segmentation, which can enhance the representation capability of the encoder without increasing the parameters.
Our approach directly utilizes the transformers to replace the conventional convolutional layers in the encoder, which not only benefits from the powerful representation capability of the transformers but also retains the spatial information.
To solve the compatibility between the transformers and the subsequent upsampling modules, we propose to introduce a simple upsampling module, named as the UNet-style upsampling module, which can gradually recover the spatial information with fewer parameters.
In addition, to adapt to the characteristics of medical images, we propose to introduce the lesion-enhancing transformation to preprocess the input images.
The experiments on the ACDC and ISBI 2017 segmentation demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which achieves the best performance of all the methods without using extra augmentation.

Diluted magnetic semiconductors (DMS) have recently been the focus of extensive research aimed at the development of spintronic devices.
The most promising materials for such applications are the II-VI semiconductor compounds.
Among various II-VI compounds, SnTe-based DMS have attracted considerable attention due to their favorable magnetic properties.
In this paper, we present a detailed investigation of the magnetic properties of Sn/1-x/CrxTe diluted magnetic semiconductors.
A comprehensive study of the magnetic behavior of these materials, including magnetic susceptibility, specific heat, and magnetization, was performed.
Our results suggest that the addition of Cr ions introduces magnetic moments in the otherwise non-magnetic matrix of SnTe, with the Curie temperature increasing with the concentration of Cr.

The method is based on an iterative process that involves training a network with labeled data and then interactively refining the network's performance through user feedback.
The user provides feedback on the network's output, which is then used to update the network's weights and biases.
The process is repeated until the network achieves a desired level of performance.
The method is evaluated on a public dataset of neuronal structures and compared to other state-of-the-art segmentation methods.
The results show that the proposed method can achieve better performance in terms of accuracy and speed.

The resulting binary image shows the object segmented from the background, with the edges of the object preserved.
The proposed method was evaluated on a dataset of images and the results showed that it achieved a high degree of accuracy in segmenting the objects while preserving the edges.

Abstract:
We use a novel method to estimate the impact of each NBA player on his team's chances of winning, based on the player's on-off court performance.
This method leverages the widely-available box score statistics as well as the similarity between pairs of players, which can be calculated using their playing time together.
Our method is a natural extension of the plus-minus statistic, which has been widely used in basketball to evaluate player performance.
This paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of our proposed method against other metrics currently used in the literature, in terms of how well each metric predicts the outcome of actual games.
We show that our proposed method performs better than existing metrics in predicting game outcomes, and that it is therefore a more effective tool for evaluating player performance.

Here is an abstract for the academic paper titled "Femtosecond resolution timing jitter correction on a TW-scale Ti:sapphire laser system for FEL pump-probe experiments":


Abstract
We have developed a femtosecond (FS) resolution timing jitter correction system for a Ti:sapphire laser system with a pulse energy of up to 1.5 J at a 1 Hz repetition rate.
The system utilizes a programmable digital delay line (DDL) and an acousto-optic modulator (AOM) for fine and coarse timing adjustments, respectively.
The DDL is programmed to correct for timing jitter on a shot-by-shot basis, resulting in an rms timing jitter of less than 5 fs.
The AOM is used to make larger timing adjustments to maintain a constant delay between the pump and probe pulses.
The system has been used to perform pump-probe experiments on a Ti:sapphire amplifier system with a pulse energy of up to 100 mJ at a 1 kHz repetition rate.

Abstract:
Inverse covariance matrix estimation is a fundamental problem in statistics, but it becomes challenging when the dimensionality of the dataset is very high.
The L0 sparse inverse covariance (LSIC) estimation algorithm provides a solution to this problem by estimating the inverse covariance matrix with a small number of nonzero elements, making it suitable for high-dimensional data.
In this paper, we provide a comprehensive review of the LSIC estimation algorithm, including its theoretical background, algorithmic steps, and applications.
We also discuss the challenges and limitations of the algorithm, and explore potential extensions and improvements.
The LSIC estimation algorithm has a wide range of applications in various fields such as finance, genetics, and machine learning.
We believe that this work will provide a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners interested in inverse covariance matrix estimation and high-dimensional data analysis.

Abstract:
A parallel corpus is a collection of translations of the same source text in different languages.
This has allowed researchers to compare words and phrases across languages.
However, such resources for Hebrew and Aramaic (and other rare languages) are scarce, despite there being a wealth of textual material available in these languages.
This paper presents a method for identifying parallel passages across a large Hebrew/Aramaic corpus and applying language model fine-tuning for subsequent translation.
Our results show that the proposed method can effectively identify parallel passages, resulting in improved performance for Hebrew-to-English and Aramaic-to-English translation tasks.

Few-shot segmentation is a challenging problem in which the goal is to segment new classes given only a few training examples.
In this paper, we propose a self-guided learning approach that utilizes a reference image to adapt a pre-trained segmentation model to new classes.
We further propose a cross-guided learning approach that utilizes a collection of reference images from multiple classes to adapt the model.
Our approaches are based on a novel adaptation module that can be easily integrated into existing segmentation models.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approaches on the VOC2012 and Cityscapes segmentation datasets, where we achieve state-of-the-art performance.

This paper examines the spectral efficiency of flexi-grid long-haul optical systems and proposes a method for optimizing it.
The authors conducted extensive simulations and found that a hybrid modulation scheme, which combines quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) and discrete multi-tone (DMT), can achieve the highest spectral efficiency.
Additionally, they found that the number of subcarriers and the width of the signal spectrum have a significant impact on spectral efficiency.
The authors propose a method for optimizing these parameters to achieve the highest spectral efficiency.
The results of this study can help designers of optical networks to improve the spectral efficiency of their systems and to reduce the cost of transmission.

Abstract:
Traditional semantic segmentation models tend to confuse objects that have similar appearances.
We propose a network structure that utilizes an ensemble of confusion classes as a mid-level feature to explicitly reduce confusion errors in semantic segmentation.
Our approach extends the atrous convolutional neural network to incorporate a multi-scale confusion class pooling (MCP) module.
The MCP module performs a series of pooling operations on different scales of the feature maps to extract a rich representation of the input image, which is then used to classify each pixel into one of the predefined confusion classes.
With the help of the confusion class labels, our proposed network learns to explicitly reduce confusion errors during the training process.
We evaluate our approach on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, and the results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in semantic segmentation.

Abstract:
Tracking objects in videos requires models that can adapt to appearance changes and object motion.
We present an approach for learning such models without requiring an abundance of labeled training data.
Our approach consists of a cell-based architecture created by composing building blocks that are automatically discovered by differentiable neural architecture search.
Each building block is an encoder-decoder network that transforms a sub-region of the input patch to its pixel-level representation.
The architecture is automatically discovered in a way that ensures the decoder networks in each building block specialize in recognizing and locating objects within their corresponding sub-regions.
We implement our approach on top of a state-of-the-art tracking framework and show that it significantly improves the accuracy and robustness of the tracker on popular benchmarks.

The key innovation in our approach is the use of a dense consensus layer, which enforces agreement among the different segments in the image.
Our method is trained using a combination of supervised and semi-supervised learning, with the goal of learning a robust and generalizable segmentation model.
We evaluate our approach on a large dataset of abdominal CT scans and show that it outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of segmentation accuracy and generalization performance.
We also show that our approach is able to learn a robust model that is able to segment multiple organs and tumors in a single image, even when the training data is only partially labeled.

An important task in computer vision is referring image segmentation, which associates each pixel in an input image with a semantic category label, and further retrieves a referring region in the image that is most relevant to the category.
However, existing referring segmentation methods mainly rely on low-level image cues, and often encounter difficulties in comprehending contextual information and capturing long-range dependencies, which limit their performance in referring segmentation.
In this paper, we propose a cross-modal progressive comprehension approach to referring image segmentation, which leverages the power of both images and texts to overcome the limitations of previous methods.
Our approach progressively comprehends the referring information from both modalities in a mutually reinforcing manner.
Specifically, we first generate object region proposals via a coarse-to-fine strategy that integrates both image and text understanding.
Then, we develop a referring segmentation network that refines the object regions by progressively reasoning about the referring relationships between objects and their referring regions.

In this paper, we present VoxResNet, a deep learning framework for automated brain tissue segmentation of MRI volumes.
VoxResNet is designed to explicitly model the inter-voxel dependencies in a feed-forward manner while maintaining voxel-level interpretability.
It achieves this by utilizing a novel voxel-wise residual network (VoxResNet) architecture, which incorporates skip connections within a 3D U-Net like architecture.
The skip connections enable the network to learn long range dependencies in the input volume.
Furthermore, we introduce a new activation function, called the spherical linear unit (SLU), which models complex non-linear interactions within voxels while maintaining the interpretability of the network.
We evaluate VoxResNet on the challenging multi-class brain tissue segmentation task from the 2016 BraTS challenge.

Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision with a wide range of applications in autonomous driving, medical imaging, and robotics.
However, existing semantic segmentation algorithms require a large amount of accurately annotated images, which can be expensive and time-consuming to acquire.
In this paper, we propose a weakly-supervised approach for multi-class semantic segmentation using FMCW radar.
Our approach leverages radar's complementary information with vision in a novel weakly-supervised learning framework to accurately segment objects in images without the need for expensive and time-consuming annotations.
We introduce a radar-based segmentation network (RSS-Net) that learns to segment objects using a weakly-supervised loss function that combines both semantic and instance segmentation objectives.
Our approach significantly improves over prior art in weakly-supervised semantic segmentation, and is shown to be effective across a range of object classes and image domains.

Academic coverage in Wikipedia has attracted significant attention from researchers and the popular
  press.
Previous research has been qualitative, with a few quantitative studies.
This paper contributes to
  the quantitative assessment of Wikipedia content, and of academic coverage in particular.
It measures
  the extent of Wikipedia's coverage of different academic occupations, its internal structure of
  articles, and the relations between these two variables, in order to assess what academic
  occupations are most prominently featured.
It also analyzes the linguistic behavior of Wikipedia
  editors with respect to academic coverage, in order to detect potential biases in coverage.
Our
  analysis reveals a strong correlation between the amount of academic coverage and the academic
  prestige of the occupation, but also a high variability among different sub-domains of science.

Abstract:
Biomedical image segmentation is challenging due to the domain shift between the training and test datasets, which can significantly degrade the performance of deep learning models.
In this paper, we propose an unsupervised domain adaptation method that leverages the category-centric prototype alignment (CCPA) technique to address this issue.
Our approach consists of two main components: a domain adaptation network (DAN) and a CCPA module.
The DAN uses a convolutional neural network (CNN) to learn a domain-invariant feature representation, while the CCPA module aligns the category-specific prototypes of the source and target domains.
We evaluate our method on three publicly available biomedical image segmentation datasets, and our results show that our approach significantly improves the performance of the baseline method in all cases.

 Normalisation by evaluation (NBE) has been a powerful technique in programming languages to trade space for time, in the pursuit for high-level compilers that perform nearly as well as hand-written code.
In this paper we argue that NBE is ill-suited for typical type theory libraries, due to the presence of side-effects.
We identify a different sweet spot for optimisation in type theory, based on a typical path in a dependent type theory proof: computation along the path, followed by simplification of the result.
We propose a method for performing optimisation based on a new notion of normality, which we call normalisation by reduction (NBR).
In an implementation in the Agda proof assistant, we achieve speedups of up to 22x over the standard normalization technique.

```

Learning effective and general neural network architectures is a core challenge in deep learning.
In this paper, we propose a method to learn the architecture of neural networks by propagating network codes.
These network codes are high-level human-readable descriptions of network structure, such as “3-3-3” (three convolutional layers with three filters each) or “4-3-2-relu” (four convolutional layers, followed by three fully connected layers with a ReLU activation function).
We show that these high-level descriptions can be learned in a data-driven manner, and that they lead to better generalization performance on a wide variety of datasets, compared to using random architectures or hand-designed architectures.
We present an algorithm to learn network codes in a supervised way, by training a neural architecture search (NAS) agent that learns to make architectural decisions to maximize the expected reward, and show that it is able to learn reusable codes that generalize across different datasets.
Finally, we show that our approach is able to outperform state-of-the-art NAS methods on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, and achieve competitive results on ImageNet.

Abstract:
A significant barrier to error correction is the sheer quantity of errors introduced by current generation language models.
Previous work has been done on mitigating output errors in language models, with recent work focusing on identifying and correcting the most detrimental errors to the generation of high-quality language.
However, these methods are not aimed at the specific task of error correction in the language model output.
In this paper, we propose a novel method to curb these errors in a way that is suitable for a downstream error correction task.
We train a language model to attend to its own mistakes, with the goal of learning which tokens to correct in order to obtain the highest-quality language.
Our method relies on a teacher model which provides additional feedback to the student model in the form of an error signal.

Articular cartilage plays a vital role in the functioning of joints, yet its capacity to repair itself following injury is limited.
This paper presents a mathematical model that links the cellular and mechanical processes involved in articular cartilage lesion formation.
The model considers the effects of mechanical loading, cellular metabolism, and the extracellular matrix on the formation of lesions in articular cartilage.
It captures the key processes including the production and degradation of the extracellular matrix, the response of cells to mechanical loading, and the feedback between cellular and mechanical processes.
The model was validated using experimental data and showed good agreement with the observed trends.
The results of the model suggest that mechanical loading and cellular metabolism are key factors in the formation of articular cartilage lesions.

With the continuous growth of cities, it becomes more and more important to map vulnerable populations to provide them with proper assistance.
However, this is a time-consuming and resource-intensive task that requires a lot of data collection and analysis.
In this paper, we present a novel approach to mapping vulnerable populations using AI.
We train a deep learning model on a large dataset of demographic and socioeconomic data.
The model is able to identify patterns and correlations in the data that can be used to map vulnerable populations.
The results show that our approach is able to identify high-risk areas with a high degree of accuracy.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "Geometric Thermoelectric Pump: Energy Harvesting beyond Seebeck and Pyroelectric Effects" would be:

'Thermoelectric energy harvesting has emerged as a simple and robust technology to power IoT devices and wearable electronics by scavenging waste heat from the environment.
The conventional thermoelectric generators rely on the temperature gradient between two different electrical conductors to produce the voltage using the Seebeck effect.
However, the performance of this technique is limited by the low figure of merit of the commercially available thermoelectric materials.
In this work, we propose a geometric thermoelectric pump that harnesses the temperature variation in a micro-channel to generate high-head pressure and high-flow rate for energy harvesting applications.
Our proposed approach relies on the principle of electroosmosis, where the surface charge on the channel wall and the electric field generated by the temperature-dependent thermoelectric voltage together drive the bulk flow in the channel.
We theoretically analyze the flow rate and head pressure in the channel and optimize the geometric parameters to achieve high performance.

An important problem in statistics is the recovery of a low-rank matrix from a limited number of observations, when the matrix is known to belong to a specific low-rank structure, defined by a given set of basis vectors, or “atoms.”
In many applications, the set of atoms is only known up to a given multiplicative factor, and the goal is to determine the atoms and the factor up to an overall scale that can be determined from the observations.
This paper addresses the question of determining the atoms and the factor when the matrix being recovered is a principal component analysis (PCA) matrix.
PCA factorizes a data matrix into a product of a low-rank matrix and a diagonal matrix whose entries are the squared singular values.
The low-rank matrix is uniquely defined by the atoms and the factor.
The problem of recovering the low-rank PCA matrix given the atoms and the factor up to a common scale is formulated as an optimization problem with a nonlinear constraint, which is shown to be strictly convex.

An important problem in computer vision is object proposal generation, which ranks candidate windows containing objects of interest.
Existing works focus on either maximizing discriminative power via re-ranking or adhering to a submodular covering criterion, resulting in a trade-off between quality and diversity.
We propose a simple yet effective method to optimize both criteria via submodular ranking, which ranks candidate windows with a learned submodular function that simultaneously considers discriminative and covering criteria.
Our approach, Discriminative Submodular Ranking (DSR), is based on a submodular cover algorithm that iteratively adds the most discriminative and submodularly covering regions.
We further propose an efficient implementation of DSR using coarse-to-fine sampling and an online learning strategy.
Experiments on the PASCAL VOC 2007 and 2012 datasets show that our approach achieves state-of-the-art object proposal generation performance.

Here is the abstract for the academic paper titled "Qubit state tomography in superconducting circuits via weak measurements":

The standard approach for quantum process tomography (QPT) of open systems is to repeatedly prepare the system in a known state, measure the final state after interaction with the environment, and then solve for the quantum channel describing the evolution.
However, this approach becomes impractical for continuous-variable (CV) quantum systems, where the dimensions of the state space grow factorially with the number of qubits, and for systems where one cannot prepare well-defined quantum states.
Here, we propose and experimentally demonstrate a weak measurement-based approach to quantum process tomography of multi-mode Gaussian states, which are relevant to continuous-variable quantum information processing.
Our approach enables the direct measurement of the process matrix without requiring the preparation of known states, and is therefore applicable to any initial state.
We demonstrate our approach on a four-mode Gaussian state, and reconstruct the process matrix to characterize the interactions between the modes.
Our approach can be extended to higher-dimensional Gaussian states and more general quantum channels.

Abstract:
Deep learning has shown promise for accurate segmentation of disease features from medical images, but the lack of interpretability and statistical estimations remains a limitation.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach that combines the strengths of deep learning and statistical methods to address these limitations.
Our approach utilizes a deep learning model, specifically a fully convolutional network, to extract features from medical images.
The extracted features are then fed into a statistical model, such as a random forest or support vector machine, to perform segmentation and provide interpretability.
Additionally, we propose a synergistic approach that combines the deep learning and statistical models to improve the segmentation performance.
The proposed approach is evaluated on a large dataset of medical images and compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Abstract:
Image co-segmentation refers to the task of partitioning an image into spatially coherent and semantically consistent regions.
It has emerged as an active field of research due to its wide range of applications in image processing, computer vision, and pattern recognition.
This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the state-of-the-art in automatic image co-segmentation.
We begin by introducing the concept of image co-segmentation and discussing the different types of approaches that have been proposed.
We then review the various techniques that have been used to tackle the problem, including pixel-level segmentation, region-based segmentation, and hybrid methods.
We also discuss the evaluation metrics that have been used to assess the performance of co-segmentation algorithms.

Abstract:
Progressive diffusion, recently introduced for image synthesis tasks, improves the conditioning of GANs training and generates images faster than conventional diffusion methods.
In this paper, we apply the concept of progressive diffusion to semantic image segmentation, a task that consists of predicting a high-resolution mask of class labels for every pixel of an input image.
We propose a progressively diffused network (PDN) that, unlike existing approaches, directly outputs a high-resolution segmentation mask and skips the commonly adopted upsampling process.
Our network is trained with a progressive diffusion scheme in an end-to-end manner, where a series of diffusion components are gradually introduced during training.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Cityscapes and VOC segmentation benchmarks, where PDN achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods while being trained approximately two times faster.
The code and models are available at https://github.com/autonomousvision/progressive_diffusion.

We find that the young (≲1 Gyr) main sequence turn-off (MSTO) and the old (≳3 Gyr) red giant branch (RGB) in the Milky Way are reproduced in the outer disks of S0s at a fixed radius, suggesting that these galaxies formed the majority of their stars in a similar manner to the Milky Way.
The inner disks of S0s are consistently younger and more metal-rich than their outer disks and also than the Milky Way disk, indicating that the accretion and merging of smaller galaxies have contributed to their build-up.
We compare the observed radial distributions of young and old stars in the S0s with chemo-dynamical simulations of galaxy formation.
The agreement between the observations and the simulations supports a top-down scenario for the formation of disk galaxies, in which the merging of dark matter halos forms galaxies that retain their stars and gas, allowing them to grow primarily through the accretion of fresh gas, rather than through the merging of pre-existing galaxies.

This paper introduces a path integral representation of the Lorentzian spinfoam model, which describes the dynamics of classical point particles without invoking any extra geometrical background structures.
We show that the path integral formulation of the model exhibits an additional symmetry, a foliation symmetry, which is absent in the original formulation.
This symmetry is generated by a new vector field, referred to as the foliation vector field, which depends on the particle trajectories.
By exploiting this symmetry, we derive a set of novel Feynman rules that are valid in any foliation of spacetime.
In particular, the foliation symmetry allows us to decouple the path integral into a product of a bulk integral and a boundary integral.
The bulk integral is shown to have a well-defined limit as the particle's proper time goes to zero, which provides an alternative way of obtaining the stationary phase approximation of the model.

Here is the abstract for the academic paper titled "Brain Tumor Segmentation using an Ensemble of 3D U-Nets and Overall Survival Prediction using Radiomic Features":

Abstract: Brain tumor segmentation and survival prediction are essential tasks in clinical imaging.
In this paper, we propose a novel ensemble of 3D U-Nets for brain tumor segmentation and radiomic features for overall survival prediction.
The ensemble of 3D U-Nets is designed to effectively segment brain tumors in 3D MRI images, while the radiomic features are extracted from these segmented images to predict overall survival.
The proposed method was evaluated on the BraTS 2020 dataset and achieved a dice similarity coefficient of 0.83 and 0.81 for the tumor and tumor core segmentation, respectively.
The radiomic features were able to predict overall survival with an AUC-ROC of 0.79.
The proposed method shows promise for clinical use, and further evaluation is required.

This paper considers a class of renewal processes with dependent interarrival times and proves renewal theorems for such processes.
It shows that the interarrival times of these processes can be represented by a hidden Markov model, allowing for the determination of the renewal distribution and the mean renewal time.


The applications of these renewal theorems in geometry are explored, particularly in the study of fractal shapes such as the Sierpinski triangle and the Koch snowflake.
It is shown that the interarrival times of the renewal process can be related to the lengths of the sides of the fractal shapes, and that the mean renewal time can be used to determine the fractal dimension of the shapes.


The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these results for other areas of mathematics and science, such as the study of random processes and the analysis of complex systems.
It is hoped that the renewal theorems presented in this paper will provide a useful tool for the study of such systems.

An effective and efficient semantic segmentation method is essential for the robots to perceive the environment.
However, the limitation of computational resources and the variation of the environment of autonomous shopping robots restrict the model's performance and the size of the model.
We present a cost-effective region-based active learning (CEREALS) framework for efficient semantic segmentation, targeting autonomous shopping robots in dynamic shopping malls.
Given the shopping robot's mobility and limited onboard computation, we focus on efficiency and effectiveness.
The proposed method first estimates the uncertainty of the model to filter out the easy-to-classify regions.
Then it plans a path to visit only the uncertain regions, named exploration regions, and simultaneously performs semantic segmentation on the captured images.

Articular cartilage is essential for the movement of joints, as it is a smooth, resilient tissue that allows for the frictionless motion of bones.
However, it is vulnerable to injury and disease, which can lead to pain and loss of mobility.
In this paper, we present a novel method for modeling and simulating the effects of cyclic loading on articular cartilage lesion formation.
Our method uses a combination of finite element analysis and computational fluid dynamics to simulate the mechanical and biochemical processes that occur in articular cartilage under cyclic loading conditions.
We find that our model is capable of predicting the formation of lesions in articular cartilage due to cyclic loading, and that the predicted lesion formation is consistent with experimental data.
We also find that our model is able to predict the effect of various factors on the formation of lesions, such as the intensity and frequency of the cyclic loading, the properties of the articular cartilage, and the presence of biochemical factors.

Abstract:
Label corruption, caused by inconsistent, inaccurate, or noisy labeling, is a common challenge in image segmentation.
It can significantly degrade the performance of image segmentation models.
We introduce Co-Seg, a novel image segmentation framework that leverages the strengths of multiple models to overcome label corruption.
Our approach combines a pre-trained image segmentation model with a corruption detection model to selectively refine the predictions on potentially corrupted regions.
The corruption detection model accurately identifies regions with a high likelihood of label corruption, while the image segmentation model provides initial predictions.
We train the corruption detection model using a contrast set, which consists of examples from the same distribution as the training data but with known labels.

Abstract:
Training deep learning models for medical image segmentation is challenging due to the scarcity of labeled data and the inherent complexity of the task.
In this paper, we address these issues by proposing a new framework that is designed to train robust models with limited data and incomplete labels.
Our approach leverages a segmentation-aware loss function that is tailored to handle incomplete labels, enabling the model to learn more effectively from limited training data.
We evaluate our method on a public dataset for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) segmentation and demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.
We also conduct a comprehensive analysis to understand the impact of label incompleteness and data scarcity on the performance of our model.
Our results show that our method is effective in handling both scenarios, making it a promising tool for medical image segmentation with limited resources.

Abstract
We present a semi-supervised segmentation approach to localize retinal layers in optical coherence tomography (OCT) images.
A fully convolutional network is trained to classify pixels in OCT images into six layers of the retina using only a small set of manually annotated images.
To handle the variability and uncertainty in both the appearance of OCT images and the layer boundaries, we adopt a segmentation approach that operates on image patches rather than the entire image.
During training, the network outputs an uncertainty measure for each pixel, which guides the selection of most informative training samples for strong supervision.
We utilize a patch-based loss function that is robust against local errors in the output.
Furthermore, to overcome the scarcity of labeled images, we propose a novel semi-supervised loss that utilizes unlabeled images to regularize the network.

We evaluate our algorithm on a set of randomly generated matrices, and we compare its performance to that of a state-of-the-art algorithm.
Our results show that our algorithm can find matrices with significantly smaller peak-sidelobe distances than the state-of-the-art algorithm, especially for large matrices.
We also present a set of theoretical results that characterize the performance of our algorithm, and we discuss its potential applications in radar signal processing and other fields.

Abstract:
Traditional semantic image segmentation methods tend to rely on hand-designed features and heuristics, which may not generalize well to complex real-world images.
This paper presents a new approach to semantic image segmentation based on a multi-layer approach to superpixel-based higher-order conditional random fields (CRFs).
Our method utilizes recent advances in deep learning to automatically learn a hierarchy of features for segmentation, which are then used to construct a higher-order CRF that models the spatial dependencies between pixels.
This allows our method to capture complex relationships between objects and background regions in an automatic and data-driven fashion.
Furthermore, our method is able to segment images with high accuracy and efficiency, making it suitable for real-time applications.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the public VOC2012 segmentation benchmark, where our method achieves state-of-the-art performance.

We then use a graph cuts algorithm to optimize the segmentation by maximizing the conditional score.
Our approach is fully automatic and does not require any manual initialization or post-processing steps.
We evaluate our algorithm on the Cityscapes and CamVid datasets, and show that it achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation quality.

Decoding is a fundamental step in most segmentation algorithms, especially for biomedical image segmentation.
It converts a label map into a binary mask, which can be used for various applications such as object detection, image registration, and image analysis.
However, the performance of the decoding step is often limited by the quality of the input label map, which may be noisy, incomplete, or inaccurate.
In this paper, we propose a new decoding method called Cascade Decoder, which is designed to handle such noisy and incomplete label maps.
Our method first applies a series of cascaded decoders to refine the input label map, and then uses a final decoder to produce the final binary mask.
Each decoder in the cascade consists of a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a conditional random field (CRF) model.

Abstract:
Domain adaptation has gained significant attention in the field of computer vision, where the goal is to learn a model capable of performing well on target domains using training data from a different source domain.
However, fully supervised domain adaptation can be challenging and expensive due to the need for labeled target domain data.
In this work, we propose a semi-supervised domain adaptation approach that leverages unlabeled target domain data and a small amount of labeled data from either the source or target domain.
Our key insight is to learn a progressive feature alignment model that gradually aligns the feature representations of the source and target domains.
Specifically, we introduce an adaptive alignment module that performs feature alignment based on a learned similarity metric and an adversarial component that encourages domain-invariant feature representation learning.
Furthermore, we introduce a progressive alignment module that enables feature representation to be gradually aligned between the source and target domains.

Abstract
Traditional saliency models suffer from lacking contextual information for accurate salient object detection.
In this paper, we propose a multi-task learning framework, namely DeepSaliency, to improve the performance of salient object detection.
The proposed method simultaneously learns the tasks of predicting salient objects and the underlying scene via a deep neural network.
We introduce a new loss function that combines the tasks of saliency detection and scene understanding, which enables the network to learn contextual information effectively.
Our experimental results on three public datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over the state-of-the-art approaches in terms of precision, recall, and F-measure.


DeepSaliency can be applied to various computer vision tasks, such as image segmentation, object detection, and image editing.

Medical image segmentation is a fundamental task in medical imaging analysis, but it remains a challenging problem.
In this paper, we present TransClaw U-Net, a novel approach that combines the strengths of two powerful architectures: Claw U-Net and Transformers.
Claw U-Net is a state-of-the-art convolutional neural network (CNN) for medical image segmentation, but it lacks the ability to capture long-range dependencies in images.
To address this limitation, we introduce a transformer block into the Claw U-Net architecture, allowing the network to capture global dependencies and improve performance on medical image segmentation tasks.
Our experiments show that TransClaw U-Net significantly improves segmentation performance on a variety of medical images, including MRI brain images and chest X-rays.
We also perform a detailed analysis of the network's performance and show that the transformer block is crucial for capturing long-range dependencies in medical images.

Abstract:
We present a method for the segmentation of facades in outdoor scenes.
Our approach is based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) that has been trained on a large dataset of images containing buildings.
The network is able to accurately segment the facade of a building from the rest of the image, allowing for the extraction of information such as the building's shape, size, and texture.
We evaluate our method on a variety of images, and show that it is able to generalize well to different types of buildings and environments.
Our approach is particularly useful for applications such as 3D reconstruction, urban planning, and disaster response.

Abstract:

Transfer learning has recently gained a lot of attention in the field of medical image segmentation.
The ability to use pre-trained models on large datasets to extract meaningful features has shown promising results on a variety of segmentation tasks.
In this work, we perform a critical assessment of transfer learning for medical image segmentation with fully convolutional neural networks.
We evaluate the performance of several state-of-the-art transfer learning models on a variety of medical image segmentation datasets, and analyze the impact of transfer learning on model performance.
Our results show that transfer learning can significantly improve the performance of medical image segmentation models, especially when the target task has a limited amount of labeled data.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "Meta Segmentation Network for Ultra-Resolution Medical Images" could be:

Medical image segmentation is crucial in the analysis and diagnosis of many diseases.
However, traditional segmentation methods often struggle with the ultra-resolution images used in modern medical imaging.
This paper proposes a novel approach to segmentation using a Meta Segmentation Network (MSN).
The MSN is based on a convolutional neural network (CNN) and is designed to efficiently segment ultra-resolution medical images.
The network is composed of an encoder-decoder architecture, with the encoder trained to extract features from the input image and the decoder trained to segment the image using the extracted features.
The MSN is trained using a novel loss function that combines both pixel-wise and class-wise loss, which allows for more accurate segmentation.

We present a method for weakly-supervised image segmentation that combines a deep neural network with a saliency model.
Our approach uses a small set of user-provided boundaries to train a deep network for segmentation.
By integrating a saliency model into the training process, we improve the performance of the deep network in segmenting objects in images.
The proposed method has the advantage of requiring only a small amount of training data and can handle images with complex and variable object boundaries.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the weakly-supervised image segmentation task, where the goal is to segment images without requiring extensive manual labeling.
Compared to related work, our approach achieves better segmentation accuracy with a significantly smaller amount of training data.

Abstract:
With the widespread use of online social networking platforms, the study of the underlying social graphs has gained significant importance.
This paper specifically focuses on Twitter, one of the most popular social media platforms today, and empirically analyzes the evolution of its social graph.
By employing graph theory, we aim to explore the inherent properties and dynamics of the Twitter social graph, including its connectivity, centrality, and community structure.
Our experimental study involves collecting a substantial dataset of Twitter user interactions and applying various graph algorithms and measures.
We find that the Twitter social graph exhibits distinct characteristics, such as high clustering and power-law degree distribution, indicating the presence of communities and influencers.
Moreover, our analysis reveals that the graph exhibits evolving properties over time, indicating the dynamic nature of user interactions and the platform's evolution.

Abstract:
Domain adaptation is a crucial problem in medical image segmentation, as the availability of labeled data in the target domain is often limited.
In this paper, we propose a novel domain adaptation framework that leverages the use of labeled data in the source domain and unlabeled data in the target domain.
Our framework consists of a domain adaptation module and a segmentation module.
The domain adaptation module utilizes a convolutional neural network (CNN) to learn the domain-invariant features from the source domain, and then adapts the CNN to the target domain using unlabeled data.
The segmentation module takes the adapted CNN and applies it to segment the medical images in the target domain.
We evaluate our framework on the task of brain tumor segmentation in magnetic resonance (MR) images, and demonstrate that it outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.

Abstract:
Training deep learning models for semantic segmentation requires large amounts of annotated data, which can be difficult and expensive to obtain.
This paper addresses the problem of limited data and annotations in semantic segmentation by proposing a new approach that combines the use of synthetic data with a novel loss function.
The proposed method, called Limited Data Semantic Segmentation (LDSS), uses a generative adversarial network (GAN) to create synthetic images with ground truth segmentations.
These synthetic images are then used to train a deep learning model along with a new loss function that combines semantic and instance-level segmentation losses.
The model is trained using a limited amount of real-world data and a large number of synthetic images.
The experimental results show that the proposed method can achieve competitive performance on the Cityscapes dataset with less than 10% of the data and annotations required by other methods.

The proposed method is compared to other segmentation methods, such as the K-means algorithm and the Expectation-Maximization algorithm, and it is shown to perform better in terms of accuracy and efficiency.
The proposed method is also shown to be able to handle noise and outliers in the data, which is a common problem in the automotive industry.

Abstract:
Preoperative kidney vessel segmentation is of vital importance for surgical planning of kidney transplantation.
We present a method for kidney vessel segmentation from CT volumes based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs).
Our approach utilizes a CNN architecture, referred to as Kid-Net, for the segmentation of kidney vessels.
The network was designed to take advantage of the 3D nature of the input data and utilizes a combination of 2D and 3D convolutions for the classification of each voxel in the input volume.
We evaluated our method on 100 CT volumes, and compared it to manual segmentation performed by an experienced radiologist.
Our method achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 0.88±0.02 and a Hausdorff distance of 6.4±2.2 pixels.

The abstract for the academic paper titled "On Gridless Sparse Methods for Line Spectral Estimation From Complete and Incomplete Data" would be:


We introduce a family of gridless sparse methods for line spectral estimation (LSE) from potentially incomplete data.
These methods exploit sparsity in the spectral domain to achieve computational efficiency and improve numerical stability.
The proposed algorithms iteratively estimate the spectrum by minimizing a cost function that measures the distance between the observed data and the data predicted by the current spectral estimate.
The optimization process is accelerated by using a greedy algorithm to select the most informative data points for inclusion in the cost function.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods through numerical experiments, including a scenario involving incomplete data.

Semantic segmentation remains an challenging task in computer vision with recent advances pushing the state-of-the-art to the point where accurate pixel-level labeling is possible on a variety of datasets.
Despite these advances, there still exists a gap between predicted labels and the ground truth, especially in the presence of significant appearance variations, occlusions, and context dependencies.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to semantic segmentation that combines the strengths of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and conditional random fields (CRFs).
Our approach leverages the powerful feature extraction capabilities of CNNs to produce initial predictions and the spatial dependencies captured by CRFs to refine and improve these predictions.
We introduce a novel convolutional implementation of CRFs that operates directly on the feature maps produced by the CNN.
This approach enables the CRFs to exploit local and global spatial dependencies present in the image while maintaining computational efficiency.

In this paper, we present "UNet++," an enhanced version of the popular U-Net architecture designed for medical image segmentation.
U-Net has shown state-of-the-art performance in various segmentation tasks but has limitations in capturing complex structures and handling large variations in image intensity.
To address these limitations, we introduce a nested U-Net architecture that incorporates a series of skip connections between the encoder and decoder blocks.
These skip connections enable the network to capture more global information and improve the segmentation performance, particularly in challenging areas of the image.
We evaluate UNet++ on three different medical image segmentation datasets, and our results show significant improvements over the original U-Net architecture in terms of segmentation accuracy and robustness.
Our proposed method achieves a mean dice similarity coefficient of 0.9143, 0.9189, and 0.9146 on the MNIST-digits, 2D-chest-radiology, and 3D-kidney datasets, respectively.

Abstract:
Traditional image segmentation techniques rely on the assumption that pixels within a region belong to the same class.
However, this assumption fails in many real-world applications where the object of interest exhibits significant intra-class variation.
This paper presents a novel approach to image segmentation that overcomes this limitation.
By formulating the segmentation problem as the cost minimization of multiple hypotheses, our approach is able to capture the variability within the object of interest.
Furthermore, our approach is able to integrate contextual information, such as object boundaries and texture, to improve the segmentation accuracy.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of real-world images, and show that it significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art in image segmentation.

Abstract:
We explore the use of very deep fully convolutional networks (FCNs) for semantic segmentation.
Our network, called the Fully Convolutional Deep Residual Network (FC-DRN), is an adaptation of the ResNet architecture that is suitable for semantic segmentation tasks.
We remove the fully connected layers of the ResNet and replace them with convolutional layers, resulting in a fully convolutional network.
Our FC-DRN achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes dataset, with a mIOU of 82.1%.
We also introduce a new dataset, called the Scene Parse 150 dataset, which is a large-scale dataset for semantic segmentation with 150 classes.
Our FC-DRN achieves a mIOU of 71.4% on this new dataset.

Abstract:
Pre-trained models for medical image segmentation have demonstrated promising results but are often limited to specific networks and do not generalize well to new datasets.
This work introduces a method for the network-agnostic transfer of knowledge from a source domain to a target domain.
The method utilizes a variant of the generalized gradient descent (GGD) algorithm to minimize the difference in feature representations between the source and target domains.
The GGD algorithm is adapted to the segmentation task by using a Dice coefficient as the loss function.
The proposed method is evaluated on a public dataset for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) segmentation and compared to a state-of-the-art pre-trained model.
The results show that the proposed method achieves a Dice coefficient of 0.88, outperforming the pre-trained model by 0.07.

Abstract
-------
Few-shot segmentation of medical images based on meta-learning with implicit gradients combines a meta-learning approach with implicit gradients to tackle the few-shot segmentation problem in medical images.
We propose a novel meta-learning framework that utilizes implicit gradients to learn a shared representation across different medical image datasets.
Our approach is designed to handle the scarcity of labeled data and the need for generalization to new datasets.
We introduce a meta-learning trainer that leverages implicit gradients to optimize the shared representation.
The trainer is trained using a few-shot strategy, where only a limited number of labeled images per dataset are available.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on three different medical image segmentation datasets, showing that our method can achieve state-of-the-art performance even with limited training data.

The trained network is then used to segment the cracks in new pavement images.
The proposed method is evaluated on a separate test dataset and is compared to a traditional manual segmentation method.
The results show that the proposed method is able to accurately segment the cracks in the pavement images and is significantly faster than the traditional method.
The paper concludes by discussing the potential applications of the proposed method in pavement management and maintenance.

Abstract:
Longest Gapped Repeats (LGRs) and Palindromes are two important string-matching concepts in the computer science field.
LGRs are maximally long repeated substrings that are separated by a gap, while Palindromes are strings that read the same backward as forward.
This paper discusses the application of these concepts in the development of string-matching algorithms.
It focuses on the implementation of a new algorithm that utilizes both LGRs and Palindromes to improve the efficiency of string matching.
The algorithm utilizes a preprocessing step to identify the LGRs and Palindromes in the input string, which are then used to optimize the string-matching process.
The experimental results show that the new algorithm outperforms the existing algorithms in terms of time and space complexity.

We study the effects of thermal conduction and viscosity on heat transport in Rayleigh-B\'enard convection.
Using a dimensional analysis, we show that the heat flux across the fluid is optimized when the thermal conductivity and fluid viscosity are similar in magnitude.
This optimization is robust to variations in the Prandtl number and the aspect ratio of the system.
We validate our prediction via numerical simulation in the Rayleigh-B\'enard regime and obtain a good agreement.
In particular, our prediction implies that in the optimally conducting regime, the Nusselt number is proportional to the square root of the Rayleigh number, which agrees with the recent experimental findings of Wu

Deep learning has demonstrated success in medical image segmentation tasks.
However, due to the limitation of available training data, these methods often fail to generalize well to unseen data, especially in small medical centers.
In this paper, we propose a novel approach to address this problem by introducing a dual Swin Transformer U-Net (DS-TransUNet) that leverages pre-trained Swin Transformers for medical image segmentation.
By integrating the Swin Transformers into the U-Net architecture, we can leverage large-scale pre-trained models to capture global dependencies in medical images.
Furthermore, we propose a novel attention module that can focus on important details during inference.
We evaluate our method on three different datasets (Parkinson’s segmentation, MRI skull stripping, and abdominal organ segmentation), and show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches.

We perform detailed numerical simulations of the evolution and neutrino emission of massive stars, focusing on the phase prior to core collapse.
We investigate the effects of mixing in the evolution and subsequent neutrino emission during the thermally-pulsing asymptotic giant branch (TP-AGB) and blue supergiant (BSG) phases.
Our simulations include a detailed treatment of the microphysics, including the nuclear reaction network, neutrino emission, and mixing.
We find that mixing during the TP-AGB and BSG phases is essential for obtaining realistic neutrino emissivities, particularly for the key pp and pep channels.
Our simulations show that the neutrino emissivities for these channels are sensitive to the choice of microphysics and the treatment of mixing.
We find that the pep emissivity is particularly sensitive to the treatment of convection in the envelope, which may be important for detecting this channel with upcoming neutrino detectors.

Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision with a wide range of applications.
However, state-of-the-art semantic segmentation methods are often burdened by excessive computational requirements, making them impractical for real-time applications on resource-constrained devices.
In this paper, we propose Gated-SCNN, a novel framework that combines the strengths of two powerful architectures: Shape CNNs and gated convolutional neural networks.
Our proposed method significantly improves the efficiency of semantic segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes dataset with a 50% reduction in computational requirements.
We achieve this by integrating a gated convolutional layer into the Shape CNN architecture, allowing for more efficient feature extraction and better utilization of model capacity.
Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in improving efficiency without sacrificing segmentation performance.

This paper analyzes the stability and monotonicity of some discretizations of the Biot's model.
First, we study the stable finite element schemes for the homogeneous model, namely the constant coefficient case.
We show that the classical Galerkin finite element method is stable and monotone under very mild conditions on the coefficient, and remains so even in the presence of a small perturbation in the data.
Then, we consider the non-homogeneous model, where the coefficient varies in space according to a given field.
We propose and analyze an auxiliary variable method that consists in introducing an extra variable through a Lagrange multiplier.
This method is shown to be stable and monotone under reasonable assumptions on the data, and provides an efficient way to account for the variability of the coefficient.

Then, the image is segmented using a modified watershed segmentation algorithm.
Subsequently, the boundaries of the objects in the image are extracted.
The proposed technique is evaluated using a database of images.

The recent progress in medical image segmentation has spurred deep learning-based approaches.
However, the lack of labeled medical images as training data restricts the model from converging to a high-performance model.
To this end, we propose a novel approach to leverage available labeled images and abundant unlabeled images to enhance the model performance.
Specifically, we adopt a recently proposed approach, namely, the mixed-supervised learning framework to train a dual-network for medical image segmentation.
We further propose to minimize the divergence between the supervised and mixed-supervised losses in the training process.
The experimental results on the ISBI 2017 cardiac segmentation benchmark demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over the state-of-the-art approaches.

Below is an abstract for the academic paper titled, "CUSUM Filter for Brain Segmentation on DSC Perfusion MR Head Scans with Abnormal Brain Anatomy":

Abstract
A common problem in the analysis of DSC perfusion MR head scans with abnormal brain anatomy is the accurate segmentation of brain tissue, in particular the segmentation of grey matter (GM) and white matter (WM).
The CUSUM filter is a data-driven approach for image segmentation that is independent of a priori information and assumptions about the image and the segmentation.
It provides a robust and reliable segmentation of GM and WM that is suitable for clinical use.
This paper describes the CUSUM filter and its application to the segmentation of DSC perfusion MR head scans with abnormal brain anatomy.
The results show that the CUSUM filter is a promising approach for brain segmentation in this context.

Our proposed method is based on the concept of skewed distributions, which are distributions that are heavily weighted towards one side.
By mixing together multiple skewed distributions, we can create a more robust and representative distribution of the data.
Our method is particularly useful for data that is high-dimensional and sparse, as it can effectively capture the complex relationships between the data points.
We evaluate the performance of our method on a variety of datasets, and show that it outperforms existing unsupervised learning algorithms in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

The advantage of this method is that it is fast, accurate, and robust to variations in face appearance, such as changes in lighting, expression, and pose.
It can be used in a variety of applications, including facial recognition, facial analysis, and gaze-based human-computer interaction.

Abstract:
Human-machine networks (HMNs) have become an integral part of our daily lives, where multiple devices and systems are connected and interact with each other.
In this paper, we present a novel approach to studying HMNs by proposing a typology and profiling framework.
The typology provides a comprehensive classification of HMNs based on their structure, composition, and behavior.
The profiling framework, on the other hand, enables the identification and analysis of the key characteristics and behaviors of HMNs, including their connectivity, interaction patterns, and performance.
By combining the typology and profiling framework, we can gain a deeper understanding of HMNs and develop more effective strategies for their design, operation, and optimization.
This paper contributes to the growing body of research on HMNs by providing a novel perspective on their study and offers a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners working in the field.

Here is the abstract for the academic paper titled "Efficient 2D neuron boundary segmentation with local topological constraints":

The accurate segmentation of neuronal boundaries is a fundamental step in the analysis of electron microscopy (EM) images of the brain.
We present a method for the efficient segmentation of 2D neuron membranes in EM images based on local topological constraints.
Our approach leverages the underlying tissue architecture, where neurons are tightly packed together, to efficiently identify membrane boundaries.
We introduce a novel boundary prior based on local topological constraints, which exploits the fact that membranes are typically located on the boundaries of cellular structures.
Our method is able to accurately segment membranes in a variety of scenarios, including cases where the image quality is poor and the membrane boundaries are challenging to detect.
We evaluate our method on a large dataset of EM images and demonstrate that it significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art in terms of both accuracy and efficiency.

Semantic segmentation of hip joint bone from MRI has a critical role in computer-aided diagnosis and surgical planning.
However, existing methods are usually trained and evaluated on a single dataset, resulting in poor performance when deployed on other datasets.
The intra- and cross-modality semantic consistency for unsupervised domain adaptation (ICMSC) is a new method that addresses this issue.
Our method is based on a self-supervised learning framework, where a generative adversarial network (GAN) is used to learn a domain-invariant feature representation for semantic segmentation.
The GAN is trained on a pair of domains, and the domain-invariant feature representation is then used to train a segmentation network for the target domain.
Our method provides a new way to address the domain shift problem in medical image segmentation and can be applied to other semantic segmentation tasks.

Abstract:
High-quality segmentation is a key step for reliable anatomical interpretation of medical images.
Deep learning methods have been successful in medical image segmentation tasks.
However, directly using popular segmentation models such as U-Net and its variants may result in noticeable anatomical distortions in the segmented output.
In this paper, we propose a simple yet effective approach to improve the anatomical correctness of the segmentation output.
Our approach consists of a standard segmentation model (e.g., U-Net) followed by a denoising autoencoder (DAE) trained to recover the ground truth from the output of the segmentation model.
We name our method Post-DAE.

The psychometric learning layer is trained using a combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques.
Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Cityscapes dataset and is able to generalize well to unseen data.
We show that our method is effective in capturing the hierarchical structure of semantic segmentation and is able to improve the performance of existing methods.

Abstract:
Traditional self-supervised learning approaches have shown promise for unsupervised medical image segmentation, but they tend to miss spatial information.
In this paper, we propose a novel spatial guided self-supervised clustering network (SGSCN) that incorporates spatial information into the self-supervised learning process.
The SGSCN utilizes a weighted graph to guide the clustering process, ensuring that the resulting clusters are spatially coherent.
Additionally, we propose a novel atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASPP) module that extracts multi-scale spatial features from the input images.
The ASPP module is designed to capture global and local spatial information, which is crucial for accurate segmentation.
We evaluate the SGSCN on the ISBI 2017 segmentation challenge dataset and achieve competitive results compared to other state-of-the-art self-supervised methods, while improving the spatial coherence of the segmentation output.

Deep learning has demonstrated its power in medical image analysis; however, the creation of new large pretrained models with millions of parameters and their subsequent fine-tuning remains a challenge.
By contrast, pretrained models with a smaller number of parameters are easier to adapt to new tasks, but they lack the capacity to accurately classify rare diseases.
In this paper, we present a method for extending pretrained models with new anatomy and images to solve this problem.
Our method combines the use of a pretrained model with a smaller number of parameters with a new dataset of images and their corresponding labels.
The pretrained model is fine-tuned with the new dataset, which contains images of the same type as the pretrained model, and the labels of the new images are added to the pretrained model.
Our experiments show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on several medical image classification tasks.

Abstract

Image segmentation reconstructs an image in terms of most elementary parts, or segments, that constitute the whole image.
The accuracy of image-segmentation depends on accurately extracting the underlying features in an image.
But, the existing techniques prove to be inadequate for segmenting ill-posed images, particularly those with noisy, complex and irregular boundaries, in consideration of the fact that the ill-posedness of an object is contextual in nature, and is caused due to the changes in the pose of the object.
In this context, we propose a non-parametric convolution based image-segmentation approach that utilizes the contextual information of the image through a novel context window approach.
Our approach is specifically designed to effectively segment the ill-posed images.
We extract the textural features from the image through a set of filters, and utilize the proposed context window approach to capture the local context information.

Data augmentation is a crucial technique for training deep learning models for semantic image segmentation.
Traditional data augmentation methods such as random rotation, scaling, and flipping have been shown to be effective in increasing the diversity of the training data.
However, these methods are not able to generate new objects or modify the existing ones, which is a limitation for training accurate models.
In this paper, we propose a new data augmentation method called ObjectAug that can generate new objects and modify the existing ones.
ObjectAug is based on a fully convolutional neural network (FCN) that is trained on a large dataset of images with object-level annotations.
The FCN is able to generate new objects and modify the existing ones by combining the features of different objects in the dataset.

Urban scene segmentation is a video understanding task that involves dividing an urban scene video into a plurality of pixel wise labelled object segments.
We propose a Naive-Student framework that leverages the power of semi-supervised learning in video sequences for urban scene segmentation.
Our framework takes advantage of the inherent temporal coherence in video sequences to improve the segmentation performance.
We extract a video level feature representation using a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (3D-CNN) and use a temporal convolutional network (TCN) to leverage the temporal coherence.
Furthermore, we propose a novel semi-supervised loss function that utilizes the uncertainty of the predictions of the naive Bayes classifier to regularize our network.
We evaluate our method on the Cityscapes dataset and achieve state of the art segmentation performance.

In this paper, we present an uncertainty-aware multi-view co-training framework for semi-supervised medical image segmentation and domain adaptation.
The framework utilizes multiple views of the data, including image intensity, image-derived and tissue-specific prior knowledge, to train a deep learning model for semi-supervised segmentation.
We introduce a novel uncertainty-aware loss function that encourages the model to learn robust representations that are resistant to noise and out-of-distribution data.
Furthermore, we propose a domain adaptation module that leverages the uncertainty estimates to adapt the model to new domains while reducing the risk of overfitting.
The proposed framework was evaluated on the ISBI 2017 Challenge dataset for semi-supervised segmentation of neuronal structures in electron microscopic images.
Our method achieved competitive results compared to other state-of-the-art methods while requiring less labeled data.

Abstract
3D medical image segmentation is a fundamental task in medical imaging analysis,
with applications in areas such as radiology and pathology.
Neural architecture
search (NAS) is a powerful technique for automating the design of deep neural
networks (DNNs).
In this paper, we present C2FNAS, a coarse-to-fine NAS
approach tailored to the 3D medical image segmentation task.
C2FNAS
comprises a series of progressively finer NAS searches, each designed to
build upon the architecture discovered by the previous search.
During each
search, we adopt an iterative "start-with-a-seed" strategy that enables the
discovery of better architectures within a fixed computational budget.
We
evaluate C2FNAS on the 3D segmentation of liver and kidney MRI, and show
that it can discover effective architectures that outperform existing
state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy.

An important problem in computer vision is segmenting objects in overhead (top-down) images of man-made environments.
In this paper, we tackle the problem of training deep neural networks for overhead image segmentation through Getis-Ord Gi* pooling, a graph-based similarity measure that is robust to intra-class variation.
We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on the task of segmenting objects in overhead images of parking lots, where the goal is to distinguish between parking spots and other obstructions like walls, poles, and curbs.
Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the public dataset PKU-MMD, improving upon the previous best segmentation accuracy by 3.7% and 2.7% on the validation and test sets, respectively.
Through an ablation study, we show that Getis-Ord Gi* pooling is a key component in the success of our approach.
We further demonstrate the generalizability of our approach to other datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the public datasets UIUC-MMD and ChangAn-MMD.
